items.descriptionOriginal: Under her courtroom table one day, Poonam Bamba found a red thread smeared with sindoor. Her peon, the court attendant who looks after the courtroom, urged her to wait. "Ma'am, please don't come to the dais yet," he said. "We are getting it cleaned, and only then should you come." A colleague once opened a case file and found cut hair inside it. The retired High Court judge says such moments belong to the part of judging that never reaches a judgment, and she keeps returning to them when she explains who sits on the bench. "People don't know that kind of pressure," she says. For Bamba, the point of these stories is simple. "Judges are not gods. They are as human as you and I are, and it is not easy to sit in that moment, listen to two people screaming at you and still maintain your calm," she tells The Better India. From the corporate world to the district bench Her own journey began far from a courtroom. In 2002, after a career in the corporate world, Bamba joined the district judiciary, the trial courts where most disputes first reach a judge . She took her oath quietly, before the district judge, in a ceremony she describes as far from pompous. From 125–150 cases a day to trials involving thousands of documents, Bamba describes the demanding realities of India's district courts. Photograph: ( Bar and Bench ) She was later elevated to the High Court , where the oath is a formal ceremony, but the quieter first one stayed with her. "I won't say that I made very big promises, but whenever I saw people appearing before me, there was always a desire that even if you help one person, your day is made," she says. A demanding routine That desire met a demanding routine almost at once. A judge's day begins with a cause list , the schedule of matters listed for hearing, and its length depends entirely on the court. Magistrates in her district handled 125 to 150 cases a day, against a pendency, or backlog of undecided cases, of 36,000, which she links largely to cheque-bouncing disputes. She corrects the common belief that every judge faces the same load. Additional sessions judges hear fewer matters, but murder trials keep them recording evidence from 10 am onwards. A judge in Canada or the US, she notes, may hear far fewer cases in a day. Her own courtroom later handled cases investigated by the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) and terror-funding trials, where evidence recording ran continuously from 10 am to 4 pm. Some of those days ended without a single disposal, the term courts use for a case that has been decided and closed. Bamba credits stenographers, police officers and court staff, whose long hours and behind-the-scenes work keep the justice system running. Photograph: (AI-Generated image) "There are 10,000 documents in a case, and there are sometimes 20,000 documents in a case," she says. A full day of careful work, in other words, may not appear in the statistics at all. Bamba is quick to credit the people who share the room. Stenographers work the same hours as the judge, and even a short break means arranging for a colleague to take their seat. "Our stenographers are not able to move from their seats," she says. Police officers, she adds, sometimes work 36-hour shifts and are then deputed to give witness testimony straight after duty. In her view, they are as committed and as underappreciated as the judges they work alongside. Their effort sits within a national picture. Law Minister Arjun Ram Meghwal told the Rajya Sabha on 23 July 2026 that 5.64 crore cases are pending across the Supreme Court, the 25 High Courts and the district and subordinate courts. National Judicial Data Grid figures as of 28 July, reported by Bar and Bench, show that 4.98 crore of those cases are in district and subordinate courts and 63.76 lakh are in the High Courts. NewsBytes reports that subordinate courts have 7,311 vacancies against a sanctioned strength of 30,868 judges. A judge answers to many people Bamba does not present the bench as a place beyond questions. The district judiciary, she says, follows the same conduct rules as IAS and IPS officers. "There is nothing different about us, as far as the district judiciary is concerned." Citizens unhappy with a district judge's conduct have a clear route. A complaint goes first to the district judge of that court, who can counsel the colleague informally or call them in separately. Lawyers can raise concerns in the same way. In one case, Bamba deputed a senior officer to sit quietly in a courtroom, observe a judge's conduct and report back. After more than two decades in the judiciary, Bamba urges young judges to approach the bench with humility, patience and empathy. Photograph: ( TNIE ) Typical complaints concern rudeness, sitting late or refusing urgent mentions, and she says citizens now notice. "Citizens are very alert these days," she says, and they increasingly record videos. Complaints with a vigilance angle, such as allegations of corruption or favouritism, go to the High Court. "The kind of scrutiny that happens in high courts, you cannot imagine," she says, adding that it reaches beyond a judge's conduct to individual judgments. She cites a sessions judge who granted bail, was criticised in the High Court for not knowing the law, and was then depicted in the Times of India in an AI-generated image walking to the Judicial Academy with a bag on his back. "What more scrutiny?" she asks. High Court and Supreme Court judges follow a different route, since the Constitution allows their removal only through impeachment. "The Constitution has already provided for that. Unless you amend the Constitution, what can we say?" she says. Scrutiny in the age of the screen Her strongest view concerns transparency. Bamba describes the judiciary as the most scrutinised institution in India. She believes audio-video recording and live streaming have opened proceedings to the public and invited more scrutiny than is warranted. "I feel we are very transparent, and still face ample scrutiny. Judges are not perfect, but they also function under umpteen pressures the public does not see. No one can be more accountable than a judge," she says. Her concern lies in how the recordings travel once they leave the courtroom. "Social media just pulls out one word that falls from your mouth and blows it up, and people react to the clip without reading the full judgment or order," she says. The same pressure, she says, changes how a judge behaves. "Even saying sorry will come out in the video, and then it will be published in full as if the judge misbehaved and then said sorry. It is stealing the natural way of being," she says. For citizens seeking justice, Bamba emphasises knowing their rights, asking lawyers for clarity and turning to free legal aid when they need support. Photograph: ( TNIE ) Technology has brought new demands as well. Video conferencing, introduced during Covid for remote appearances, is now sometimes misused. In her own court, a senior advocate appearing online said mid-hearing, "Excuse me, ma'am, my turn has come in the High Court," and vanished from the screen. "That was actually a serious misconduct. You just cannot run away from a district judge's court," she says. District judges have no contempt power of their own and must send a reference to the High Court, yet she chose another path. "I never believed in making references. I would rather decide a case at that time," she says. She doubts that artificial intelligence can ease the load in district courts yet. "AI can help you find similar judgments, but not this," she says, referring to the summarising of petitions. Most district courts still receive hard copies, while the Delhi High Court is fully digitised. What she tells young judges For young judges and lawyers, Bamba's advice begins with the self. "Power is given to us to dispense justice and not to flaunt," she says. "One's behaviour and attitude go a long way, so I would tell them to work on themselves first. When you can manage yourself, you can manage human resources, whether it is court staff, a litigant or a lawyer." Her method is practical, and she illustrates it with an example from her own bench. On several occasions, Bamba has spent hours, even days, studying evidence and preparing a judgment, only for one of the parties to seek an adjournment and delay the case further. "This has happened many times even though the case is more or less through. But instead of losing my cool, I learnt it is better to give a shorter date as requested. These are accommodations judges have to make all the time, despite packed schedules, workload and pressures," she says. She also trained herself to let provocation pass. "There have been times when lawyers or others have been rude to me and other judges. Lack of respect is very common and in these situations it is easy for any human to lose their temper. Over time, I trained myself to just ignore it as if I have not heard," she says. Whenever one gets angry, she adds, one should keep a little humility. In one such instance, a heated exchange ended and the day's cases were done, and she treated the matter as closed. The lawyer later apologised, and she considered it over. "They are not always bad or intentionally disrespectful. Empathy and placing ourselves in others' shoes is vital in this line of work," she says. What citizens can do Bamba believes citizens can ease the workload too, and she starts with the conversation between a litigant and a lawyer. "A citizen has every right to question their lawyer, ask for clarity, and push for a hearing date that feels realistic to them. Most of them are unaware of their own rights and some lawyers take advantage. Being aware as a citizen is important if they are visiting the court," she says. Understanding courts, however, takes effort, and Bamba admits it is hard to build. "Nobody wants to go to court," she says. Many people cannot afford to lose a day's wages to attend hearings, and even educated citizens and journalists tend to rely on media reports rather than reading the judgments themselves. The pressures that don't end there For judges, the strain does not stop at the courtroom door. Bamba recalls that in the days of typewriters, a single typing error could ruin an entire page and force the typist to start over. That pressure kept filings short and precise. Today, with copy and paste, lawyers can pad petitions to 100 or 200 pages with little effort. "We judges are also humans, and it takes us days to go through those files. But upon reading, we often realise that the same fact is stated in at least 20 ways, just to show the client that they have made such a comprehensive petition for them," she says. Unscrupulous lawyers, she adds, make the process harder for everyone. Some tell clients, "Give me Rs 50,000 and the matter will be decided in your favour," while the judge has no idea who is selling their name and judgment outside the courtroom. "Generally, unscrupulous lawyers play a very dirty role and judges bear the brunt," she says. Where to find help Bamba points to the services already in place. Legal services authorities run legal literacy campaigns and deploy paralegal volunteers to explain court procedures, though she says few people make use of them. The most direct help is free legal aid. "The National Legal Services Authority (NALSA) runs a toll-free helpline on 15100 for those who qualify: women, children, members of Scheduled Castes or Scheduled Tribes, persons with disabilities, persons in custody, and anyone whose annual income is below Rs 1,00,000 (or the limit notified by the Central or state government)," she explains. Applicants can submit an application on plain paper to the relevant legal services authority or fill in an e-form on the official portal. They can also visit legal aid clinics at courts and police stations, where legal aid lawyers and trained paralegal volunteers offer advice in person. A quieter kind of justice For Bamba, all of this returns to the people on both sides of the bench. Judges who work on themselves, litigants who plan realistically with their lawyers and citizens who know where to find help can make the process gentler for the stenographers, police and court staff who hold it together. The red thread under the table, the hair in the case file and the 20,000 documents in a single trial will never appear in a judgment or a statistic. They are the unseen weight of the job, and Bamba wants people to know it is carried by someone who is, in her own words, as human as everyone else in the room. It is the same belief she carried into that modest oath in 2002: that if she helps even one person, the day has been worthwhile.

items.descriptionOriginal: In the 1960s, Norman Roth and his band, The Glass Cage, were Canadian indie rockers who played small local shows and built enough of a following to land gigs in bigger cities. When Roth was 18, the band recorded a live performance that was never officially released and was eventually lost after they broke up shortly afterward. Now, thanks to a four-dollar thrift store purchase, the band’s music is reaching a wider audience, 58 years later . In 2016, veteran rock music promoter Marcus Pollard bought an unlabeled vinyl record at a thrift store on a whim, despite the album being physically damaged. He fell in love with the six songs recorded on it and spent the next two years trying to track down any band members connected to the record. “I searched in vain for two years trying to get any clue as to who was on the record, but to no avail,” Pollard wrote on Facebook . “Then, in a last ditch effort I posted a clip on the Canadian Artists Records Appreciation FB page and… I got a hit!” The reply that solved the mystery Pollard eventually received a reply that read, “Hey, that’s my record!” from Roth, now 77 and working as a warehouse manager. Roth was floored that his band’s long-lost recording had resurfaced, and he was able to listen to songs he hadn’t heard in more than 50 years. Turning a lost record into a real album After reuniting Roth with his lost music, Pollard went a step further. After consulting with the other band members, he set out to bring The Glass Cage’s music back to life after remaining dormant for generations. Pollard spent the next eight years using his industry connections and expertise to officially release the album. Working with a team of professionals, he refurbished the damaged record, digitally remastered the songs, designed elaborate packaging, and developed a booklet detailing the band’s impact on the Nanaimo indie rock scene of the 1960s before they broke up. The finished vinyl album, titled Where Did the Sunshine Go? , was released on February 24, 2026. View this post on Instagram “I feel like everyone has done something in their life that was dismissed,” Pollard told CTV News . “And I wanted them to feel like what they created was actually important.” What this all means to the band now While Roth and his former bandmates are excited about the album’s release, they aren’t trying to relive their youth or chase the rock star dreams they once had. They’re just happy that others will now have access to their music and are enjoying the ride. “I’m not looking for accolades or super stardom, that’s long gone,” Roth told CTV News . “It’s just saying to the world, ‘I was here.’ And I hope they enjoy it.” If you’d like to hear Roth’s music, you can stream tracks by The Glass Cage on Bandcamp and purchase the vinyl now that it’s out. This article originally appeared in January. It has been updated. The post Guy finds long-forgotten album in a thrift shop, reunites the band, and is sharing their music with the world appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Norway is known for the distinct folk art designs of its knitted sweaters, with geometric snowflakes and nature motifs, but did you know that the reason they look the way they do isn’t purely aesthetic? The clothing expert behind The Iron Snail clothing brand shares all kinds of fascinating facts about textiles on the company’s social media site, and his video about Norwegian sweaters is particularly fascinating. Anyone who has owned a traditional, authentic Norwegian sweater knows that they are warm. Not like normal sweater warm, but warmer than a full-on coat warm. But why? Here’s the secret behind the warmth As the video explains, Norwegians perfected the art of stranded knitting to create a sweater that’s warmer than a fur coat or a wool coat, and without all the bulk. Instead of knitting with one strand of yarn, this method uses two strands, essentially creating a double layer of wool that insulates heat incredibly well. The designs serve as a way to anchor the two different yarn strands together, in addition to looking beautiful. Being able to wear a sweater outside instead of a hefty coat makes it easier to do work in the cold, snowy mountains. And people had a lot to say about it With over seven million views and over 2,000 comments, it’s clear people are intrigued: “I’m a big fan of stranded colorwork, but I had only thought of the visuals. It hadn’t occurred to me that all the floats would in fact make wearables warmer! And one thing about it is that the strands would add an insulation layer of yarn, and a second layer with the air between the floats and the knitting (which if you’ve got a comforter or duvet, you know how warm that air can keep you), but it takes way less yarn than a full knit layer, so it definitely saves on material!” “I get it from a materials perspective. It’s an insulating layer with its own bulit-in mesh liner. More negative space near the skin, better breathability/moisture control and less heat loss.” “I always figured that elaborate patterns like this serve a purpose beyond looks, most likely ease of making or strengthening the knitting, but it’s nice to get confirmation.” “I was lucky enough to receive a Dale sweater as a gift when I was 15. At the time I didn’t realize the story behind these sweaters, and I had no idea how expensive they are. Believe me when I say that these things truly last a lifetime – 20 years later, I still have and use the same sweater, and it’s still in almost perfect condition. It’s one of the only cherished items in my wardrobe and I also think it’s one of the ugliest things I own.” “I thrifted a Norway sweater years ago without really fully knowing how awesome they were (I knit and liked it for that) it is literally the BEST thing I have ever thrifted by a long shot. So warm! So comfy! I also get a lot of compliments on it and people recognize the knit style which makes my fibre art loving heart happy.” “AND as you wear it, if the sweater is 100% wool, the yarns will felt together a little bit, making those floats on the inside super sturdy and even less likely to catch your fingers.” So what does one of these actually cost? Norwegian sweaters are functional works of art, and the price reflects that fact. A traditional Norwegian sweater will easily run in the $200–$300 range. The official sweater of the Norwegian Olympic team, made by Dale of Norway (a company that has been making sweaters for nearly 150 years), costs $350. But this style of sweater isn’t only found in Norway . Often referred to as Nordic sweaters, they can be found all over Scandinavia and Iceland. They may set you back some dough, but they’re worth the investment if you’re looking for a high-quality, heirloom textile that keeps you as warm as a wool coat without the bulk. You can follow The Iron Snail on YouTube for more cool clothing history and facts. This article originally appeared in January. It has been updated. The post Clothing expert explains how Norwegian sweater designs make them warmer than a wool coat appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: People who work with children, teachers , coaches, mentors, are often beloved by the kids they serve, especially if they’re good at what they do. Those caring adult relationships are important in a child’s life, but they can also lead to some awkward situations as kids learn appropriate ways to show affection to different people. A baby might cover their mother’s face with slobbery kisses, but other adults may not appreciate that very much. As kids grow, they learn what’s okay and not okay, not just from their parents but from the village of adults in their lives as well. A perfect example of what boundary setting can look like with a young child was shared in a video showing Superhero Swim Academy instructor Jacob Siegel at the end of a swim lesson. The toddler Siegel was teaching hugged him and then went in for a kiss. The hug was expected and welcome. “Thank you, Mila. I love Mila hugs!” the coach said. But when she started to go in for a kiss, he immediately pulled back, gently saying, “No, no kissy. No kissy ’cause I’m coach. You only kiss Mommy and Daddy, okay?” The little girl looked a bit dejected and started to cry, and he quickly gave her an acceptable alternative. “Okay, hey! High five!” he said, while holding up his hand. “High five ’cause we’re all done!” She calmed right down, gave him a high five, and then he moved on to clean-up time. Watch: Teaching boundaries to children by u/alucard_axel in MadeMeSmile Behind the scenes with Coach Siegel Siegel’s expression at the end of the video says it all, he knew that was a teachable moment that could have gone another way, but he handled it with professionalism and toddler-friendly expertise. “Moments like that are actually powerful teaching opportunities,” Siegel tells Upworthy. “I want kids to know they can love and trust their coach, but also that some kinds of affection belong at home with family. It’s about helping them understand safety and respect through love.” People appreciated the example he set, sharing supportive comments on a Reddit share of the video: “So sweet… I sometimes have young clients who want to give kisses and it’s so cute but you do have to tell them “no” because it’s an important boundary to learn. Not everyone wants kisses!” “On top of knowing not to do it to other people, it also teaches them for themselves that other people shouldn’t be just giving them kisses.” “The kid is absolutely adorable but that coach is on another level. Creating the boundaries while keeping it cool and recording the whole thing so the parents are extremely comfortable. Dude is setting a hell of example.” “It sounds like he’s got a good balance between encouraging her growth and setting appropriate boundaries. Kids can be incredibly affectionate, and it’s important to gently guide them in understanding what’s suitable.” “I also think it’s important for the parents’ comfort that a grown man swimming with their young girl isn’t overstepping boundaries/being predatory. From the outside looking in, it’s hard to know for sure when something is innocent or not. It’s better to just stay away from those situations as a whole.” “The little girls I used to babysit always tried to give me kisses (they were between 2-5) and I had to tell them that I’m not related to you, so you can’t kiss me. You can hi-five or hug me, but no kisses! They still give me running tackle hugs when they see me!” Not every culture draws the line the same way A few commenters pointed out that some cultures see kissing as totally acceptable, as it’s frequently used as a friendly greeting for people of all ages and genders. But even in those cultures, boundaries based on relationships and contexts are important to learn, and it’s helpful when adults help teach those lessons so it doesn’t all fall on the parents. In an article titled “Teaching Kids About Boundaries: Why empathy and self awareness play a major role,” Child Mind Institute includes a helpful video about teaching boundaries to children, and it confirms that the coach handled things in exactly the right way. In a section entitled “Rules work both ways,” the institute notes that when people model their boundaries, it’s important for children to empathetically listen. “People are in charge of their own bodies,” writes Rae Jacobson, author of the article and senior editor at the Child Mind Institute, “and it’s not okay to touch them if they don’t want you to, just like it’s not okay for someone to touch [you] in a way you don’t like.” By calmly modeling his boundaries, the swim coach gave his young swimmer a gentle but clear message about what was and was not okay and embodied both empathy and autonomy for her in a way she can understand and mirror when she’s older. Well done, Coach. Thanks for giving us all such a fabulous example to follow. With: Coach Siegel has shared various videos showing how he teaches kids much more than just how to swim. Well done, Coach. Thanks for giving us all such a fabulous example to follow. You can find more from Coach Siegel on the Superhero Swim Academy Instagram page . This article originally appeared last year. It has been updated. The post Swim coach’s reaction when toddler tries to kiss him is a masterclass in teaching boundaries appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: One of the most dangerous conditions for older adults is also one of the most surprising: Loneliness. Sometimes when we’re in the younger, busier time of our lives, it’s easy to forget, or not even realize, that our elderly friends and neighbors might be lonely. But very often, people who have long been retired , who may have already said goodbye to many of their friends or who have physical limitations that make it difficult to get out to visit people, can find themselves alone most of the time. Feelings of loneliness can lead to depression and other health risks, and even shorten one’s lifespan . Being actively engaged in everyday life and interactions with friends, family, and community is critical to living a long and fulfilling life. A viral social media post offers a good reminder of this fact, but in the most heartwarming way. A letter that made the internet cry A poster named u/SnooCupcakes8607 shared a photo of a typed letter with the caption: “I went on a vacation 2 weeks ago, and let my neighbor babysit my pets. Shortly after I got back home, I received this letter from him in the mail that made me smile and cry. I’d like to share it here.” “Good afternoon,” the letter begins. “This letter is regarding your vacation two weeks ago and how you let me babysit Smokey, Oreo, and Jennifer. I’d just like to give you a letter of thanks.” (The letter doesn’t specify what kind of pets Smokey, Oreo and Jennifer are, but the original poster later shared that they are a German shepherd, “the crankiest little beagle you’ve seen in your life,” and a cat named Oreo.) Then the neighbor continued: I went on a vacation 2 weeks ago, and let my neighbor babysit my pets. Shortly after I got back home, I received this letter from him in the mail that made me smile and cry. I’d like to share it here. by u/SnooCupcakes8607 in MadeMeSmile “As you know, I’m an old man. You don’t see me outside often anymore, as these joints aren’t as lively as they used to be. To add to that, two years ago, in the midst of the pandemic, my dad got diagnosed with stage four colon cancer. After his death, I was left alone in my home. I don’t have a wife or kids. I could go to sleep one day and never wake up again. Every day is just sitting around and wondering what I have done for this world. Until I met Smokey, Oreo, and Jennifer. Representative image of Robert Photo credit: Tim Doerfler/Unsplash Your pets are the cutest, funniest, and most troublesome (In a good way, don’t worry, they didn’t mess up my house too much!) individuals. They gave me the motivation to restart my life again. I started waking up early in the mornings. I began to take walks outside with your pets for the first time in years. Every 10 minutes, whenever I felt sad for a second, they would bark or rub against my leg and make me laugh. The highlight of their stay was when I took them to the park. It was the longest time I’ve spend outside in a while. It didn’t just bring back pet interaction, I also met other people, started talking, and made friends with a handful of fellow human beings. I was so happy to finally be able to talk with friends again, interact with others, and feel like I’m part of the human race. I realize I sound very existential right now, but I’m telling the truth. It’s nice knowing that I’m doing something for someone, even if it’s my neighbor. I adopted two dogs soon after. (You may have been hearing noise from my home, pardon them!) I now take regular walks to the park with them and talk with friends I made there. Anyways, I’d just like to say: thank you so much. You brought back meaning to my life. And that’s all that matters. Sincerely, Robert (P.S. I think it’s time for you to mow the lawn, haha!) Walking a dog is good for the body, mind, and soul. Photo credit: Canva The comments were just as sweet People absolutely loved Robert’s letter, and Robert himself, judging from some of the comments: “Robert is a national treasure and I take anything less to be an insult!” “I wouldn’t just mow my lawn, but Robert’s too. Forever.” “Robert really is the good in all of us. He must be protected at all costs.” Some people related to Robert, having found a new zest for life after getting pets of their own. Others had seen the same phenomenon occur in their own parents or other older folks they know. “My Grandma is 93 and losing her mobility. She loves cats but doesn’t think she can take care of one. Enter, Rent-a-Kitty! The neighbor’s cat! He comes over and they hang out and she’s tickled by his visits, but then he goes to his own house at night. It’s a pretty big win for her.” One user was inspired to make a change in their own life: “I’m so glad no one can see me right now. Tears everywhere. I’ve been so worried that I will become that old man. This year has been such a low and trying to get out of it has been the worst. I can’t have dogs where I live but maybe a cat. I need to get my life in order and perhaps having a pet (or really anything more than a plant) will help get me there Thank you.” Others joked that the whole letter was just an elaborate, “Midwest-nice” way to tell the poster their lawn needed attention. Some doubted the veracity of the letter, but even if it’s not real, the comments from people sharing how their elderly loved ones had been helped by neighbors sharing their pets with them show that animals really can help people who are lonely find more connection and purpose in their lives. The science backs this up too Pets can bring much love into our lives and, according to the American Heart Association , can also help us live longer. Interacting with dogs boosts the production of “happy hormones” such as oxytocin, serotonin, and dopamine, which reduces stress levels and provides a greater sense of well-being. Regular walking with a dog is also a great way to exercise. Plus, as Robert mentions in his letters, caring for a dog forces you out into the world where you’re more likely to interact with other dog owners or just random passersby. Those little interactions can make a world of difference. Dog owners also have a unique advantage when overcoming a serious health problem. Dog owners who suffer from a heart attack or stroke are less likely to die than those who are not. It’s a good reminder to check in with older folks around us and to share the joy of our pets with people who might be lonely. You never know whose life you might touch with your furry friends. This article originally appeared four years ago. It has been updated. The post Man asks older neighbor to watch his pets and receives emotional and unexpected letter in return appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: In football (or soccer, as Americans and a few others around the world call it), the highs and the lows can be equally powerful. One second, you’re kicking a winning goal, causing an eruption like no other. The next, medics help you off the field. Unfortunately for Georgian player Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, the latter happened this week in their win against Barcelona . Paris Saint-Germain left-winger Kvaratskhelia tore his ACL , an extremely painful injury that often requires a long recovery. The 25-year-old player, so full of passion, seemed devastated to leave the game in such a way. But support from 2.7 million Instagram followers and one of his biggest heroes, Cristiano Ronaldo, is helping him heal. View this post on Instagram Preparing his hardest On his Instagram page , Kvaratskhelia shared a deeply personal message, translated from Georgian: “Many people asked me about this stand, many said that if all the footballers in the world prayed, the game would end in a draw. This could be true, but before every game I play, I ask God to leave the field healthy, but in vain. It hasn’t been a long time, but it’s still on my mind: why me, anyway? I have never missed anything; probably I prepared for this game the best I have ever prepared for.” He adds, “I thought I was prepared for everything, but not, and I realize that God chose me, and if I protected the players on another field, I’m ready to go through these months in labor, pain, tears. I know I have to come back stronger for my people who always have my back. I won’t let you down, I promise. I won’t waste a second. Thank you all for your support. See you soon.” ‘Never forget what brought you so far’ There were nearly three million likes in just 10 hours. There were also over 40,000 comments, including one from none other than Cristiano Ronaldo. He wrote, “The hardest battles in football are often ones nobody sees. I know that feeling, Kvara. But never forget what brought you this far, and don’t let a difficult moment make you doubt how far you can go. Keep that fire on. Your best is still to come.” (This comment alone got one million likes.) Kyle Bonn from Yahoo!Sports shares that Kvaratskhelia isn’t particularly injury-prone and has always been an incredibly hard worker. “This is the first major injury that Khvicha Kvaratskhelia has suffered in his football career. Previously, he had never missed more than six games in a row with an injury, and even that was back in 2021, when he was still playing for Rubin Kazan. Since moving to Napoli in the summer of 2022, Kvara has been a workhorse. He has never missed more than two club matches for any particular injury.” View this post on Instagram ‘A true inspiration’ Italian sports journalist Fabrizio Romano also shared a post highlighting Ronaldo’s kind words, calling it a “beautiful message.” This led many in the comments to call Ronaldo the GOAT (seemingly in a toss-up with Messi). One adds, “More than an idol, a true inspiration.” The post Cristiano Ronaldo shares powerful message with soccer star Khvicha Kvaratskhelia after devastating injury appeared first on Upworthy .

items.titleOriginal: How kites and ancient design are replacing fuel in Antarctic exploration
items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST Την τελευταία φορά που μια ομάδα ολοκλήρωσε μια παρόμοια διέλευση του εσωτερικού της Ανταρκτικής, έκαψε περίπου 170.000 λίτρα (περίπου 45.000 γαλόνια) καυσίμου για να το κάνει. Η αποστολή Wind Sled που έφυγε από την Ισπανία στις 18 Οκτωβρίου σχεδιάζει να μην χρησιμοποιήσει κανένα. Ο Ισπανός πολικός εξερευνητής Ramón Larramendi οδηγεί τέσσερα άτομα σε 3.400…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM The last time a team completed a comparable crossing of Antarctica’s interior, they burned through roughly 170,000 liters (about 45,000 gallons) of fuel to do it. The Wind Sled expedition that left Spain on October 18 plans to use none. Spanish polar explorer Ramón Larramendi is leading four people across 3,400 kilometers (about 2,100 miles) of Antarctic interior on a kite-powered platform he has been designing for 25 years, with 16 research projects running the entire way. The vehicle runs on wind and solar energy , meaning no combustion engine at all. Twenty-five years of design, rooted in Inuit tradition Larramendi has spent 25 years developing the Wind Sled and has logged more than 28,000 kilometers (about 17,400 miles) across ice on earlier expeditions while refining it. The platform is built on Inuit sled-building techniques, which is an unusual starting point for a cutting-edge scientific research vehicle, and Larramendi doesn’t try to make it sound otherwise. “The wind sled is something completely unique in the world,” he says. “This sled combines Inuit techniques, which can look like old-fashioned and slightly strange bits of technology. That makes it a very, very unusual mix, but hugely efficient.” The sled is 15 meters (about 49 feet) long across four modules, capable of carrying up to 2,100 kilograms (about 4,600 pounds). This expedition is running lighter, around 250 kilograms (about 550 pounds) of instruments. The crew has 20 kites ranging from five to 150 square meters (about 54 to 1,615 square feet) in sail area, swapped out as conditions change. The sled can hit 80 kilometers per hour (about 50 miles per hour) in a strong wind; average cruising speed is around 25 (about 15 miles per hour). Sixteen research projects in terrain that rarely gets visited The route goes from Russia’s Novolazarevskaya base in Queen Maud Land, through the Pole of Inaccessibility and near the Pole of Cold, finishing at the Concordia research station at Dome C. Five scientific stations will be established along the way. The 16 projects were selected by Spain’s polar research committee, with collaborators including NASA’s Ames Research Center , six Spanish universities, and several national research bodies. One of the NASA projects is asking whether salt rocks sitting on Antarctica’s surface could harbor microbial life. Sensors embedded in the rocks will measure temperature, humidity, and electrical conductivity to determine whether liquid water could form inside them despite conditions that make that seem impossible. It’s the kind of question that sounds like astrobiology because it basically is. The Dinglac project will use ground-penetrating radar to map the top 10 meters (about 33 feet) of snow to track how ice layers accumulate and shift. The campaign will also sample for microplastics and chemical pollutants, test for microorganisms and viruses, and run assessments of the European Galileo navigation system . The location makes all of it harder to get any other way. Satellites and permanent stations have limited reach into this interior. “It is taking place in an area for which there are practically no data,” Larramendi says. The crew are their own experiment All four team members are Antarctic veterans: Larramendi; Hilo Moreno , a polar guide and mountain technician; Mariusz Potocki , a researcher at the University of Maine; and Javier Selva , a documentary filmmaker who crossed Antarctica with Larramendi in 2011-2012. They’re also research subjects. The WindSled Mind project, led by Gabriel G. de la Torre of the University of Cádiz, will monitor the team’s psychological responses, sleep, and social dynamics across the 85 days. The data is meant to inform planning for long-duration space missions, where small crews face confinement and extreme isolation from Earth, conditions the interior of Antarctica replicates about as well as anywhere. “We are the experiment ourselves,” Larramendi says. “Four people isolated for 85 days in the interior of the Antarctic continent.” A route designed to be repeated The point isn’t just to complete this crossing. Each return trip lets researchers compare data across seasons to track real changes in ice, climate, and polar ecosystems over time. “Repeated data collection is absolutely key to tracking variations,” Larramendi says. When the team arrives at Concordia, they’ll fly out and leave the sled dismantled at the station, ready for the return journey. The fuel comparison says most of what needs saying: the last comparable crossing burned through about 45,000 gallons. This one runs on kites and a design that’s been in development since the 1990s, and when it’s done, the plan is to come back. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post How kites and ancient design are replacing fuel in Antarctic exploration first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM You’re doing everything right at bedtime: you stay away from screens after nine, take a soothing dark shower , sip on that herbal tea cooling on the nightstand, and maintain a reasonably consistent sleep schedule. Yet some nights the ceiling still has your full attention past midnight, and you can’t quite figure out why. If you’ve been treating sleep as mostly a habits problem, a recent nutritional review suggests there’s a variable you might be overlooking: what you eat in the evening. The review, published in the journal Nutrients , made the case for pistachios as a bedtime snack, and the reasoning holds up better than most food-and-sleep claims do. There’s no single magic compound, but what’s unusual is that one ounce of pistachios stacks five separate sleep-relevant nutrients at once, each arriving via a different route. That’s a rare combination to find in a single snack. Why diet is an underused sleep lever Most sleep advice focuses on behavior such as consistent wake times, a cool and dark room, or no caffeine past the early afternoon. Diet gets surprisingly little attention, even though a lot of research connects eating patterns to how well people sleep. People who follow the Mediterranean or DASH diets tend to sleep better, and both lean on nuts and legumes. That link pushed researchers to look more closely at which nutrients might be responsible. With pistachios, there turned out to be several working at the same time. Vitamin B6, tryptophan, and the sleep hormone chain One ounce of pistachios provides close to 40 percent of your daily vitamin B6, more than any other tree nut. This is noteworthy because B6 is what your body uses to turn tryptophan into serotonin, and serotonin is the raw material for melatonin. B6 also helps produce GABA, the neurotransmitter that tells your nervous system to settle down at night. The same one-ounce serving contains about 71 milligrams of tryptophan. In a survey of more than 11,000 Spanish university students, higher tryptophan intake was tied to longer sleep and a lower likelihood of insomnia. In a separate trial , adults between 55 and 75 who ate tryptophan-enriched cereal for a week fell asleep faster, slept longer, and produced more melatonin than those eating standard cereal. Plant-made melatonin, found in the nut itself Plants make their own melatonin, called phytomelatonin, and it has nothing to do with the melatonin your body makes from tryptophan. One analysis of American pistachios found roughly 18.7 micrograms per serving, which puts them in the same range as tart cherry and tomato, two foods with a reasonable body of sleep research behind them. Other analyses have found lower amounts, so the exact number varies, but phytomelatonin shows up in pistachios consistently. Magnesium, fiber, and the gut Magnesium supports melatonin production and plays a role in deep sleep through GABA activity. Pistachios have about 31 milligrams per ounce, around 10 percent of the recommended daily amount. Almonds have more (76 milligrams in the same serving), but every bit adds up. The CARDIA study , which tracked a large group of young adults over many years, found that those with the highest magnesium intake slept better and were less likely to get fewer than seven hours a night. A one-ounce serving of pistachios also covers about 11 percent of your daily fiber. Gut bacteria ferment fiber into short-chain fatty acids like butyrate, which have been linked to sleep quality. In a lab comparison of common nuts, pistachios produced the most of these compounds. They also rank second among tree nuts in polyphenols, and a recent meta-analysis found polyphenol supplements helped people with sleep disorders fall asleep faster and sleep longer, though most of those trials used extracts rather than whole foods. The clinical trials that haven’t happened yet No study has directly tested whether eating pistachios helps people sleep better. The review draws a reasonable line through a lot of supporting research, but connecting individual nutrient mechanisms to actual sleep outcomes still requires human trials that don’t exist yet. It’s also important to note that the review was partially funded by American Pistachio Growers . If you already snack in the evening, a small handful of pistachios, around 28 grams, is an easy substitution to run for a week. The usual sleep hygiene advice still stands, and matters more than any snack. But if you’ve already worked through that list and you’re still not sleeping well, what you eat before bed is a reasonable next thing to look at. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post Is this nut the most underrated sleepy-time snack? Here’s what the sleep research says first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.title: Η μινιμαλίστρια μαμά χρησιμοποιεί 10 κόλπα από το «σύστημα καθαρισμού της Disney» για να κρατήσει το σπίτι της καθαρό το Magic Kingdom
items.titleOriginal: Minimalist mom uses 10 tricks from ‘Disney cleaning system’ to keep her home Magic Kingdom clean
items.description: Εκατομμύρια άνθρωποι επισκέπτονται τα πάρκα Walt Disney World κάθε χρόνο. Το 2024, 52 εκατομμύρια άνθρωποι έκαναν ένα ταξίδι στα έξι πάρκα της εταιρείας. Παρά τους τρελούς αριθμούς επισκεψιμότητας, τα πάρκα έχουν σταθερή φήμη για την καθαριότητα. Η Robyn Buchanan, μια YouTuber γνωστή ως Minimalist Home, εξήγησε σε ένα πρόσφατο βίντεο πώς διατηρεί το σπίτι της οργανωμένο και τακτοποιημένο με την Disney…
items.descriptionOriginal: Millions of people visit Walt Disney World parks every year. In 2024, 52 million people made a trip to the company’s six parks. Despite insane attendance numbers, the parks have a solid reputation for cleanliness. Robyn Buchanan , a YouTuber known as Minimalist Home , explained in a recent video how she keeps her home organized and tidy with Disney-inspired cleaning tips that its parks use to stay spotless despite “tens of thousands of people walking around every day with turkey legs, ice cream, sticky children, Dole Whips, and churros.” She adds that Disney has built “an entire system around keeping the parks clean.” Disney’s cleaning systems Disney employees, known as cast members, follow specific cleaning systems, procedures, and expectations that do not rely on motivation to get cleaning done, a major selling point Buchanan points out about home cleaners looking to Disney for inspiration. She notes a major downfall for home cleaning is the phrase: “I’ll clean when I feel like I should.” Instead of waiting for motivation to strike, she offers a few ways to get little jobs done each day, including: After dinner, wipe down the countertops. When the dishwasher finishes, empty it. Before bed, do a five-minute reset. On garbage day, empty all little bins in your home. “You don’t have to have a conversation with yourself every single time. The trigger is what makes the decision for you,” she added. View this post on Instagram 10 Disney cleaning tips Tip #1: Don’t save the mess for later Disney takes care of messes right away. Spills are cleaned up, and litter is immediately thrown into a bin. “Cleaning is happening continuously while the park is operating,” she said. “They’re not waiting until closing time going, ‘Right, well, let’s see what 50,000 people have done today.’” By utilizing small cleaning resets, which Buchanan refers to as the DASH Method, she explained, “You deal with little things as you move through your day” to avoid needing a full day of cleaning (along with a motivational speech to get you going). “You’re not constantly cleaning. You’re just preventing tomorrow’s cleaning job from becoming enormous,” she said. Tip #2: The 30-step trash can rule This rule was created by Walt Disney himself. Buchanan stated that Disney “wanted his guests to be roughly 30 steps from any garbage can.” The reason? “If throwing away something is easy, people are so much more likely to do it. If the garbage can is nowhere near you, suddenly that tiny wrapper becomes a logistical problem,” she explained. This translates into homes. “If garbage constantly collects beside your son’s computer, maybe you need a little garbage bin in a better spot,” Buchanan suggested. “If clothes always land on your bathroom floor, but your hamper is in your bedroom, maybe the hamper is in the wrong place.” She emphasized that putting in cleaning systems within your house where certain behaviors naturally happen is key for helping to keep your home clean. Tip #3: Put things at the point of performance Buchanan stated that Disney utilizes this tip by placing garbage cans near where garbage is likely to happen “near food, near exits, near places where somebody suddenly realizes they’re carrying what they don’t want anymore.” Buchanan explained that, in the home, this can look like keeping “cleaning cloths in the bathroom, a hamper where clothes come off, keep box cutters where you’re constantly opening up packages, putting a donation box near the closet where you usually decide you don’t want something.” She added, “Disney organizes according to what people actually do.” Tip #4: Design for prevention Disney specifically designs its parks for fewer messes to happen in the first place. Buchanan assured her viewers the same can be done at home. “If the front entrance is constantly exploding with shoes, bags, and jackets, the answer may not be: ‘I need to tidy this more often.’ Maybe you need hooks or fewer shoes there. Maybe every person needs one basket,” she said. This includes keeping cleaning tools and supplies close to where you use them in the home so they are easily accessible when needed. “I have toilet cleaner in every bathroom. I have cleaning cloths in every bathroom. I even have a few broom and dustpan sets a few places in my house—by the fireplace, down where the cat’s litter box is—where I feel like I need them!” said Buchanan. Tip #5: “Go Away Green” Buchanan explained that Disney uses muted colors, including one called “Go Away Green,” which doesn’t draw eyes or attention to things such as utility boxes, doors, and equipment. “The idea isn’t that the object disappears—it’s just that your brain really doesn’t pay much attention to it,” she noted. “I feel like Disney gave clutter a boring dress code, and I’m here for it.” At home, you can adopt the same method. She explained how “Bright cords, random containers, different colored baskets, a black charger hanging down a white wall” can all shout for attention. For boring functional items in the home, she suggested blending them into the room using “matching baskets, neutral storage, cord covers.” Tip #6: The utilidors Disney has a unique underground system of tunnels called utilidors that help keep behind-the-scenes operations of the parks, including moving cast members around, storing supplies, and other necessary logistics, out of sight. Buchanan compared it to managing a well-run home that needs discreet places to keep “cleaning supplies, tools, overflow pantry food, returns, recycling, half-finished projects, the vacuum—all the boring infrastructure required to operate a household. We need things neat, tidy, and organized.” In her home, Buchanan has a basket where she keeps returns, a linen closet, and a broom closet where she keeps things intentionally stored and out of sight to prevent clutter. Tip #7: Everybody picks up the trash This Disney rule is Buchanan’s favorite because parks are kept clean not just by custodial staff—but by all staff. When they see something that needs attention, they see to it. She added that it means “cleanliness has become part of the culture. It’s not just one person’s job.” She urged using the same philosophy in homes, with every family member contributing to help keep the house clean. “Everyone who lives in the house has some ownership of the space,” she added. View this post on Instagram Tip #8: Give people actual zones Custodial work at Disney is divided up into clear zones with clear responsibility. Designating the same format to family members at home (i.e., someone is responsible for taking out the trash, putting shoes away, or unloading the dishwasher on specific days) is another easy way to make sure the house stays clean. Tip #9: The overnight reset Buchanan pointed out that overnight at Disney parks, a lot is happening when guests aren’t paying attention. This includes landscaping, maintenance, and more before the next day begins. At home, the same reset can be implemented. “Not a deep clean, not an hour,” said Buchanan. But giving the kitchen a final wipe down, clearing off counters, and starting the dishwasher to ensure a fresh start for the morning can make a big difference. Tip #10: Clean in the same order Disney uses the same general cleaning sequence every time, which Buchanan thinks is an underestimated benefit that can also be done at home. “When you clean a room in different order every time, you keep having to think about what comes next,” she explained. “I like to take the ‘think’ out of everything.” She recommended creating a sequence for yourself. “For example: garbage, laundry, things that don’t belong, surfaces, floors, done.” She continued, “You can use whatever order makes sense for you. But the point is that your brain eventually learns it so it just goes on autopilot so you can just zone out.” The post Minimalist mom uses 10 tricks from ‘Disney cleaning system’ to keep her home Magic Kingdom clean appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Ο ειδικός στην επικοινωνία μοιράζεται το «κόλπο της Taylor Swift» για τέλεια ολοκλήρωση μιας ομιλίας σε 3 βήματα
items.titleOriginal: Communication expert shares ‘Taylor Swift trick’ for perfectly wrapping up a speech in 3 steps
items.description: Το 2022, η Taylor Swift έδωσε μια εναρκτήρια ομιλία στο Yankee Stadium σε αποφοίτους του Πανεπιστημίου της Νέας Υόρκης. Μίλησε για σχεδόν μισή ώρα και έλαβε επίσης επίτιμο διδάκτορα. Ενώ ορισμένοι μπορεί να θεωρήσουν μάλλον ανόητη την έννοια των επίτιμων διδακτορικών που δίνονται σε διασημότητες, σύμφωνα με πληροφορίες, πολλοί από τους φοιτητές είχαν μια έκρηξη. Αλλά ένας ειδικός στην επικοινωνία έχει χρησιμοποιήσει…
items.descriptionOriginal: In 2022, Taylor Swift gave a commencement speech at Yankee Stadium to New York University graduates. She spoke for nearly half an hour and also received an honorary doctorate. While some might find the notion of honorary doctorates given to celebrities rather silly, reportedly many of the students had a blast. But one communication expert has used the speech to exemplify an excellent trick for winding down a speech. Author Dorie Clark analyzed Swift’s words to illustrate how beautifully the singer crafted her speech. She noted that there are three “powerful public speaking strategies” Swift used and made it clear that these methods can be helpful for anyone who has to give a speech. Clark stated, “Taylor Swift has a trick for turning a good speech into a great one. Once you see it, you’ll want to use it every single time.” View this post on Instagram Trick for closing a speech In an Instagram clip captioned “The Taylor Swift trick for closing a speech,” Clark first introduced herself. “I taught communications at Duke University for over a decade, and I’ve coached hundreds of senior leaders from top companies. And I have rarely seen someone close a speech as well as Taylor Swift’s 2022 commencement address at NYU when she received an honorary doctorate. So watch how she closes the speech.” The clip then cut to Swift, clad in a purple (and somehow stylish) graduation gown, her cap perfectly tilted like a French beret. Swift said, “And as long as we are fortunate enough to be breathing, we will breathe in, breathe through, breathe deep, and breathe out.” Swift paused and half-smiled. “And I am a doctor now, so I know how breathing works.” This got a big laugh from the audience. Back to Clark, who broke down why Swift’s closing was so effective. “Watch what she’s not doing. Lots of speakers want to end on an ‘up’ note. So they’re too eager to assure people, ‘You can do it. It will all be fine!’ It’s too easy. Taylor didn’t do that. Instead, she used three easy, powerful public speaking strategies that you can use in your next talk. 3 public speaking strategies “First, she’s meeting the audience where they are. They’re nervous about their future. They’re worried about the direction. And she acknowledges that. Breathe in. Breathe out. It’s also a very good Easter egg, if you listen to her music.” Next, Clark noted, is humor. “Second, she ends with a joke! She’s a ‘doctor’ now. Humor always helps.” “And third, and most importantly,” Clark continued, “She shows them that she’s one of them. That’s one of the most powerful things that speakers can do. Unite people that they’re speaking to and show them ‘we are all in it together.’ That’s true whether you’re a rock star like Taylor Swift, showing you’re also just another NYU grad. Or a regular person who has influence in your company or your club or your school.” Clark reiterated that anyone can use this approach. “So the next time you give a speech, think about those three things. How can you meet the audience where they are? Use humor. And show them that we’re all in it together.” Many commenters appreciated the advice, though a few noted that Swift wasn’t exactly “one of us.” One Instagrammer did playfully point out, that while Clark’s points are helpful and true, Clark just might also be a “Swiftie.” View this post on Instagram The post Communication expert shares ‘Taylor Swift trick’ for perfectly wrapping up a speech in 3 steps appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Το 1975, ένας ηθοποιός ξεδίπλωσε μια σεξιστική αγανάκτηση κατά του Τζόνι Κάρσον. Η Shelley Winters αρνήθηκε να καθίσει σιωπηλή.
items.titleOriginal: In 1975, an actor unfurled a sexist rant on Johnny Carson. Shelley Winters refused to sit silently.
items.description: Οι ηθοποιοί και οι διάσημες προσωπικότητες λαμβάνουν εκτεταμένη επίσημη εκπαίδευση στα μέσα ενημέρωσης και δημοσίων σχέσεων. Εξάλλου, τα στούντιο δεν μπορούν να κάνουν viral βίντεο με τα αστέρια τους επειδή βάζουν το παροιμιώδες πόδι τους στο στόμα τους. Αλλά πριν από μερικές δεκαετίες; Τα πράγματα ήταν πολύ πιο γρήγορα και χαλαρά. Το κοινό αποκτούσε πρόσβαση σε διασημότητες μέσω talk show και ζωντανών συνεντεύξεων για τους…
items.descriptionOriginal: Actors and mainstream celebrities today receive extensive formal media and PR training. After all, studios can’t have clips of their stars going viral for putting their proverbial foot in their mouth. But a few decades ago? Things were a lot more fast and loose. The public was gaining access to celebrities via talk shows and live interviews for the very first time. It didn’t always go smoothly and led to some pretty tense yet entertaining moments on live television . Oliver Reed goes off on “women’s liberation” and Shelley Winters responds perfectly It was September 26, 1975, when Johnny Carson welcomed renowned actor Oliver Reed to the Tonight Show stage. The English actor starred in the film Oliver! , which won an Academy Award for Best Picture a few years earlier. Reed was invited on the show to promote a new film. Shelley Winters, herself a highly acclaimed, Oscar-winning actress, was interviewed on a previous episode. In addition to her Oscar, Winters also won a Golden Globe and a Primetime Emmy and was twice nominated for a BAFTA Award. During the interview, Winters sat just off-camera, to Reed’s side. It got off to a cheeky start when Reed, talking about Americans, said, “Some of them behave themselves, and some of them are quite loud.” He then glanced pointedly at Winters. Some more good-natured banter went back and forth before Reed, feeling too often interrupted by a chatty Winters, cut her off and said, “I’m sorry, I thought it was my turn.” It was all in good fun, or at least mostly. Eventually, Winters left the stage, claiming she “had to go.” That’s when Reed began taking his shots. “She’s alright, she can’t shout at us now,” he told Carson. “So much for women’s lib.” Carson asked him about the women’s liberation movement in the U.K., to which Reed responded: “The women in England are quite good. They’re always in the kitchen, so you can’t hear them when they shout. I think most women are happy in the kitchen.” He then added that men make better chefs. The audience booed, and Reed shushed them. Carson couldn’t help but chime in with a classic quip that earned him some applause: “I think if they paid women what they pay chefs, women would love to be in the kitchen.” Reed went on to say he believed a woman’s place was to take care of “her children and her man.” He received applause for this, and a small smattering of jeers and boos. Again, he shushed the audience, even going as far as to say, “Quiet woman!” to a particular jeerer. Then, he saw Shelley making her way back to the stage. Winters dumped her drink on Oliver Reed following sexist comments Winters didn’t say a word when she returned to the stage, yet Reed seemed to know what was coming. He stood up, held his arms at his sides, and stood still as she poured an entire glass of liquid directly onto his head. Then she left the stage again, and Reed sat down to continue the interview. Reed, to his credit, took it in stride with excellent comedic timing and attempted to continue his monologue without missing a beat: “I believe that women’s liberationists…” he began, to raucous laughter. “I believe that women’s liberationists sometimes do extraordinary things,” he finished, to more laughter. But it was clear he took issue with what Winters had done: “I don’t think, in actual fact, that it gives them much armament to their cause. I mean, the fact that I have been covered in whiskey, and it is whiskey, pays no cause to the lady. There are a lot of people that watch this program that will probably laugh at that, and there will be several who will probably be quite indignant. I am not indignant, because this is indicative of the bad manners of a lot of chauvinist ladies.” Carson wrapped it all up with a sly smile. “I like this show myself,” he said. A bit? Perhaps, but Reed was open about his beliefs It’s hard to say for sure whether the conflict and the whiskey dumping were entirely authentic or played up for entertainment. However, Reed had a reputation for being outspoken against the women’s liberation movement. He was also known as something of a volatile personality. In an infamous appearance on David Letterman’s show, Reed’s interview became quite hostile and was cut short. Another talk show appearance, After Dark in 1991, devolved into chaos when Reed clashed with the female guests, tried to kiss one of them, and was ejected from the studio. Reed later discussed the incident with Winters in an interview , saying it took him off guard. “I didn’t know what to say, so I said absolutely nothing,” he admitted before adding, “She’s a showman, and I’m a showman. That’s our business.” Reed died on May 2, 1999, after a drinking contest at a bar in Malta got out of hand while he was filming the movie Gladiator . Weirdly enough, he predicted this almost exactly five years earlier, quipping that he would die of laughter in a bar after taking on a ridiculous bet. 1970s, and previous decades, were rife with sexism in Hollywood and beyond Though Shelley Winters was a beloved movie star, understanding the Hollywood she came up in helps put her actions into greater context. Hollywood was not typically a friendly place for women like Winters. Star power often rested solely on beauty, with even top-billed actresses relegated to eye-candy roles or simple tropes. Winters herself debuted in film in the 1940s, when “ casting couch ” culture was at its worst and most pervasive. Even safe, lighthearted spaces like late-night talk shows often demeaned actresses. They would be grilled about their love lives and appearance rather than their career achievements. Winters, for her part, was known for not sitting idly by and tolerating sexism or discrimination of any kind. Vanity Fair writes, “Throughout her life she was a progressive, feminist, and civil rights advocate.” She attended a Democratic National Convention and spoke at a White House Correspondents’ Dinner around 1960. She also called out John F. Kennedy, directly to his face, for his father’s antisemitic views. She died in 2006, at the age of 85, as an iconic Hollywood trailblazer. She fought for women’s rights, defied ageism in Hollywood, and stood up to any and all loudmouths who tried to stand in her way. The post In 1975, an actor unfurled a sexist rant on Johnny Carson. Shelley Winters refused to sit silently. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Ο σύζυγος της Debbi Fields πόνταρε ότι δεν μπορούσε να βγάλει 50 $ σε πωλήσεις μπισκότων. Μια τελευταία ιδέα μάρκετινγκ της έχτισε μια αυτοκρατορία.
items.titleOriginal: Debbi Fields’ husband bet she couldn’t make $50 in cookie sales. A last-ditch marketing idea built her an empire.
items.description: Η χρονιά ήταν 1977 και η 20χρονη Debbi Fields μόλις είχε ανοίξει το Mrs. Fields Chocolate Chippery, το ταπεινό της κατάστημα με μπισκότα στο Palo Alto της Καλιφόρνια. Το πάθος της για το ψήσιμο ξεκίνησε στην εφηβεία της και μέχρι τότε είχε τελειοποιήσει τη συνταγή της. Χρησιμοποιώντας τα 5 δολάρια την ώρα που έβγαζε ως «ball girl», αγόραζε μόνο τα καλύτερα συστατικά. Αλλά δεν ήταν μόνο το εμπόρευμα…
items.descriptionOriginal: The year was 1977 , and 20-year-old Debbi Fields had just opened up Mrs. Fields Chocolate Chippery, her humble cookie shop in Palo Alto, California. Her passion for baking began in her teens, and by then she had perfected her recipe. Using the $5 an hour she made as a “ball girl,” she bought only the best ingredients . But it wasn’t just the ingredients that made Fields’ cookies stand out. Unlike the hard, small, crumbly, mass-produced cookies common at the time, her cookies were served warm, soft-baked, gourmet-style, and oversized. Baking despite the odds Although friends and family loved Fields’ baking, no one seemed to believe it could become a business. According to the University of New Hampshire’s Rosenberg International Franchise Center , Fields had to approach several banks before finally securing financing to open her debut shop. Even Debbi’s business-tycoon husband, Randall Fields, didn’t expect it to succeed. She later told the Los Angeles Times that he predicted she wouldn’t make a measly $50 in sales on opening day. As noon approached without a single sale, it looked like Randall was right. Then, Debbi had an idea. A Hail Mary tactic that turned into a genius marketing ploy She walked out of the shop with a tray of her freshly baked signature cookies and began handing them to passersby on the street. The strategy was pretty simple. Instead of trying to convince strangers to spend money on a cookie they had never tasted, Fields gave them a reason to come inside: let them try one first. And it worked. After one sample, folks were hooked, and they went in to buy more. Fields would end up making $75 that day, surpassing her husband’s cynical expectations. And the rest is cookie history As we all know, that first-day success grew to be something much bigger. Fields continued building her business, and over the years it grew from a cookie shop to a multi-million-dollar cookie empire. Fields became a celebrity of sorts, appearing on shows like Hollywood Squares and the new Mickey Mouse Club , writing several best-selling cookbooks, and appearing as a judge and mentor on Supermarket Superstar , a reality television series where culinary entrepreneurs compete to get their product into grocery stores. Although she sold the company to an investment firm in the ’90s, she remains the brand’s spokeswoman. At its height, Mrs. Fields operated hundreds of locations across the United States, as well as in Canada, England, Japan, Australia, and Hong Kong. And that little opening-day experiment of free samples became an important (and delicious) part of the company’s identity. Fields might not have had a business background, but she certainly had a natural entrepreneurial spirit. She had no real way to know whether free cookie samples would actually resonate with potential customers. Still, she believed she had something people wanted, and she was right. Her cookies would eventually become such a familiar part of American mall culture that it’s hard to picture a trip to the mall without encountering a Mrs. Fields sample. Which, of course, has a funny way of turning into a Mrs. Fields purchase. Fields had plenty of reasons to doubt her idea, especially with everyone else doubting her. But she kept believing in it, proving that sometimes you just have to trust your own special recipe and know the result will eventually speak for itself. The post Debbi Fields’ husband bet she couldn’t make $50 in cookie sales. A last-ditch marketing idea built her an empire. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: 2 μόρια μπορεί να βοηθήσουν στην επιβράδυνση της ανάπτυξης του καρκίνου του παγκρέατος
items.titleOriginal: 2 molecules may help slow pancreatic cancer growth
items.description: Τα καρκινικά κύτταρα του παγκρέατος είναι εξαιρετικά καλά στην ανάπτυξη, αλλά νέα έρευνα δείχνει ότι δύο μικροσκοπικά μόρια που υπάρχουν ήδη στο σώμα μπορεί να βοηθήσουν στην επιβράδυνσή τους. Ερευνητές στο Texas A&M College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences (VMBS) και στο College of Education and Human Development διαπίστωσαν ότι τα αυξανόμενα επίπεδα δύο microRNAs, kn…
items.descriptionOriginal: Pancreatic cancer cells are remarkably good at growing, but new research suggests that two tiny molecules already present in the body may help slow them down. Researchers at the Texas A&M College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences (VMBS) and the College of Education and Human Development found that increasing levels of two microRNAs, known as miR-15a and miR-16, reduced protein synthesis and slowed the growth of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) cells. In a study in Physiological Reports , the researchers also shared that patients with higher levels of the microRNAs in their tumors tended to live longer, further supporting their potential as targets for new pancreatic cancer treatments. “Cancer cells continually proliferate, or grow and divide,” says James Fluckey, associate dean for research and a professor in the kinesiology and sport management department and the study’s principal investigator. “To do that, the cells need to increase processes like protein synthesis that give them what they need to grow. If you disrupt that protein synthesis, you can slow the rate at which those cells can grow.” MicroRNAs are short strands of genetic material that help regulate which proteins a cell produces. Rather than providing instructions for making proteins themselves, they can bind to genetic messages and prevent those instructions from being translated into proteins. That gives microRNAs considerable influence over what happens inside a cell. Peter Nghiem, an associate professor in the VMBS veterinary integrative biosciences department, compared their role to the brakes on a car. “Their expression can prevent something very bad from happening—like accelerating to the point where you crash or develop cancer,” he says. When levels of miR-15a and miR-16 are reduced, as the researchers observed in pancreatic cancer, that braking effect may be diminished, so the team explored what happens when those microRNAs are added back. “The whole goal with this study was not to repair the brakes but bring the brakes back into the cell to see if we can slow down the progression of these cancer types,” Fluckey says. To test that idea, the researchers increased miR-15a and miR-16 in cultured PDAC cells. Doing so reduced both protein synthesis and cell proliferation. The study builds on the team’s previous research into miR-15a and miR-16 by examining how the two microRNAs influence protein production and cell growth in pancreatic cancer. The team also used computational analysis to identify the biological processes potentially influenced by the two microRNAs, revealing connections to a broad range of genes and pathways involved in cancer, protein metabolism, cell adhesion and other cellular processes. That broad influence could be particularly important because cancer is rarely driven by a single malfunctioning process. “We would love to find that magic bullet to say, ‘This is the molecule that causes cancer,’ but we can’t,” Fluckey says. “What we can say is that these microRNAs seem to have a vital role in the protein balance of the cell. When they are in abundance, we can dramatically slow the progression of that cancer.” The researchers next turned to publicly available patient data to determine whether the patterns they observed in cultured cells were also reflected in people with pancreatic disease. They found that miR-15a and miR-16 levels were lower in pancreatic tumors than in healthy pancreatic tissue. They also found that microRNAs were also reduced in samples from patients with pancreatitis, an inflammatory condition of the pancreas. Most notably, pancreatic cancer patients whose tumors had higher miR-15a and miR-16 expression had better survival outcomes than those with lower expression. Together, the patient data reinforced the researchers’ laboratory findings, showing that the same microRNAs that slowed cancer cell growth in cultured cells were also associated with better outcomes in people with pancreatic cancer. While the results point toward therapeutic possibilities, turning miR-15a and miR-16 into a treatment will require solving a major challenge: getting them to the right cells. The researchers’ next goal is to develop a delivery method capable of restoring the microRNAs specifically in cancer cells while leaving healthy cells alone. “We’re becoming more and more confident that the miR-15a and 16 interventions may truly have therapeutic potential,” Fluckey says. “Now we just have to figure out how to get it to cells in a way that we’re only treating the cells that are cancerous.” That specificity will be critical, Nghiem says, because microRNAs also perform important regulatory functions in healthy cells. The researchers also caution that restoring miR-15a and miR-16 is unlikely to become a stand-alone cure for pancreatic cancer; instead, it could eventually provide one component of a combination of treatments targeting the many biological processes involved in the disease. “It’s just not going to be one treatment for a disease,” Nghiem says. “MicroRNA-15a and 16 can be one important arm of a treatment regimen. As we do research, we’re going to find all of the pieces that come together eventually to effectively treat and hopefully cure patients with these devastating diseases.” For Fluckey, one of the most promising aspects of the research is that those potential tools already exist naturally within the body. “The therapeutic intervention that we’re looking at is already in your body,” he says. “We just have to figure out how to get it back in working order.” Source: Texas A&M University The post 2 molecules may help slow pancreatic cancer growth appeared first on Futurity .

items.descriptionOriginal: Meet Kolkata’s Alpona Didi. 🌺❤️ Every year before Diwali, 74-year-old Ratnabali Ghosh steps out at 5 AM to draw intricate traditional Alponas on the doorsteps of strangers. What may look like simple patterns carries a deeper meaning. In a city where many young people have moved away and elderly parents may be left feeling alone, her colourful artwork brings unexpected joy to people’s mornings. Inspired by generations of Bengali artistic tradition, Ratnabali is doing more than decorating doorsteps. She’s helping keep a fading cultural art form alive while reminding people that even a small gesture can make someone feel noticed and valued. Her story shows us that kindness doesn’t always need grand gestures. Sometimes, it begins with a few lines of art outside someone’s door. 🎨 Know someone who would love this story?
