items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Creating a More Sustainable Workplace Reading Time: 3 minutes Sustainability has moved from being a nice extra to something many businesses are expected to think about as part of everyday operations. Sustainability has moved from being a nice extra to something many businesses are expected to think about as part of everyday operations. Customers, employees and clients are increasingly interested in how organisations manage energy, waste and travel, but creating a greener workplace doesn’t necessarily require a dramatic redesign or a huge environmental budget. The good news is that creating a greener workplace does not always require major investment. Often, the most effective changes are simple adjustments that reduce environmental impact while improving day-to-day operations. The workspace itself can play a big part. For some businesses, this could mean looking at how they use their office space, while others are reducing unnecessary travel and allowing their staff to work from home and only meeting face-to-face for genuine reasons. Those trying to reduce travel emissions find that some cities offer flexible office space, like Leeds . These coworking and flexible office options can reduce the need for employees to travel into a permanent office every day when face-to-face collaboration is only required occasionally. Businesses that require regular in-person collaboration are increasingly choosing locations with strong public transport connections. This can help reduce reliance on car travel and make lower-carbon commuting a practical choice for more employees. Make Energy Efficiency an Everyday Habit Energy efficiency sounds like a major infrastructure project, but plenty of improvements begin with ordinary workplace habits. Lights left on in empty meeting rooms, computers running overnight and heating operating when nobody is in the building all represent avoidable energy use. Reducing energy use can lower operating costs while also helping organisations cut the emissions associated with powering their workplace. Motion-sensitive lighting, sensible heating controls and making sure equipment is switched off when it isn’t required can make an immediate difference. Businesses can also look at practical ways to reduce workplace energy consumption , including reviewing heating schedules, monitoring usage and considering smarter controls. Make Greener Commuting Easier Supporting cycling, walking and public transport can be as simple as providing secure bike storage, showers or clearer information about nearby transport connections. Flexible and hybrid working can help too. Fewer commuting journeys can also help lower transport-related carbon emissions, making hybrid working beneficial for both employees and the environment. If employees don’t need to be physically present every day, reducing unnecessary journeys may be more practical than expecting everyone to commute simply because that’s how the working week has traditionally been structured. The key is making greener choices convenient. People are far more likely to change their habits when the alternative actually works for their lives. Reduce Waste Without Making Work More Complicated Sustainability initiatives tend to lose momentum when they create additional hassle. Waste reduction works best when the greener option is also the easiest one. Moving routine documents online can reduce unnecessary printing, while clearly labelled recycling points make it easier for employees to dispose of things correctly. Reviewing purchasing habits can help as well. Ordering fewer disposable supplies, reusing equipment where possible and resisting the temptation to replace perfectly serviceable office furniture all add up. Get the Team Involved Finally, no workplace sustainability plan will get very far if it exists only in a policy document nobody reads. Employees need to understand what the organisation is trying to achieve and, ideally, feel that they have some ownership of it. That might mean creating small team targets, inviting staff to suggest improvements or simply making recycling, energy saving and sustainable travel part of everyday workplace conversations. Progress doesn’t need to be turned into a competition, but sharing the results can help people see that individual actions genuinely add up. Over time, small changes to energy use, commuting habits and waste management can reduce a workplace’s environmental impact while supporting wider sustainability goals. The post Creating a More Sustainable Workplace appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Cloud Technology Can Support Business Sustainability Goals Reading Time: 2 minutes Businesses across the UK are facing more and more pressure to reduce their environmental impact while maintaining operational efficiency. Both customers and investors are paying closer attention to sustainability commitments, and many organisations are being encouraged to look for practical ways to make a real impact with long-term environmental goals. While most initiatives often focus on transport , energy use and supply chains, technology decisions also play an important role. Many organisations are now reviewing how their IT infrastructure contributes to their wider sustainability strategy. By adopting scalable digital solutions and working with providers that offer Managed Cloud services for improved efficiency and resource management , businesses can reduce unnecessary energy consumption while maintaining the performance and flexibility needed to support growth. Reducing reliance on energy-intensive on-site infrastructure Traditional on-site IT infrastructure can require significant resources to operate and maintain. Physical servers consume electricity around the clock and often require dedicated cooling systems to prevent overheating. As equipment ages, performance can decline, leading to increased maintenance demands and higher operating costs. Moving workloads into efficiently managed cloud environments can help reduce the energy demands associated with maintaining multiple on-site servers. For example, your business may replace ageing server equipment with cloud-hosted applications and storage solutions rather than investing in additional physical infrastructure. Supporting flexible and remote working Cloud technology has transformed the way employees access business systems and collaborate with colleagues. Staff can securely access files and data from different locations, whether they are working from home or visiting client sites. This flexibility can support your objectives by reducing the need for daily commuting and frequent business travel. For example, team members can collaborate on projects remotely using cloud-based platforms. Alongside environmental benefits, flexible access can improve employee satisfaction and help organisations attract and retain talent. Businesses that support remote working and secure access to business systems can often create a more agile, environmentally friendly operating model. Making better use of business resources Another advantage of cloud technology is scalability. Unlike traditional infrastructure , businesses do not need to purchase large amounts of hardware in anticipation of future demand. Instead, you can increase or decrease capacity as requirements change. For example, a retailer may temporarily increase storage or computing resources during a busy trading period without investing in additional physical equipment that may sit unused for much of the year. This approach helps reduce waste and prevents overinvestment. Improving monitoring and reporting Accurate data is essential for sustainability targets. Cloud-based platforms often provide advanced reporting and monitoring capabilities that can help you gain better visibility into your operations. You could use cloud-based dashboards to analyse performance metrics and identify inefficiencies across different departments or locations. This information can support more informed decision-making and help businesses prioritise areas for improvement. Better access to data can also assist with reporting, making it easier to measure progress against environmental goals and demonstrate accountability to stakeholders. To summarise… While sustainability requires a broad business commitment, being fully sustainable for many businesses is not something that can be achieved quickly. Cloud adoption can be an important step towards reducing resource consumption, improving operational efficiency and supporting long-term environmental goals. The post How Cloud Technology Can Support Business Sustainability Goals appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Examples of Medical Errors That May Lead to a Malpractice Claim Reading Time: 3 minutes Examples of Medical Errors That May Lead to a Malpractice Claim According to a study published in Patient Safety and highlighted by the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ), diagnostic errors accounted for 26.6% of closed medical malpractice claims reviewed over a 20-year period. Among all claims related to the diagnoses, 39% were fatal. Misdiagnosis and delay in diagnoses were the most often made claims. Medical malpractices have severe implications for patients, which may range from delays in treatment to deterioration of medical conditions or even disability and death. In the USA, one is entitled to filing medical malpractice if a healthcare professional fails to adhere to the acceptable level of care, resulting in preventable harm. There are actually more malpractice cases that happen in the healthcare industry than people realize. But it’s also important to understand that not all unfavorable medical outcomes qualify as malpractice. A claim will require evidence of negligence and resulting injury. But what is an example of malpractice ? Let’s take a closer look at the common medical errors and what steps you need to take to seek a possible claim. Diagnosis Is Where Most of It Happens In the AHRQ systematic review of ED care, the rate of diagnostic errors was found to be 5.7% with an extrapolated estimate of 7.4 million diagnostic errors and 371,000 severe harms per year associated with diagnostic errors. These overall rates were based on results from three prospective studies conducted outside of the U.S. in Canada, Spain, and Switzerland. AHRQ commissioned an independent review after its publication because of the high numbers that were cited. This is an order of magnitude, not a number count. Rates of disease-specific errors have higher validity. On average, physicians fail to diagnose stroke in about 17% of patients. The list is completed by myocardial infarction, aortic dissection, spinal cord compression, and venous thromboembolism. These conditions share a profile. They present atypically often enough that a physician working quickly can reach the wrong conclusion. The Procedure Itself Surgical and anesthesia errors sit at the opposite end of the evidentiary range. Wrong-site surgery. A retained sponge. An anesthesia dosing failure during a routine case. Proof of breach in wrong-site and retained object surgeries is seldom disputed since there is evidence of negligence in the records. Firms handling this work tend to sort it by mechanism rather than by specialty. Medical malpractice lawyers in Marietta, GA , separate birth injuries such as cerebral palsy, brachial plexus injury, and hypoxic ischemic encephalopathy from anesthesia errors, emergency room errors, and surgical errors. Medication Errors More defendants get implicated in medication cases than any other type. A prescriber orders a prescription, a pharmacist dispenses the prescription, a nurse delivers the prescription, and the electronic health record alerts for a possible drug interaction or not. Wrong dosage, lack of allergy information, and drugs with similar appearances on the screen cause claims. Each individual has his own employer and his own insurance. Birth Injuries Obstetric negligence claims hinge more on timing than anything else. Whether or not someone interpreted the fetal monitoring properly. How quickly the decision was made to utilize the C-section procedure. Whether or not the procedures used were appropriate for shoulder dystocia. These cases require more time than adult claims. In fact, some states also set a separate limitations period for minors in malpractice cases that ends well before adulthood. What Turns an Error Into a Claim Expert testimony does most of the work. A plaintiff cannot establish the standard of care without a qualified physician stating what it was. A number of states, including Georgia, require a sworn expert affidavit filed alongside the complaint. That single requirement can end a case before anyone takes a deposition. Damage caps are the other structural variable. It’s important to understand, though, that these caps could shift. The non-economic damage cap in California remained unchanged at $250,000 for decades before AB 35 changed it to $350,000 for cases other than death. It is at $500,000 for wrongful death starting from 2023, increasing by $40,000 and $50,000, respectively, each year for ten years. The distance between a medical error and a malpractice claim is mostly documentary. Whether the chart recorded the symptom the patient actually reported. Whether the monitoring strip survived. Whether anybody wrote down a time. Errors are common and claims are not, and most of what fills the space between those two facts is records that either exist or do not. The post Examples of Medical Errors That May Lead to a Malpractice Claim appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: October is a good time to grow spinach on your terrace in many parts of India, as temperatures begin to ease after the summer heat. With a few containers, suitable soil, and regular care, even a small terrace can provide fresh palak for everyday meals. The key is to give the plants enough light, maintain moisture in the soil, and choose growing conditions suited to the season. Vijay Sharma, a swimming coach at SP College in Bikaner , Rajasthan, knows the satisfaction of harvesting vegetables at home. He began gardening in 2017 after noticing that the quality of market-bought cluster beans was declining. Pleased with the results, he started growing spinach, okra, chillies, and other vegetables. During the COVID-19 lockdown, he expanded his garden to cover 1,500 square feet, growing more than 150 varieties of vegetables and medicinal plants. In a conversation with The Better Indi a published in October 2021, he shared how he prepared his growing medium, reused household materials as planters, and cared for his plants. His experience offers useful lessons for those planning to grow spinach this October. 1. Choose a suitable container Spinach grows well in containers, making it a practical choice for terrace gardeners. Choose a pot or grow bag at least six to eight inches deep, with drainage holes to prevent water from collecting around the roots. A wider container allows you to grow several plants together. October is a good time to grow spinach on your terrace in many parts of India. Photograph: (The Arbor Gate) The expert found creative ways to expand his garden when gardening supplies were difficult to access during the lockdown. He reused discarded drums, old tyres, and broken plastic containers as planters. For spinach, use a clean container that allows excess water to drain freely. Avoid overcrowding the plants, as adequate space helps leaves develop well. 2. Prepare a nutrient-rich growing medium Healthy leaves begin with good soil. Spinach needs a growing medium that retains moisture without becoming waterlogged. Sharma explains that he uses soil mixed with cow dung manure or cocopeat, with these materials accounting for around half of his growing mix. For spinach, combine garden soil with well-rotted compost and cocopeat to create a loose, moisture-retentive medium. Use mature compost rather than fresh manure, which can damage plants and is unsuitable for direct application to leafy vegetables. 3. Sow seeds directly into the pot Spinach seeds can be sown directly into the container where the plants will grow. Place them in shallow furrows, cover lightly with soil, and water gently. Keep the soil moist while the seeds germinate. Once seedlings appear, thin them out if they are growing too close together. This gives the remaining plants room to develop healthy leaves. October is suitable for sowing spinach in many parts of India, particularly northern regions where temperatures begin to fall. In warmer areas, choose a cooler spot on the terrace and avoid exposing seedlings to excessive afternoon heat. 4. Give spinach adequate sunlight Spinach needs sufficient sunlight for healthy growth, but intense heat can cause it to struggle. Choose a spot that receives several hours of sunlight, preferably in the morning if your terrace becomes very hot later in the day. The gardener has observed how vegetation can influence temperatures in his garden. He explains that creepers shelter his plants from direct sunlight and help cool the garden during summers when temperatures in Bikaner can approach 50 degrees Celsius. For spinach, aim for a balance. Avoid deep shade, but provide some protection from harsh afternoon sun in warmer regions. 5. Water regularly without soaking the soil Spinach needs consistent moisture, especially during germination and early growth . Dry soil can affect leaf development, while excess water can damage the roots. Spinach grows well in containers, making it a practical choice for terrace gardeners. Photograph: (Nature & Garden) Sharma advises beginners to pay attention to watering. "Watering the plants is equally important for their healthy growth," he says. Check the soil regularly and water when the surface begins to dry. Water gently around the base of the plants, allowing excess moisture to drain through the container. Pots exposed to strong sunlight or dry winds may need more frequent checks. 6. Feed the plants and keep an eye on their leaves A growing medium enriched with compost gives spinach a good start. If the plants remain in the same container for several weeks, add a light layer of mature compost around them to replenish nutrients. Inspect the leaves regularly for holes, discolouration, or pests. Remove damaged leaves and avoid overcrowding, which can restrict airflow. The gardener advises beginners to grow seasonal vegetables and says that plants need occasional trimming. For spinach, remove damaged foliage while leaving healthy leaves and the central growing point intact. 7. Harvest without uprooting the plant Once the outer leaves are large enough to use, harvest them carefully while leaving the central growing point undisturbed. This allows the plant to continue producing leaves. The first harvest may be ready in around four to six weeks , depending on the variety, temperature, and growing conditions. For a more regular supply, sow small batches of seeds at intervals rather than planting everything at once. For spinach, use a clean container that allows excess water to drain freely. Photograph: (Gardener's Path) Sharma's terrace garden shows how growing vegetables at home can begin with a simple experiment and expand over time. For beginners, a couple of spinach containers are a good starting point. TBI Gardening Calendar brings together what to plant, grow, and care for each month of the year, helping home gardeners make the most of their balconies, terraces, backyards, and small growing spaces. Each story focuses on seasonal plants and crops, with simple, practical guidance on when to sow or plant, how to care for them, and what to expect as they grow.

items.title: Είμαστε πολύ πιο κοντά στην προστασία του 30% του πλανήτη από όσο γνωρίζαμε. Αλλά υπάρχει μια σύλληψη.
items.titleOriginal: We’re way closer to protecting 30% of the planet than we knew. But there’s a catch.
items.description: Πρώτον, τα καλά νέα: Ο κόσμος μπορεί να είναι πολύ πιο κοντά από ό,τι πιστεύουμε σε έναν διεθνή στόχο προστασίας του 30% της γης έως το 2030. Τα κακά νέα: Μάλλον δεν είναι η σωστή γη. Τα έθνη του κόσμου έχουν θέσει προστασία στο 27% περίπου των χερσαίων μαζών του πλανήτη, πολύ περισσότερο από το 19% που πιστευόταν προηγουμένως, σύμφωνα με έρευνα που δημοσιεύθηκε πρόσφατα…
items.descriptionOriginal: First, the good news: The world might be a lot closer than we think to an international goal of protecting 30% of land by 2030. The bad news: It’s probably not all the right land. The nations of the world have placed protections on roughly 27% of the planet’s land masses, far more than the 19% previously thought, according to research recently published in Nature . There has been much hand wringing among conservation-minded folks that countries were woefully behind on land protection pledges made in 2022 to shield 30% of Earth’s land and 30% of the ocean from development as part of an update to the Convention on Biological Diversity, the main international agreement aimed at the current extinction crisis. But “our analysis suggests that much more of the land is in some type of conservation area than currently recognized,” said lead author Helen O’Neill, a postdoctoral researcher at the United Kingdom’s Institute of Zoology, London. The official tally tracking protected lands is a database at the Protected Planet website , a collaboration between the United Nations and the International Union for Conservation of Nature. While this is the authoritative source, it’s incomplete. Some protected land hasn’t been registered there by countries. And it doesn’t include significant acreage that falls into a kind of gray area – land that isn’t formally protected chiefly for wildlife, but where regulations provide many of the same benefits. Known as “other effective area-based conservation measures” or OECMs, this might include land protected as sacred by Indigenous groups or managed to improve water quality. O’Neill and 35 other scientists from across the globe set out to tally this overlooked land to create a more complete picture. To reduce the massive effort required to scrutinize the status of every piece of land on the planet, the researcher selected pieces totaling 10% of all the world’s land masses. That included terrain scattered across the world and covering major types of ecosystems, from the Rocky Mountains in Montana to the Amazonian jungle to the desert of the Arabian Peninsula. .IRPP_ruby where regulations and management practices made them good candidates for being OECMs. The scientists used the results to create a computer model that estimated how this pattern would apply to the entire world. The result was the encouraging estimate that 26.8% of all land is protected, at least on paper. But that doesn’t mean conservationists can cruise across the 2030 finish line with their arms raised. Because the research also revealed troubling holes in where these lands are being conserved. Of the 173 different ecological regions scientists have mapped around the world, fewer than 100 have greater than 17% of their land protected, the scientists estimated. Regions that are primarily ice and rock – polar and alpine landscapes – are significantly overrepresented in the catalog of protected areas. That’s not a big surprise, since those regions are often less attractive for human settlement or exploitation by farming or other activities. By contrast, deserts, woodlands, grasslands and temperate forests all fall below the 30% target. Then there is the question of whether land that’s conserved on paper is really being protected . The new research points to the potential gains that can be made, particularly with the recognition of the conservation potential of these OECMs. But “conserving 30% of land and seas is not sufficient on its own,” said Heather Bingham, a co-author who heads the Protected Planet Initiative. “The target also calls for these areas to be managed effectively for positive biodiversity outcomes, and to be placed where they will have the greatest impact on biodiversity.” O’Neill, et. al. “ Global conservation area coverage substantially exceeds current estimates .” Nature. items.descriptionOriginal: Scientists have turned blood cells from an 80-year-old into neural stem cells with a molecular age of less than 20, effectively reversing more than 60 years of cellular aging in the laboratory. The discovery offers a new way to investigate how cells become younger and could help researchers better understand age-related diseases such as Alzheimer's.

items.title: «Thermocol Out, Clay & Shola In»: Αυτά τα είδωλα Durga των καλλιτεχνών της Καλκούτα δεν θα πνίξουν το Hooghly This Pujo
items.titleOriginal: ‘Thermocol Out, Clay & Shola In’: These Kolkata Artisans’ Durga Idols Won’t Choke the Hooghly This Pujo
items.description: Στο Joy Durga Bhandar, ένα εργαστήριο στο Kumartuli της βόρειας Καλκούτα, ο Koushik Ghosh ξεκινά ένα είδωλο με ένα πλαίσιο από μπαμπού και ξύλο δεμένο μεταξύ τους με σχοινί από γιούτα. Από αυτή τη βάση προέρχονται οι γλυπτές φιγούρες, οι διακοσμήσεις και τα στρώματα χρώματος που βλέπουν οι θιασώτες κατά τη διάρκεια της Durga Puja. Ο Koushik ξέρει καλά αυτή τη διαδικασία. Για γενιές, οι τεχνίτες στο Kumartuli φορούσαν…
items.descriptionOriginal: At Joy Durga Bhandar, a workshop in north Kolkata's Kumartuli, Koushik Ghosh begins an idol with a framework of bamboo and wood tied together with jute rope. From this base come the sculpted figures, decorations and layers of colour that devotees see during Durga Puja. Koushik knows this process well. For generations, artisans in Kumartuli have worked with bamboo, straw and clay, shaping idols by hand for Kolkata's Durga Puja celebrations. Over time, many workshops also adopted thermocol decorations, synthetic paints and plastic ornaments because they were quicker or cheaper to use. Koushik is looking for ways to bring more traditional materials back into his work. "The frame, the clay, the straw, those were always ours. The thermocol and the chemical colours came later, because they were cheaper and faster. I am going back to what was here before," he says. The straw framework gives the idol its shape before artisans add the first layers of clay. He is working towards idols decorated with natural clay, shola (the soft pith of a plant used for delicate ornaments) and natural colours instead of thermocol. Every year, after Durga Puja, thousands of idols are immersed in the Hooghly River and other water bodies. In 2025, around 5,200 idols were immersed across 34 major Hooghly ghats and approximately 30 other water bodies in Kolkata and nearby suburbs, according to The Times of India . Civic workers clear debris from immersion sites, but thermocol and plastic decorations need careful collection and disposal because they can persist in the environment. Neel, a volunteer who has spent several seasons cleaning the Hooghly's banks near Babughat, remembers finding thermocol floating on the surface, coloured residue near the banks, and plastic decorations gathering along the ghats. Kumartuli's workshops have produced clay idols for Kolkata's Durga Puja for generations. For Koushik, the challenge is to make the decorations less wasteful while keeping the craft affordable for the families who depend on it. From bamboo frames to Durga's eyes: Inside the craft of Kumartuli Walking through Kumartuli's narrow lanes, the smell of wet clay is difficult to miss. The neighbourhood, whose name comes from kumor (potter) and tuli (neighbourhood quarter), has been home to idol makers for more than three centuries. Its workshops stand between Rabindra Sarani and the Hooghly, the river that has long supplied the fine alluvial soil used in their craft. Traditionally known as Ganga maati , this clay is softer and finer than ordinary earth, allowing artisans to sculpt delicate features. Artisans shape clay over the bamboo-and-straw framework before adding finer details and colour. At Koushik's workshop, everything begins with the kathamo (a framework made from bamboo and wood). "The frame is not just engineering," he explains. "It is the first thing she stands on." The structure must support the central Durga figure, accompanying figures, a lion and other sculpted elements. Next comes khar bandha (tying straw around the frame). Carefully shaped bundles of straw form the arms, waist, chest and other features. If the straw is tied incorrectly, the figure may lose its balance or the clay may crack. The first clay layer is entel mati (sticky clay mixed with tush , or rice husk). It takes about three to four days to dry. Straw and clay form the idol's limbs, which must be balanced before the finer layers are applied. Artisans then apply bele mati (finer, smoother clay), allowing another five or six days for drying, depending on the weather. Any cracks are repaired with fresh mud. Faces, hands and other delicate parts are often made separately using chhach (moulds), helping workshops manage the large number of orders they receive. The final detailing includes chokkhudaan (painting the eyes). Some artisans specialise in this stage because even a slight difference in the brushstrokes can change the expression of the figure. This process has remained largely familiar across generations. A Durga idol includes accompanying figures and a lion, all assembled before the final decoration. The changes have come in the materials used for decoration and finishing. Earlier, artisans relied on bamboo, straw, jute, shola and natural pigments. Tamarind-seed gum, chalk powder and starch made from boiled arrowroot were used to prepare and finish colours. As demand grew, thermocol became popular for chaal (decorative backdrops), mukut (crowns) and ornaments. Synthetic paints offered brighter colours, while plastic jewellery entered some workshops. These alternatives were quicker, cheaper and easier to work with when deadlines were approaching. The extra work behind a natural finish Gopal, a veteran artisan who remembers making idols before thermocol became common, understands why workshops adopted it. He recalls decorating traditional sabeki pratima (traditional-style idols) with shola, cloth, zari and daaker saaj (traditional decorative work). Handmade clay figures require repeated shaping and drying, adding to an artisan's working hours. "Shola was beautiful, but it took time. Thermocol came because it was fast and cheap. If you remove thermocol now and don't give me shola at the same price and within the same time, I am just working slower for the same money," he says. Thermocol is lightweight, easy to cut and relatively inexpensive. Shola, jute, handmade paper, paper pulp, bamboo and clay ornaments may require more time and skill, and sometimes cost more. Natural colours create another difficulty. Asha, who manages colouring and finishing work at a Kumartuli studio, says buyers have grown accustomed to the bright, uniform finish of synthetic paints. "Natural colour is more beautiful if you know how to look at it. But the buyer is standing under LED lights in the pandal. They want brightness. Softness looks like less work to them, even when it is more," she explains. Colouring and decoration come after sculpting, with buyers often expecting a bright, even finish. This expectation has financial consequences. Koushik points to raw-material prices, labour, drying time and the risk of damage as factors that can raise the cost of working with natural materials. Handmade decorations take more hours. Natural colours need careful application. During the monsoon, wet clay can also take longer to dry. In the final weeks of a season, artisans often work long hours to meet delivery dates, using fans and tarpaulins to manage damp conditions. Koushik has not lost an idol to rain, but the possibility remains with every order that needs additional drying time. Artisans use fans and tarpaulins to manage damp conditions while working to Puja deadlines. The bigger challenge is recovering these expenses. There is no fixed price for a Durga idol. The cost depends on its height, design, decorations, arrangement of figures and the buyer's budget. Even two idols of the same height can have different prices. Costs differ by design, materials and year, so there is no single price difference between idols using natural decorations and those made with synthetic alternatives. For a small workshop, even a modest unplanned expense can make a difference. "If the idol has to be eco-friendly and the client wants the same finish as a synthetic-painted one, one of us has to absorb the difference. Usually, it is us," Asha says. The cost of an idol depends on its size, design, decorative materials and time spent finishing it. A South Kolkata Puja committee organiser, who requested anonymity, describes the buyer's dilemma. His committee relies on contributions from neighbourhood families, so any increase in an idol's price or change in its appearance must be discussed with the people paying for it. Gopal believes buyers and artisans should agree on materials and costs when placing an order. That would help workshops plan their purchases without bearing unexpected expenses themselves. After the idols are immersed, what is left in the Hooghly? Idol immersion is an important part of Durga Puja. The environmental concern lies with synthetic decorations and paints that may enter the water or be left on the banks unless they are removed and collected. Thermocol and plastic do not biodegrade easily and can break into smaller fragments that remain in the environment. Some synthetic paints contain heavy metals that can affect water quality. Decorative paints and plastic ornaments may leave residues that require post-immersion collection. A Central Pollution Control Board study conducted between 1993 and 1995 estimated that idol immersions released 32 tonnes of colours and 16.8 tonnes of varnish and garjan oil annually into the Hooghly during that period. These colours contained metals including lead, mercury and chromium, according to findings reported by Down To Earth . These are historical findings, not a measure of present-day pollution. They help explain why safer materials and careful post-immersion clean-ups matter. The CPCB's revised guidelines of May 2020 call for natural, biodegradable idols, discourage toxic synthetic paints and restrict thermocol, plastic and plaster of Paris. CPCB guidelines favour biodegradable idols and discourage thermocol, plastic and toxic paints. West Bengal's 2018 immersion rules require natural clay and bamboo, prohibit plaster of Paris and toxic colours, and place responsibilities on Puja committees and local authorities. Decorative thermocol has also been prohibited under national single-use plastic restrictions effective from July 2022. For workshops, switching materials works best when decisions are made before production begins. In August 2025, The Times of India reported that police were conducting awareness drives and inspections at Kumartuli and other idol-making centres. West Bengal's immersion rules call for natural clay and bamboo and prohibit toxic colours. Artisans interviewed for that report asked for guidance six to eight months before Durga Puja, when orders and material choices can still be changed. Koushik agrees that natural decorations need to be planned from the start. A 25-YO idol maker puts paper pulp & plant colours to the test A few workshops have already begun experimenting with alternatives. Ritwik, a 25-year-old third-generation idol maker, has been testing paper pulp for ornaments and plant-based colours for the faces of idols. After attending an awareness workshop, he brought back samples of gerua (an earth-based red pigment), turmeric-based colours and dyes derived from plants. He began trying them on small clay surfaces before using them on larger figures. "The look is different. Not worse, actually; I think it is more beautiful. But it is older-looking. Some clients like that. Some think I made a mistake. It depends on whether they know what they are seeing," he says. Artisans testing plant-based pigments say their finishes can look different from synthetic paints. The softer, slightly uneven appearance resembles the finish of traditional idols made before synthetic paints became widespread. There is no reliable figure for how many Kumartuli workshops have completely moved away from thermocol. During the reporter's visits, thermocol decorations and synthetic paints were still visible in workshops. Experiments with natural alternatives were promising, but had yet to become the norm. With thousands of idols made in Kumartuli each season, these material choices can add up. According to a September 2026 report in The Telegraph , around 166 studios produce close to 8,500 idols in a season, with turnover exceeding ₹200 crore in the previous year. A 2026 report estimated around 166 Kumartuli studios making close to 8,500 idols each season. Koushik and other artisans say a broader shift will depend on affordable traditional materials, clear specifications from buyers and guidance shared well before production begins. A reliable supply of shola, jute and natural pigments would also make it easier for workshops to plan ahead. What a painted tile shows about the choice At Gopal's workshop, a painted tile offers another way to compare the materials. One strip was coloured with synthetic paint, the other with natural pigment. Gopal left both exposed through the previous monsoon to see how they changed. The synthetic strip remained uniform; the natural one developed warmer, slightly uneven edges. Gopal did not declare either better. For him, the contrast shows how a natural finish may differ from what buyers are accustomed to. Natural pigments can create a different finish, while handmade ornaments take time. These differences need to be part of the discussion when an idol is commissioned. Traditional clay figures are moulded and dried before receiving their colours and decorations. Koushik is working to bring more of the materials his craft has long relied on back into use. Buyers can help by agreeing on materials and budgets early; timely guidance and access to affordable supplies could help more workshops do the same. Behind every idol are weeks of skilled labour. Choices about paint, decorations and post-immersion waste collection matter both to the artisans and to the river near their workshops. For Koushik, the goal is practical: honour an old craft, reduce the amount of synthetic waste entering the Hooghly and make sure artisans can still earn a fair living. All images courtesy Akhil Rajarathinam

items.title: «Δεν είχα πτυχίο μηχανικού»: Ο γιος του Almora Mechanic έμαθε από το Διαδίκτυο και κατασκεύασε ένα ιπτάμενο αυτοκίνητο
items.titleOriginal: ‘I Had No Engineering Degree’: Almora Mechanic’s Son Learnt From the Internet & Built a Flying Car
items.description: Τα ιπτάμενα αυτοκίνητα καταλαμβάνουν και πάλι το διαδίκτυο, με τα σχέδια της Tesla να τροφοδοτούν συζητήσεις για ένα μέλλον όπου οι άνθρωποι θα μπορούσαν να ταξιδεύουν στον αέρα αντί να κάθονται στην κίνηση. Αλλά στην Almora του Uttarakhand, ένας καινοτόμος έχει περάσει 13 χρόνια δουλεύοντας για μια παρόμοια ιδέα, οδηγούμενος από ένα πρόβλημα πολύ πιο κοντά στο σπίτι. Ο Ράβι Τάμτα μεγάλωσε στο βουνό…
items.descriptionOriginal: Flying cars are once again taking over the internet, with Tesla's plans fuelling conversations about a future where people could travel through the air instead of sitting in traffic. But in Almora, Uttarakhand, an innovator has spent 13 years working towards a similar idea, driven by a problem much closer to home. Ravi Tamta grew up in the mountains of Kaflikhan village near Jageswar Dham, where reaching a hospital could mean hours on winding roads. He began wondering if there was another way to travel through the hills, one that did not depend on roads or require an airport. Inspired by the challenges of reaching hospitals in the hills, Ravi Tamta spent 13 years developing a flying vehicle that can take off and land vertically. Photograph: ( Zee News) That question led him to build HAPIDA SKYNeX, an electric flying vehicle prototype that can take off and land vertically. After years of experiments, the vehicle completed its maiden test flight in August, taking off from an army helipad in Almora and remaining airborne for nearly a minute. A mountain problem sparked the idea For people living in hilly regions, distance is not always measured in kilometres. Winding roads and difficult terrain can turn a relatively short journey into a long trip, particularly when someone needs medical attention. Tamta began exploring whether a flying vehicle could help people cover such distances faster. His idea was to develop a vehicle that could rise vertically, travel over difficult terrain, and land without needing a runway. View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Better India (@thebetterindia) The aim is to make air travel more accessible in hilly regions, particularly during medical emergencies and in areas that are difficult to reach by road. Developed under his venture, Hapida Sky Private Limited, the HAPIDA SKYNeX combines modified, scaled-up multirotor drone technology with an electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) system. In simple terms, it uses the same basic principle that lets a multirotor drone take off and hover, but applies it to a prototype designed to carry a person. Unlike conventional aircraft that need a runway to gain enough speed for take-off, an eVTOL vehicle is designed to lift off and land vertically. This could make the technology particularly relevant to mountainous areas, where finding suitable space for runways can be difficult. How the flying vehicle works HAPIDA SKYNeX uses multiple electric motors and propellers mounted on external arms to generate lift. Working together, these components are designed to raise the vehicle off the ground, sustain a hover, and help control its movement through the air. This multirotor arrangement is similar in principle to the technology used in drones, although scaling it up to carry a person presents additional engineering and safety challenges. The prototype also features a lightweight frame, a cockpit designed for a single pilot and a transparent canopy. Its electric propulsion system is battery-powered, eliminating direct exhaust emissions during operation. From a mobile-charging shoe to a smart walking stick for visually impaired people, Ravi Tamta's earlier inventions also focused on solving practical, everyday problems. Photograph: ( Business Today ) However, its practical flight range, battery endurance, and overall efficiency will depend on factors such as the battery capacity, the vehicle's weight, and the power required to sustain flight. The intended use is short-distance travel across difficult terrain. According to the reported project details, a journey of around 40 kilometres that takes approximately 90 minutes by mountain road could potentially be completed in 10 to 15 minutes by air. This is an intended travel-time goal, rather than a demonstrated operational capability at this stage. Thirteen years of learning through experiments Tamta did not have an engineering degree or access to a fancy laboratory. Instead, he turned to the internet to learn, relying on his parents' support and repeated experiments to develop his idea. Over 13 years, the concept gradually took shape under his venture, Hapida Skynex. The maiden flight was an important step in testing whether his idea could work beyond the drawing board. The single-seater prototype features a lightweight frame, a cockpit for one pilot and a transparent canopy, with multiple electric motors and propellers designed to generate lift. Photograph: ( Influencer Book of World Records ) The prototype is still at an early stage and requires further testing. While the test flight offers a glimpse of what the vehicle might eventually do, it is too soon to know how it will perform in regular use. Before a vehicle of this kind can be used for routine passenger travel, it would need to demonstrate reliable flight control, sufficient battery performance, structural stability and safe responses to component failures. Operating in mountainous terrain would bring additional considerations, including changing weather, wind conditions, landing-site availability and emergency procedures. From everyday inventions to flying vehicles The flying vehicle is not Tamta's first attempt at solving practical problems through invention. His earlier creations include shoes that charge mobile phones on the go, a smart walking stick for visually impaired people, a bamboo-splitting machine and firefighting equipment. Ravi Tamta hopes HAPIDA SKYNeX will one day make travel across Uttarakhand's mountains faster and more accessible. Photograph: ( Instagram/@ravi_tamta3 ) Each project began with a practical challenge, leading him to explore how a device could make a task easier. HAPIDA SKYNeX has a longer journey ahead before it can carry passengers or help people reach hospitals faster. For now, its first flight marks a step forward for an idea shaped by life in the mountains. As conversations about flying cars continue online, Tamta's work offers a different way to look at the technology: not just as a futuristic mode of transport, but as a possible answer to the everyday challenges of getting from one place to another. Sources: 'Uttarakhand Man Conducts Test Flight Of Drone-Based Flying Vehicle: Watch' by NDTV, Published on 8 August 2026. 'This Uttarakhand youth built an electric flying vehicle. Here's why everyone is talking about Ravi Tamta' by The Times of India, Published on 7 August 2026.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News The innovative approach of Ocean Cleanup Reading Time: 4 minutes From a Dutch teenager’s question in 2013 to 50 million kilograms of debris removed, Ocean Cleanup proves ingenuity can still tackle one of the ocean’s most overwhelming problems. Our oceans cover 71% of the planet’s surface, plunging down nearly 11,000 meters at their deepest point in the Mariana Trench, deeper than Mount Everest is tall. Below the waves lies home to billions of species spread across coral reefs, mangrove forests, seagrass beds, and hydrothermal vents. The deep-sea bed alone hosts an estimated 500,000 to 10 million species, with scientists believing 91% of ocean species remain unclassified to this day. Despite this astounding biodiversity, humans continue to put large portions of it at risk with persistent detrimental activities. In 2023, the 5 Gyres Institute, set up by Marcus Eriksen and Anna Cummings to carry out in-depth research on plastic pollution, published data revealing that 82-358 trillion plastic particles currently float on the ocean’s surface, equal to between 2.4 and 4.9 million tonnes. However, this figure is only the portion of plastic that floats; the United Nations Regional Information Centre for Western Europe (UNRIC) estimates that in total from rivers, lakes and oceans, between nine and 23 million tonnes of plastic waste reach aquatic ecosystems annually. These are the statistics that led Boyan Slat, at the age of only 18, to ask himself why no real progress was being made to tackle the plastics that had found their way into our world’s seas. In 2013, Slat set up Ocean Cleanup, which has now grown into a globally recognized non-profit organisation that utilises sustainable innovation to systematically clear non-biodegradable waste from oceans. The idea was brought to life when the Dutch innovator designed a system that harnesses the natural movement of waves and currents to push plastic into the curve of a U-shaped inflatable barrier which floats on the ocean’s surface, with both ends steered by a boat. Once the retention zone is full, it is detached from the main inflatable system, emptied into a third boat and replaced, continuing the process. The plastics on board the collection boat are taken back to shore and recycled. At 18, Boyan Slat designed a U-shaped floating barrier that uses natural wave and current movement to concentrate ocean plastic into a collection zone, creating the foundation of what Ocean Cleanup has become today. Photo courtesy of Ocean Cleanup . A perfected process now allows the organization to use an Automated Debris Imaging System (ADIS), which not only keeps track of plastic collected, but also monitors and maps the distribution of plastic debris using embedded AI. This helps to plot where to place their cleanup systems as efficiently as possible. The crew onboard also includes independent observers to monitor interactions with marine life, such as protected turtle species or whales. The key to the design is that ocean animals can easily swim under or around the system without harm. The retention zone has numerous inbuilt safety measures, including acoustic deterrents, escape aids for any animals caught up in the rubbish, and breathing hatches for mammals to ensure they can access a clear patch of ocean surface. In 2025, Ocean Cleanup launched System 03, which is almost three times larger than previous systems and measures up to 2.2km long, hoping to make even more impact on the effects of the climate crisis. The organisation has found that ocean plastics accumulate mainly in five different zones called ocean garbage patches, the biggest of them all being the Great Pacific Garbage Patch. This is bounded by the North Pacific Subtropical Gyre, a network of ocean currents, which rotates clockwise around an area of 20 million square kilometres. As the currents churn the plastics piled up in the Patch, they break down further, becoming microplastics which are known to build up in food chains that are reaching humans. Turtles are eating plastic bags mistaking them for jellyfish, albatrosses are feeding resin pellets to young instead of fish eggs, and a phenomenon known as ‘ghost fishing’ is becoming ever more common as marine mammals get tangled in discarded plastic fishing nets. This is why this Patch has become a main target zone for the organisation. However, by weight 70-80% of ocean plastic actually arrives there by rivers, with studies suggesting that just a few major rivers are the worst offenders. This is why Ocean Cleanup tackles the root of the problem as well, working with government leaders, individuals and private companies to set up interceptors at points along some of the most polluted rivers, like the Sandy Gully in Kingston, Jamaica. These interceptors include barriers, barricades, guards and the Interceptor Original: an autonomous, 100% solar powered craft that utilises a conveyor belt to continuously extract debris and distribute it evenly between containers that can store up to 50m 3 of trash combined before needing to be emptied. All of which work together to drastically reduce the trash flow from rivers into the wider sea. In March 2026, Ocean Cleanup reached 50 million kg of debris removed. This organization is living proof that with perseverance and ingenious solutions we can come together to tackle some of our world’s largest problems. But how can you play your part to help reduce plastics in our oceans? So how can you help reduce plastic in our oceans? Every little bit counts. Refuse single-use plastics like straws, and bring reusable bags when you shop. Recycle properly, following your local program’s rules closely. Avoid microbeads in products like face scrubs, usually listed as “polyethylene” or “polypropylene” on ingredient labels. Share what you’ve learned with others. Support organizations fighting plastic pollution. Join a river or beach cleanup, and never flush non-biodegradable items down the toilet. The post The innovative approach of Ocean Cleanup appeared first on Happy Eco News .

Η διατήρηση του Cuatro Ciénegas ξεκινά σε μια κοιλάδα που έχουν οι περισσότεροι άνθρωποι…
items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Cuatro Ciénegas Conservation Restores Mexico’s Ancient Desert Oasis Reading Time: 3 minutes Cuatro Ciénegas conservation efforts in Mexico’s Chihuahuan Desert are reviving ancient pools and returning bison to the land, offering a model for desert restoration worldwide. Cuatro Ciénegas conservation begins in a valley most people have never heard of. Tucked into the Chihuahuan Desert in Coahuila, the basin holds hundreds of crystal-clear pools called pozas that Fundación Pro Cuatrociénegas has spent years working to protect. These pools support life found nowhere else on the planet. The valley became a UNESCO biosphere reserve in 2006. It spans more than 413,000 hectares, an area larger than Los Angeles. Within that space live over 800 plant species and roughly 360 animal species, many found only here. The pools themselves hold something even stranger. Scientists have traced microbial life in the pozas back nearly 500 million years. Researchers believe these microbes descended from an ancient sea trapped underground when mountains rose around the basin. Some pozas also contain stromatolites, layered rock structures built by microbial colonies. Scientists consider them living relatives of some of Earth’s earliest life forms, similar to formations found in Australia’s Shark Bay. Few places on the planet still host stromatolites forming under natural conditions today. Mexican scientists Valeria Souza and Luis Eguiarte made that discovery, turning a quiet desert valley into a living laboratory. Their work found more bacterial diversity in a single pool than scientists had documented across China’s entire Pearl River. The find helped convince Mexico to take the area’s protection more seriously. Protection came just in time. Decades of irrigation for alfalfa farming, much of it feeding dairy operations, drained the aquifer feeding the pozas. Nearly 90 percent of the valley’s surface water has disappeared since the 1960s. Churince, once the basin’s largest lagoon, dried up completely in 2016. That loss sparked a wave of local action. In 2018, conservationists won a court order forcing officials to close a canal draining two major pools. The ruling marked a turning point for regional water policy. Fundación Pro Cuatrociénegas has since built on that momentum, becoming the driving force behind on-the-ground Cuatro Ciénegas conservation. The nonprofit works to protect the valley’s water, restore native habitat, and support ranching methods that use less water. Its programs also train local students in environmental science, turning former skeptics into active partners in the valley’s recovery. That shift in local support matters. Many families once saw conservation as a threat to their livelihoods. Years of education and dialogue changed that view for many residents, who now see healthy pozas as tied to their own future. The clearest sign of progress arrived in December 2025. Forty-four American bison arrived at a reserve called El Santuario in Coahuila, marking a major step in Cuatro Ciénegas conservation efforts. The animals came from a managed herd at Rancho El Uno in Chihuahua’s Janos Biosphere Reserve, overseen by the conservation group Cuenca Los Ojos. American bison graze on restored grassland in Coahuila, part of a new Cuatro Ciénegas conservation effort to bring the keystone species back to northern Mexico. Photo courtesy of Fundación Pro Cuatrociénegas . Bison do more than roam grasslands. Their grazing improves soil structure and helps native plants recover. Unlike cattle, bison tolerate drought well, making them a natural fit for a region growing hotter and drier. The project brought together Mexico’s environment ministry, SEMARNAT, along with its national parks commission, CONANP, and several conservation groups. Fundación Pro Cuatrociénegas partnered with the N’dee/N’nee/Ndé Indigenous nation to open reserve land for the herd. The Mexican Fund for the Conservation of Nature also supported the effort, reflecting the broad coalition needed to pull off a reintroduction of this scale. Officials involved called the partnership a model for Cuatro Ciénegas conservation going forward. Government agencies, scientists, ranchers, and Indigenous communities rarely align this closely. Their shared success offers a template other desert regions could follow. Cuatro Ciénegas conservation still faces real challenges. Water rights in Mexico remain tangled in overlapping laws, and some irrigation canals draining the basin remain open. Full recovery of dried lagoons like Churince could take years, if it happens at all. Even so, the signs of resilience are hard to ignore. Researchers have found that dormant microbes can survive in dry mud for years, springing back to life once water returns. A desert valley that nearly vanished is showing what patient, collaborative Cuatro Ciénegas conservation can achieve. Scientists study its microbes, ranchers adjust old habits, students learn to protect their backyard, and American bison once again roam land shaped by their ancestors. What happens next in Cuatro Ciénegas may show the rest of the world how to save a dying ecosystem before it is too late. The post Cuatro Ciénegas Conservation Restores Mexico’s Ancient Desert Oasis appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Urban Food Forest Transforms Singapore’s Skyscrapers into Edible Landscapes Reading Time: 3 minutes An urban food forest thrives 51 floors above Singapore’s streets, proving hyperdense cities can grow far more than ornamental greenery. Permaculture educator Andrew Millison traveled to Singapore to answer a deceptively simple question: how much food, greenery, and habitat can a hyperdense urban environment actually produce? What he found reshaped his understanding of what cities can grow. At the top of one Singapore skyscraper sits what is described as the world’s highest rooftop farm, an urban food forest producing roughly a ton of organic food annually on the 51st floor. Bananas, mulberries, star fruit, and water apples grow alongside pumpkin vines. Bees pollinate crops despite the extreme elevation, including kadong , a native fruit with a tart, green-apple flavor whose edible leaves are traditionally used in local salads. A nearby miracle berry temporarily transforms sour flavors into sweet ones, delighting visitors encountering the effect for the first time. Unlike conventional rooftop farms arranged in single horizontal rows of vegetables, this urban food forest layers vertically within a tight footprint. Tree layers rise above shrub layers, herbs fill the understory, and vines climb through the structure, creating a legitimate multi-tiered food production system rather than a novelty garden. The restaurant sourcing from this rooftop describes the space as inseparable from its culinary philosophy, using every part of each harvest to minimize waste while drawing creative inspiration directly from what grows above the kitchen. Beyond this single example, Millison explored how urban food forest principles could scale across Singapore’s built environment. The island nation has almost no farmland and imports nearly all of its food, yet government policy already mandates extensive greenery integration. A landscape replacement policy requires developers to replace any land they build on with equivalent greenery elsewhere on the structure, driving widespread adoption of vertical gardens and rooftop plantings across the city. One striking example of this policy in action covers roughly 200% of its building footprint in combined horizontal and vertical greenery, effectively treating the high-rise as a small mountain, with the ground extending upward through multiple stories. The landscape architect behind the design explained that root space is the central engineering challenge, requiring sufficient soil depth or widened planters, root barriers to prevent structural damage, built-in drainage systems, maintenance walkways, and anchor cables to stabilize mature tree canopies as they grow denser over time. Currently, Singapore maintains roughly 2,000 hectares of green rooftop space, but most of this greenery consists of exotic ornamental plants rather than food-producing species. The country spends approximately one billion dollars annually managing this urban vegetation. Replacing ornamental plantings with productive alternatives, while maintaining the same underlying infrastructure, could transform this investment into a genuine urban food forest network spanning the entire city, rather than a purely decorative one. Singapore’s landscape replacement policy has created roughly 2,000 hectares of green rooftop space citywide, with Edible Garden City working to transform this largely ornamental urban food forest infrastructure into a genuine perennial food production network using resilient native and traditional crops. Photo by Cyrill on Pexels. Edible Garden City, a Singapore-based urban farming social enterprise, is actively developing the plant genetics needed to make this transition possible. At Gardens by the Bay, the organization experiments with diversified, multi-tiered plantings that move away from monoculture rows toward genuine food forest design. This approach reduces pest pressure by diluting concentrated crops across diverse species, minimizes pesticide use, and incorporates flowering plants that attract pollinators while producing edible blooms. Perennial plants form the backbone of this urban food forest model, since street-side and terrace plantings cannot practically be tilled and replanted annually like conventional vegetable plots. Species proven successful at the test site are introduced to industry partners and community gardens, spreading resilient, low-maintenance crops including lemongrass, pandan, cassava, sweet potato, and Brazilian spinach, alongside traditional vegetables once grown by earlier generations before industrial food systems replaced them. Singapore currently allocates only about 1% of its land to farming, yet its extensive rooftop and vertical greening infrastructure suggests far greater capacity remains untapped. The research, plant trials, and structural engineering needed to convert ornamental cityscapes into a genuine urban food forest have already been completed and proven at scale within the city itself, requiring policy rather than new invention for wider implementation. What makes Singapore’s example significant extends beyond any single rooftop or building. The city demonstrates that food production and dense urban living are not inherently incompatible, provided cities are willing to reimagine landscaping budgets, structural design, and plant selection around productivity rather than appearance alone. An urban food forest at this scale offers a template other hyperdense cities worldwide could adapt, transforming skylines already covered in decorative greenery into genuine sources of food, habitat, and community resilience. The post Urban Food Forest Transforms Singapore’s Skyscrapers into Edible Landscapes appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Emanuel Kuntzelman has a special relationship with trees. Sitting in an apple tree at the early age of six, he decided to dedicate his life to serving the universe. Under an oak in college, he formulated an idea to unite people in a common purpose. Reading under a weeping willow, the name Holomovement came to him for that common purpose, a movement he later helped realize. People also appeared along the way as if on cue to point him in a direction when he didn’t know which way he was going. “Sometimes the universe makes things so easy for us — if you're on that quest for truth, and you're willing to say it here and there.” Emanuel believes each person has a calling, a purpose, and trees and people are there to help us as long as we keep learning and seeking. In doing so, all can join in the Holomovement “to unite humanity through our collective purpose.”

items.descriptionOriginal: In November 2018, conservationists working in North Bengal's Dooars region raised an alarm about a barrier that was increasingly obstructing elephants: razor-sharp fencing around tea estates. The Wildlife Trust of India (WTI) reported on a series of stakeholder meetings organised by its conservation partner, the Society for Protecting Ophiofauna and Animal Rights (SPOAR), between 11 and 16 November that year. It described how randomly installed razor-blade fencing was forcing elephant herds to divert from their usual routes. The organisation reported that the sharp wires caused serious injuries to elephants and other wildlife, and that some animals died while attempting to cross the fences. The report did not identify individual animals or provide a tally of razor-wire injuries . But it highlighted a problem that extended beyond the fences themselves: when elephants could no longer follow familiar routes, their movement could bring them into closer contact with people. In August 2026, WTI and SPOAR brought tea estate representatives, government agencies and conservation organisations together in Chalsa, Jalpaiguri, to discuss elephant-friendly management. Photograph: (csmonitor) Seven years later, a reassessment by WTI and SPOAR would offer a measurable indication of how much the landscape had changed. Between 2019 and 2026, the length of razor-wire fencing mapped across the assessed tea-estate landscape fell from approximately 134.7 km to 34.8 km, a reduction of 74.2%. The change followed years of engagement with tea estate management, local communities and government agencies. It also raised a question: how much safer can an elephant's journey become when a landscape begins to accommodate its movement? A corridor is not always a forest Across North Bengal's Terai and Duars, elephant movement does not stop at the edge of a forest. Routes run through forest patches, tea plantations, worker settlements, roads and railway lines. These connections allow elephants to move between habitats in search of food, water and space. But when land is divided by fences, trenches and other obstacles, a familiar passage can become difficult or dangerous to navigate. For tea estates, fencing may be intended to protect workers, crops and property. Yet barriers placed across elephant movement routes can also redirect herds towards labour lines, roads and settlements, creating risks for people and wildlife alike. To understand the extent of the problem, WTI and SPOAR conducted a year-long field survey in 2019 across eight identified elephant corridors in North Bengal. The survey documented how elephants used tea estates and identified barriers that could impede their movement. From a survey to a shared commitment The findings became the starting point for discussions with those managing the landscape. On World Elephant Day in August 2019, nearly 50 representatives from tea estates, the Forest Department , tea associations, the administration and conservation organisations gathered for a consultative workshop on securing elephant passage through tea gardens. The discussions focused on practical measures such as identifying problematic barriers, keeping movement routes open and reducing losses for both people and elephants. Camera trap footage of a wild #elephant herd crossing the Apalchand-Kalimpong corridor via the Meenglass Tea Estate in North Bengal. These cameras were installed by WTI's Green Corridor Champion (GCC) partner in the landscape, @SPOAR_India https://t.co/ZF4RgSGE3a — Wildlife Trust of India (@wti_org_india) November 22, 2024 Some tea estate representatives shared examples of areas being left open for elephants. Others discussed commitments to remove existing razor wire or to avoid installing it in the future. WTI, SPOAR, the Forest Department and tea estate management continued engaging with the landscape, while awareness initiatives helped workers and residents understand elephant movement and the risks posed by obstructed routes. What changed between 2019 and 2026? A reassessment by WTI and SPOAR in 2026 offered a way to measure changes in the fencing landscape. In 2019, the survey had mapped 291.7 km of fencing across the assessed area. By 2026, the total had fallen to 104.5 km. The decline in razor-wire fencing was particularly notable in 2026: from 134.7 km to 34.8 km. However, the figures do not mean that all the missing fencing was deliberately removed. WTI's account attributes the reduction to a combination of removal, deterioration and fencing not being reinstalled. Nor do the figures establish how many elephant injuries or h uman-elephant encounters have been prevented. They measure a change in the physical barriers across the landscape, not a verified reduction in casualties. Still, the reassessment suggests that estate practices have changed over time, following sustained engagement and discussions about safer elephant movement. The next danger is overhead The same reassessment identified another concern: low-hanging electrical infrastructure. The survey documented 54 power lines below a height of 13 feet, with 47.4% hanging below 10 feet. These were flagged as serious hazards to elephants. An elephant may be able to move past a fence only to encounter a low electrical line or another obstacle along its route. The findings are intended to guide joint verification and corrective action involving tea estate management, the Forest Department, the West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Company Limited (WBSEDCL) and conservation partners. A charter for coexistence In August 2026, WTI and SPOAR brought tea estate representatives, government agencies and conservation organisations together in Chalsa, Jalpaiguri, to discuss elephant-friendly management. The consultation introduced the Elephant-Friendly Tea Estate Charter. The proposed framework focuses on keeping known elephant routes open, reviewing hazardous fencing , improving electrical safety, preparing workers and residents for encounters, managing crowds and strengthening monitoring. The fall from 134.7 km to 34.8 km of razor-wire fencing is a measurable change. It is not, on its own, proof that elephants are safer. Establishing that will require continued monitoring of injuries, deaths, movement patterns and encounters with people. Sources: 'SPOAR lobbies to Mitigate Human-Elephant Conflict in Elephant Corridors of Dooars in Northern West Bengal' : By WTI 'From Commitments to Change: How North Bengal's Tea Estates are Making Space for Elephants' : By Upasana Ganguly, Published on 8 October 2026
