items.descriptionOriginal: "Earlier, it was very difficult for me," says Bengaluru resident Rashmi Sampath, recalling every family outing with her 16-year-old daughter, Deeksha, who has spinal muscular atrophy. "She weighs 55 kilograms, and lifting her into the car was exhausting. But now, since the seat rotates 90 degrees, it is very comfortable." The difference has been more than convenience. A journey that once demanded careful planning, physical effort, and frequent compromises has become something the family can look forward to. Last year, they drove nearly 1,000 kilometres from Bengaluru to Kanyakumari without the travel itself becoming an obstacle. "She was very comfortable throughout," Rashmi says. "We took just two breaks. She could even sleep on the seat. Earlier, we couldn't have imagined travelling such a long distance like this." For millions of Indians living with disabilities or age-related mobility challenges, the hardest part of a journey often begins before the vehicle even starts moving. Getting into a car can require multiple people, unsafe lifting techniques, or simply deciding that the trip isn't worth the effort. It is this overlooked challenge that Bengaluru-based TRUE Assistive Technology set out to address. Founded by engineers Naina Padaki and Anand Kutre, the company designs assistive mobility solutions, including swivel seats, portable ramps, transfer systems, and wheelchair-accessible vehicle modifications, that make everyday travel safer and more accessible. TurnPlus rotates towards the car door, making it easier for passengers to get in and out with less physical strain. Since beginning its journey, the company says it has enabled mobility for over 1,000 users across India, supporting people with conditions ranging from paralysis and Parkinson's disease to post-polio complications and age-related mobility issues. A project that uncovered a larger problem Neither Naina nor Anand had initially planned to build an assistive technology company. Both spent over two decades working as engineers — Naina in software and compliance engineering, Anand in the automotive sector. Their journey into accessible mobility began unexpectedly in 2013, when Toyota approached them with a project to design a swivel seat for the Corolla Altis. The prototype was showcased at an auto show, but it failed to gain traction because of its high cost. "We went on to see how we could bring the solution to the Indian market," recalls Naina. Naina Padaki and Anand Kutre spent years developing mobility solutions that work with existing cars, without permanent modifications. The idea had also been shaped by another experience. Having lived in the United States before returning to India, the couple had seen people with disabilities participating independently in everyday life. "We had seen a lot of people in the US who were disabled but still living day-to-day life with full potential. We thought we should do something similar in India," she says. The path, however, was anything but straightforward. Without external funding, they bootstrapped the venture using income from consulting assignments. "Sometimes we had money but no people, and sometimes we had people but no funds," Anand recalls. "That's why it took about four years to bring the whole thing together." Interest slowly began building after an article about their work led families to reach out directly. Once they had served their first hundred customers, the founders realised there was a genuine demand for accessible mobility solutions in India. They expanded the design to fit nearly 80 percent of Indian car models before formally establishing TRUE Assistive Technology in 2022. Designing for Indian conditions As Anand began designing the products, one principle remained non-negotiable. "I didn't want to do anything like jugaad ," he says. Instead of permanently altering vehicles, the founders focused on creating solutions that could fit existing cars without affecting warranties, insurance, or resale value. Their flagship innovation, TurnPlus , is a patented swivel-seat mechanism that transforms an existing car seat into one that rotates outward. Rather than climbing or being lifted awkwardly into the vehicle, the passenger can first sit on the seat while it faces the door. The seat then swivels back into the cabin, making transfers smoother for senior citizens and people with conditions such as paralysis, Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis, post-polio complications and spinal injuries. Unlike many vehicle modifications that require structural changes, TurnPlus uses the car's existing seat. The mechanism is installed beneath it, allowing the seat to rotate without permanently altering the vehicle. TRUE Assistive Technology's portable ramps and transfer systems help wheelchair users navigate everyday barriers at home and on the move. "We didn't want people to leave their vehicles in garages for days," Naina explains. "You don't have to leave the vehicle with us. We bring the product to your doorstep." Because the original seat remains intact, the system can also be removed later if the owner decides to sell the vehicle, helping preserve its resale value. As they worked with more users, the founders realised that mobility challenges rarely end once someone gets into a car. Some wheelchair users needed a safer way to enter vehicles without being manually lifted. Others struggled with small staircases outside homes, clinics or public buildings. That led to the development of RamPlus , a lightweight portable ramp that can be carried in a vehicle and unfolded whenever a step or raised entrance blocks wheelchair access. The company later introduced TransPlus and HoistPlus , assistive systems and transferring devices that help caregivers lift and transfer people safely between wheelchairs, beds and vehicles, reducing physical strain for both users and families. For individuals who require more extensive support, TRUE also undertakes end-to-end vehicle modifications, including wheelchair ramps, hydraulic lifts and roof-height adjustments that convert standard vehicles into wheelchair-accessible ones. Before reaching users, every solution undergoes automotive safety testing, including front and rear crash tests, seat belt anchorage testing and durability assessments across temperatures ranging from minus 20 C to plus 60 C. The above tests are only for their products and not for vehicle modifications. "If I had to sell it across India , it had to be as reliable as the vehicle itself," Anand says. 'To be dependent on anybody is very painful' For Amritsar resident Jatin Gandotra, the technology came into his life after someone close to him suffered a stroke. His relative, now in her 60s, has severely restricted mobility and has spent nearly two years confined to bed. Jatin first discovered TRUE Assistive Technology while reading about a collaboration with Maruti Suzuki. "I found the technology very fascinating because my close relative is a stroke patient," he says. "I wanted to see how we could help her." After a relative suffered a stroke, Jatin Gandotra turned to accessible mobility to make family outings easier for her. Today, the family uses TurnPlus to help her get into the car more comfortably. Speaking about the emotional impact, Jatin says it goes far beyond the physical act of travelling. "To be dependent upon anybody is very, very painful," he says. "When you look through the patient's eyes, you can see that satisfaction that they are being cared for." For him, accessible mobility is ultimately about giving families more choices. "See what freedom you can bring to their life," he says. More than easier journeys The founders say stories like these continue to reinforce why they chose this path. Among their earliest customers was a woman who completed her PhD sooner because she could travel to college more frequently after installing the mobility solution. Another user, Vijay Kannan, fulfilled a long-held dream of driving his parents to Ayodhya after equipping his vehicle with an accessible ramp. "It's not just for the person using it," says Naina. "It helps the entire family. When they see how conveniently they can travel together, it changes things for everyone." Rashmi has witnessed that change firsthand. "The more we socialise these children, the happier they become," she says. "We shouldn't confine them to a single room." Her daughter now plans trips with the confidence many teenagers take for granted. "She says, 'We'll go anywhere. We'll explore this place.' She feels nothing is limited for her anymore." For families like Rashmi's, accessible mobility means fewer limitations, more shared experiences and the freedom to explore the world beyond their homes. According to the Census 2011, India is home to over 2.68 crore persons with disabilities, alongside a rapidly growing elderly population. Yet for many, something as ordinary as getting into a vehicle remains one of the biggest barriers to participating in everyday life. For families like Rashmi's and Jatin's, accessible mobility is not simply about modifying a car. It means visiting relatives without anxiety, travelling to school or work more comfortably, taking a long-awaited road trip, or stepping outside after months of staying indoors. Sometimes, restoring independence begins with making the first step into a vehicle a little easier. All images courtesy True Assistive Technology team

items.descriptionOriginal: Frankie Robertson had spent years helping families navigate premature birth. But nothing could have prepared her for sitting in a neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) with her own newborn daughter. Robertson had spent nearly a decade in leadership at March of Dimes, an organization whose work includes premature birth prevention. She had listened to parents’ stories, supported families and cried alongside mothers whose babies arrived too soon. But experiencing it herself was entirely different, revealing a gap often overlooked in conversations about pregnancy and childbirth: Mothers need care and support long after their babies arrive. It’s a critical need that philanthropists Olivia and Tom Walton are working to address. In September 2026, the couple announced an initial $100 million commitment over five years to Healthy Moms, Healthy Babies America , a national initiative aiming to cut the country’s maternal mortality rate in half by 2031. The investment is intended to help states expand promising approaches to maternal healthcare, particularly in rural and underserved communities where women face significant barriers to care. That includes expanding access to virtual appointments for women who live far from healthcare providers, training more midwives and community health workers, and strengthening postpartum care during the critical first year after childbirth. Olivia Walton's 0 million dollar commitment to maternal health Rather than creating an entirely new healthcare system, the initiative aims to help states put proven solutions into practice on a larger scale. The Waltons’ $100 million commitment will support state matching grants, partnerships, and improvements in healthcare infrastructure , with the goal of attracting additional public and private investment to sustain those efforts long after the initial five years. The ultimate measure of success is ambitious but straightforward: cutting the nation’s maternal mortality rate in half by 2031. The risks aren’t the same for every mother The United States has one of the highest maternal mortality rates among wealthy nations, and those risks aren’t shared equally. In 2024, non-Hispanic Black women were more than three times as likely to die from maternal causes as non-Hispanic white women, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention . This disparity is driven by a combination of systemic inequities in healthcare, including unequal access to quality prenatal and postpartum care, higher rates of certain underlying health conditions, and racial bias within the medical system. Research also shows that Black women’s concerns about their symptoms are sometimes dismissed or inadequately addressed by healthcare providers, potentially delaying lifesaving treatment. Geography matters, too. In rural communities, women may have to travel long distances to reach maternity care, making consistent prenatal and postpartum support difficult to access. Robertson, who has spent much of her career advocating for maternal health equity in Louisiana, believes improving outcomes also requires recognizing the circumstances women bring into pregnancy. Researchers call one aspect of this weathering : the cumulative physical toll of chronic stress, discrimination and systemic inequities. First proposed by public health researcher Arline Geronimus , the hypothesis explores how these experiences may contribute to poorer health outcomes over time. “It’s not simply about experiencing an isolated act of discrimination,” Robertson explained. “It’s about the overall effect, physiological toll of navigating just environments where you constantly have to confront, recover from inequities, or anticipate them.” Improving maternal health means looking beyond medical emergencies and recognizing the importance of consistent care, emotional support and access to resources before, during and after childbirth. What if better maternal care looked like this? Imagine a new mother returning home from the hospital, exhausted and overwhelmed. She’s anxious, struggling to sleep and unsure whether what she’s experiencing is a normal part of recovery or a sign that something is wrong. Now imagine someone comes to check on her. A postpartum home visit could help identify complications, answer questions and connect her with additional care. A midwife or community health worker could help another mother navigate appointments and find needed resources. A doula could provide emotional and practical support during childbirth, helping a woman understand her options and communicate her needs. Photo by Sarah Chai For mothers experiencing postpartum depression or anxiety, better access to mental health services could mean receiving help before symptoms become a crisis. These are among the approaches Healthy Moms, Healthy Babies America hopes to help states expand, building on programs already showing promise rather than starting from scratch. In October, the initiative announced its first state-level investments: $10 million each for Arkansas and Kentucky over five years. The grants are intended to strengthen maternal healthcare access, particularly in rural communities, through workforce development, postpartum support and improved maternal health data. The initiative hopes successful approaches can eventually be adopted in other states. Photo by Healthy Moms and Healthy Babies America The investments are still in their early stages, and it will take time to see how many families benefit and whether improvements can be sustained. The Waltons hope their commitment will also attract additional public and private funding to help effective services reach more communities beyond the initial five years. Helping mothers find joy, even when pregnancy doesn’t go as planned For Robertson, the importance of having someone looking out for mothers is deeply personal. Her experiences with postpartum recovery and her daughter’s premature birth inspired her to become a doula and establish Black Joy Doula Firm, a maternal health practice focused on supporting Black women through pregnancy and childbirth. Her goal is to help mothers facing unexpected complications manage their fears, understand their options and hold on to some of the joy they felt when they first imagined becoming parents. “I wanted to be a doula to work with moms who get this news and then show them how to protect their peace, help them with coping mechanisms, help them slow down, help them maintain that joy,” she explained. It’s a philosophy that reflects what meaningful maternal care should look like: someone who listens, recognizes when a mother needs help and understands that her well-being matters, too. Frankie Robertson at the Joyful Birth Advocacy session with expectant moms, partners, and families at the Community Baby Shower Robertson knows firsthand that even mothers with extensive knowledge and resources can find themselves overwhelmed by the unexpected. But protecting maternal health shouldn’t be a responsibility women carry alone. That’s what makes the Waltons’ investment an opportunity worth watching. If it helps more communities provide consistent, compassionate care, fewer mothers may have to navigate pregnancy and recovery without the support they deserve. Because when a baby arrives, a mother’s need for care doesn’t end. A healthier start for families begins with making sure someone is looking out for her, too. items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST DAILY Κάθε φθινόπωρο, κάτι συμβαίνει στο σώμα πριν συμβεί στο μυαλό. Η μυρωδιά του καπνού του ξύλου που παρασύρεται μέσα από ένα ραγισμένο παράθυρο, το ιδιαίτερο βάρος του φωτός του Οκτωβρίου που γέρνει στο πάτωμα, και ξαφνικά βρίσκεστε κάπου αλλού εντελώς, πίσω σε μια κουζίνα που δεν έχετε σκεφτεί εδώ και χρόνια ή αισθάνεστε τεταρτημένοι…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Every fall, something happens in the body before it happens in the mind. The smell of wood smoke drifting through a cracked window, the particular weight of October light slanting across the floor, and suddenly you’re somewhere else entirely, back in a kitchen you haven’t thought about in years, or feeling fourteen again for no apparent reason. Then you reach for the show you always watch this time of year, or the book with the cracked spine, and the evening softens. If that pull toward the familiar feels like something you should probably resist, it isn’t. Mental health professionals describe what happens each autumn as a predictable response to something real: the season changing registers in your nervous system as a small form of loss. The nostalgia that follows isn’t a distraction from fall; rather, it’s a part of how you move through it. Seasonal transitions are a form of small loss “Transitions mean something is changing, and change inherently means something is being lost,” says Janna Sayfie , L.M.S.W., co-founder and psychotherapist at Urban Mind Psychotherapy. “These ‘endings,’ however small, register to us as a form of loss. Looking back at something familiar anchors us to a sense of continuity and stability that we try to find when it feels like the ground is shifting beneath us.” That sense of loss takes different shapes for different people. For a lot of adults, the end of summer is the end of a looser way of moving through the week, a rhythm that’s harder to hold onto once September arrives. For parents, back-to-school season carries a weight that’s difficult to articulate, the passage of time made suddenly visible. And even without children in the picture, fall tends to settle in with a certain pressure attached: fresh starts implied, intentions expected, a vague sense that you should be doing more with the season than you are. Matt Sosnowsky , L.C.S.W., founder and psychotherapist at Philadelphia Talk Therapy, compares it to New Year’s, with all the same weight and none of the festivities. Your body recognizes fall before your brain does Part of why autumn nostalgia can feel so sudden and strange is that it often bypasses the thinking mind entirely. Sarah Haugh , L.M.H.C., founder of North Shore Professional Therapy, describes these as somatic memories: body-based recall that surfaces through sensory cues before any conscious recognition has kicked in. “Even before we know what these triggers remind us of, we’re swept away into visceral or nervous system memory,” Haugh says. She explains that this kind of implicit memory, a felt sense rather than a story you can retrieve, is the same part of the memory system that holds experiences from before we had language. Fall is unusually thick with these triggers. Wood smoke through a cracked window. The low angle of October light that somehow reads as different from September even when the temperature hasn’t shifted. Damp leaves, a candle you only bring out once a year, the sound of a school bus on a Tuesday morning. Any of these can pull a decade-old feeling into your chest before you’ve had a chance to ask where it came from. Why reruns feel better than something new Once the nervous system has registered the season as a kind of ending, it tends to steer toward the known. Sayfie puts it plainly: “Our brains tend to favor the predictable over the unpredictable.” We associate the unknown with risk, and when things are shifting, even in the small seasonal way they do every year, the familiar offers something new experiences can’t: you already know how it ends. Revisiting a favorite show or book is one way of meeting that need without quite naming it. The characters feel like company you trust. There’s no uncertainty about whether it will be good. Sosnowsky describes this as a form of safety-seeking, not a failure to engage with what’s ahead, but a way of steadying yourself so that you can. Nostalgia as a tool, not just a feeling Sosnowsky calls nostalgia “an engine for positive emotions,” pointing to research showing that wellbeing draws from three sources: anticipating the future, savoring the present, and looking back at the past. “Taking time to sink into a memory with gratitude and appreciation can help us elevate seminal experiences of joy, connection, and deep meaning,” he says. Nostalgia works that third channel. Don’t think of it as wallowing but as a return to something that still has something to give. Sometimes it carries grief alongside the warmth, which is its own kind of usefulness. A young person packing for college while their mind keeps wandering back to high school. A parent watching a kid start middle school while some part of them is still at kindergarten drop-off. Someone moving through a first round of holidays without a person they love. Looking backward in these moments isn’t getting stuck; it’s how the past gets processed. “Looking back, though sometimes difficult, helps us to integrate our past and make meaning from life,” Sosnowsky says. “In this way, we benefit from the people, places, and experiences that helped shape our lives by recognizing what remains a part of us as we move forward.” So when October settles in, and you find yourself scrolling down to the same playlist, reaching for the same worn-out novel, or clicking on the same show you’ve already seen more times than you can count, that pull isn’t something to override. It may be your nervous system holding onto who you are while the season changes around you. Remind yourself that you can gift yourself that return. At some point, when you’re ready, you can always put something new on. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post Fall nostalgia: why your nervous system reaches for reruns when autumn arrives first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM The world’s tallest wind turbine just reached full height in Germany. GICON ‘s pilot turbine in Schipkau, eastern Germany, now stands 365 meters (1,197 feet) tall from base to blade tip, making it Germany’s second-tallest structure after Berlin’s TV tower . Official commissioning is set for November. Higher altitude, stronger winds Higher up, winds are faster and more reliable. That translates to more hours of generation per year, and GICON says its design could produce roughly twice the electricity of a conventional turbine with the same rotor diameter. One thing to flag: that’s a claim about cumulative generation over time, not rated power. The turbine’s rated capacity is 3.8 megawatts; future versions are designed to go past seven. The rotor hub sits 300 meters (984 feet) above the ground. Building that high required rethinking construction. A crane capable of reaching 1,197 feet wasn’t realistic, so GICON used a telescoping tower instead. A specialized lifting system raised an inner tower through a surrounding lattice structure, then locked it at full extension. “365 meters – this is an overwhelming moment for our entire team,” said GICON founder and CEO Jochen Großmann. “What was long a challenging idea and then an equally challenging construction project now stands as a globally unique facility in Schipkau.” A second tier for existing wind farms GICON and its funder, Germany’s Federal Agency for Disruptive Innovation (SPRIND), aren’t pitching these turbines as replacements for existing wind farms. The plan is to stack them above. A “second tier” of tall turbines with their rotors spinning above those of conventional turbines already in the ground, adding generation without touching any new land. Germany’s existing wind farms could potentially fit up to 4,000 of them, per the companies’ own estimate. That’s a significant amount of added capacity without a single new wind farm permit. The Schipkau turbine is still a pilot, and the yield projections haven’t been proven in operation yet. GICON and SPRIND are in talks with wind energy companies about commercialization, with series production as the goal. Everything depends on what the numbers look like once it’s running. items.description: Ένα παντρεμένο ζευγάρι από την Καλιφόρνια έχει κάνει αποστολή του να φωτογραφίσει και τα 40 είδη άγριων γατών στη Γη — και έχουν μόνο ένα ακόμα μπροστά τους. items.descriptionOriginal: A married California couple has made it their mission to photograph all 40 wild cat species on Earth — and they only have one more to go. The stunning images serve to raise awareness about the animals, many of which are vulnerable or endangered. So far, Sebastian Kennerknecht and Rachel Tobias have traveled to 33 countries across five continents and photographed 39 species in the Felidae family, often using camera traps in forests, deserts, and grasslands where the elusive cats roam. SWNS / Sebastian Kennerknecht The San Francisco-based duo has captured images of a cheetah in Tanzania, a tiger in India, and an ocelot in Panama. The only species they have yet to cross off the list is the northern oncilla, found in Central America. It’s a rarely seen animal, and one of smallest wild cats in the Americas. View this post on Instagram Kennerknecht, 41, has been photographing cats since college: He studied ecology at the University of California, Santa Cruz, to understand animals and became particularly interested in bobcats. Tobias, 37, grew up loving wildlife and was always drawn to the ocean and photography. The two met online, and they instantly connected over their love of nature. Fittingly, their first date was searching for bobcats. SWNS / Sebastian Kennerknecht In 2024, Kennerknecht realized he had photos of 30 of the world’s wild cats, so he and Tobias decided to go for the full 40. In addition to photography, the couple run cat expeditions together, taking out small groups to observe the felines in their natural habitat and learn how to photograph them. They’ve raised hundreds of thousands of dollars through their work. One photo of a Borneo Bay cat brought in $120,000 for conservation efforts, and they collected around $70,000 per year for five years to protect lion species in Zambia’s Kafue National Park. They are partnered with Panthera, the world’s leading wild cat conservation organization. Kennerknecht told Talk to the Press that the couple’s work is “99% frustration and 1% joy,” noting that they’ve seen elephants crush their expensive camera traps, insects get into them, and humidity fog up lenses, rendering images unusable. “We set up a studio in the forest,” Tobias explained, adding: “In Malaysia, we set up six traps; we had to sleep in the jungle full of bugs and carry 60 pounds of gear.” SWNS / Sebastian Kennerknecht Despite the project’s challenges, the couple is dedicated to ethical photography. They don’t use any bait or lures to attract the cats towards the cameras, so they can observe their natural behavior. “It’s much more successful for telling a story about the species,” said Tobias. “Telling a story between the viewer and the animal is really powerful for conservation.” SWNS / Sebastian Kennerknecht A large part of their aim is to introduce the world to the 33 small wild cat species that are relatively unknown, so more can be done to protect them. “If you protect small cats, you protect big cats,” she added. The pair also wants to prove humans can coexist with big and small wild cats. “There are lots of human activities that might negatively impact cats without people knowing,” Tobias said. “People want to protect natural spaces and help with coexistence.” View this post on Instagram In Paraguay at the time of this writing, the team has had camera traps set up since April to capture the northern oncilla, with a ground crew frequently checking on them, but the cat has remained elusive. View this post on Instagram “It’s been pretty incredible,” Kennerknecht said, “but measuring local awareness has been tough.” They’ve set up billboards in areas with wild cats, featuring pictures of the local cats with the slogan, “I’m your neighbor.” SWNS / Sebastian Kennerknecht As for their favorite species, Kennerknecht said his is a bobcat, as that’s the feline that launched his photographic journey in Santa Cruz. But for Tobias: “There’s nothing more beautiful than a female leopard.” SWNS / Sebastian Kennerknecht Below are the cats they’ve photographed so far: Lion — Zambia Jaguar — Brazil Tiger — India Snow Leopard — Kyrgyzstan Leopard — Zambia Mainland Clouded Leopard — Malaysia Sunda Clouded Leopard — Malaysia African Golden Cat — Uganda Caracal — Yemen Serval — Tanzania Geoffroy’s Cat — Argentina Southern Oncila — Brazil Andean Mountain Cat- Argentina Pampas Cat- Bolivia Ocelot — Panama Margay — Panama Marbled Cat — Malaysia Borneo Bay Cat — Malaysia Asiatic Golden Cat — Indonesia Bobcat — U.S. Canada Lynx — Canada Eurasian Lynx — Kyrgyzstan Iberian Lynx — Spain Mountain Lion — Chile Cheetah — Tanzania Mainland Leopard Cat — Malaysia Sunda Leopard Cat — Malaysia Flat-Headed Cat — Malaysia Rusty-Spotted Cat — India Fishing Cat — Thailand Pallas’s Cat — Mongolia Jungle Cat — India Sand Cat — Western Sahara Black-footed Cat — South Africa European Wild Cat — Spain Afro-Asiatic Wild Cat — Botswana Chinese Mountain Cat — China Jaguarundi — Location Unconfirmed/South America Güiña — Location Unconfirmed/Chile/Argentina This article was originally written by William Ormes Roder for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets.

items.description: Η ζωή είναι λίγο πιο εύκολη τώρα για ένα νότιο κέρας στην Ολλανδία, χάρη στις τρισδιάστατες προθέσεις για το πάνω και το κάτω ράμφος του. Το πουλί στο μέγεθος της γαλοπούλας στον Βασιλικό Ζωολογικό Κήπο ARTIS του Άμστερνταμ υπέστη σοβαρό τραυματισμό που έσπασε και τα δύο τμήματα του λογαριασμού του και του άφησε δύο κολοβώματα, δυσκολεύοντάς του να πάρει φαγητό και να περιποιηθεί τον εαυτό του.…
items.descriptionOriginal: Life is a little easier now for a southern ground hornbill in the Netherlands, thanks to 3D-printed prostheses for his upper and lower beak. The turkey-sized bird at the ARTIS Amsterdam Royal Zoo suffered a severe injury that broke both sections of his bill and left him with two stumps, making it difficult for him to pick up food and groom himself. “He managed reasonably well with them, but he could no longer do everything a hornbill naturally does,” ARTIS veterinarian Martine van Zijll Langhout said in a press release . To improve his well-being, the team perfected custom prostheses that are “virtually identical” to his original beak. “A bird uses its beak all day long, to pick up food and, for example, to preen its plumage. Especially with a young bird that can still live to a very old age, we felt it was important to see if we could improve its quality of life,” van Zijll Langhout added. ARTIS Although several birds have been fitted with artificial beaks, this hornbill is believed to be the first to receive replacements for both the upper and lower beak. Should the beak parts continue to function well for the long-term, the team plans to publish a scientific paper detailing exactly how they created the prostheses, so veterinarians around the world can help similar patients. The process is technically complex, as every bird has a unique beak that perfectly aligns to its skull and other anatomy. If the shape isn’t exactly right for either part of the bill, the animal will struggle to use the prosthesis. To ensure their creation would be a success, van Zijll Langhout and her colleagues performed a CT scan of the bird’s head as well as the broken beak pieces. The prostheses were then 3D-printed from plastic, and orthopedic surgeons meticulously attached them using titanium components. View this post on Instagram One of the biggest risks with a procedure like this is that the bird will reject the new beak, which could result in the animal refusing to eat. The zoo staff planned for that possibility and were prepared to have the prostheses removed if need be — but so far, all is going well: The team reported the bird settled in right away after the beak attachment operation and even appeared to be “smiling” afterward . And the day following the surgery, he began eating independently. “That was an incredibly important moment for us,” said van Zijll Langhout. “He understood that he could use his beak and began to discover for himself what was possible with it.” RELATED: From a Dolphin’s Tail to a Bird’s Beak: 7 Innovative Prosthetics That Have Helped Animals

items.descriptionOriginal: The treatment delivers a light-sensitive algae protein to the retina. Paired with special goggles, it can restore limited vision and lasts for years. The patients sit perfectly still as a needle inches toward one of their eyes. After the injection, they’ll no longer be completely human. The syringe is filled with a gene therapy that installs a light-sensitive algae protein into failing retinas and could reboot some lost vision. When scientists first proposed using algae proteins to restore human eyesight, the idea seemed like science fiction. Could alien proteins integrate into our intricate visual system? Even if they did, could the brain translate the resulting signals into sight, rather than nonsensical bursts of light? A new study suggests yes, with caveats. The team treated people with retinitis pigmentosa, a genetic disease that gradually destroys light-sensing cells in the retina. Seven of ten patients showed improved light sensitivity. After patients donned goggles that deliver pulses of light to activate the algae proteins, the team tested their eyesight. Roughly half could reach for and touch objects or identify the orientation of a black bar, a common test of visual recovery. The treatment is still far from restoring full vision. What patients saw was too blurry and the field of view too narrow to discern texture or fine detail. The boundaries of objects looked squiggly. But those who responded to the treatment continued to improve over roughly five years. One participant, whose story made headlines in 2021 , can now recognize and count different objects, and white stripes on a crosswalk pop out. The study, called PIONEER , is an ambitious clinical trial combining gene therapy with optogenetics. The first goal was to assess safety, and it met the mark. Most participants experienced a brief bout of inflammation in the eye receiving the injection. The only patient to suffer a severe side effect was quickly treated with medication. The findings suggest the initial success wasn’t a fluke. The study “represents an important milestone for optogenetic vision restoration,” said study author Stefan Futterknecht at the Institute of Molecular and Clinical Ophthalmology Basel, in a press release . Setting Sights High Around two decades ago, Karl Deisseroth was hunting for new ways to control brain cells. Electrical bursts and chemicals, which are how neurons communicate, seemed like obvious choices. But nature had something stranger to offer: algae. Algae produce a protein called channelrhodopsin. When activated by light, the protein changes neuron activity using a mechanism that works similarly in mammalian cells. In a foundational paper , Deisseroth’s team inserted the protein into rodent neurons, and voilá—the neurons could now be controlled using light. The technology, called optogenetics, revolutionized neuroscience. By genetically tagging specific neurons with channelrhodopsin, scientists can now dial the cells’ activity up or down like a dimmer switch. Optogenetic experiments have revealed brain circuits that shape feelings, memory, and cognition with unprecedented precision. Researchers panning for more genes in different algae strains struck gold again. One channelrhodopsin variant they found, ChrimsonR, was particularly exciting. Unlike the classic version that’s activated by blue light, ChrimsonR responds to amber light, which penetrates tissues better and is less damaging. More recently, scientists have begun to use generative AI to redesign natural proteins to make them even more sensitive to light. “Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of,” said Per Svenningsson, Chair of the Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine, when the technology won the coveted prize this year. Still, it has mainly been considered a research tool. Light It Up Retinitis pigmentosa gradually robs people of their eyesight. Researchers have linked over 100 genetic variations to the condition, which kills off light-sensitive cells in the retina. “The replacement (or editing) of a single gene would not help most persons,” wrote Deisseroth in the New England Journal of Medicine . Instead, adding channelrhodopsin could offer a more universal solution by rewiring surviving neurons. Early successes bolstered the idea. In one study , scientists equipped cones—a type of retinal light-sensing cell—with channelrhodopsin in mice with retinitis pigmentosa. The therapy boosted their light sensitivity. It also reactivated cones that had stopped responding to light in human retina samples. The new study took a different approach. In advanced disease, cones may have already degenerated beyond the point at which they could be saved. So instead, the gene therapy targeted ganglion cells. These cells process signals from light-sensitive cells and pass that information to the brain, but don’t detect light themselves. Ganglion cells are, however, more resilient than cones. Add channelrhodopsin, and they could become substitute light sensors. The team packed genetic instructions for ChrimsonR into a harmless viral delivery system and injected it into the poorer seeing eye of 10 patients aged 40 to 73. All were legally blind, and each received one of three escalating doses. As the patients gradually built up levels of the algae protein in their eyes, the team faced another challenge: Translating visual scenes from the outside world into amber light that the engineered ganglion cells could recognize. They developed specialized goggles that look a bit like Apple’s Vision Pro. The goggles use a camera to scan the field of view thousands of times per second, monitoring for light changes in every pixel. When the device detects a change, it pulses amber light from that pixel into the eye. Because our eyes naturally dart around—often without us noticing—this dynamic method may better mimic normal vision. With the goggles on, 6 of 10 participants showed clinically meaningful improvement in light sensitivity, with more than a fourfold boost over baseline readings. One participant improved over 62-fold. Of the eight who agreed to further eyesight tests, roughly half could touch a notebook, grab a small staple box, and detect changes in a rotating bar. Of those who initially responded to the treatment, improvements lasted for years. Their brains also seemed to adapt to the alien light sensors. In one test, participants were asked to open or close their eyes while looking at a tumbler. Electrical brain signals related to vision were more coherent with eyes open, suggesting their perception depended on improved visual input. Any gene therapy carries risk. In an already worsening eye, inflammation and other side effects could cause further damage. Overall, the injection appeared relatively safe. Most participants experienced a temporary increase in eye pressure, but no detectable side effects throughout the body. The retina’s overall structure remained unchanged. One person suffered a blockage in a major eye artery that cleared within minutes after treatment with an FDA-approved eye drop. For now, the participants still can’t read or see faces. The therapy reaches only a fraction of their ganglion cells, making sharper vision harder to restore. More advanced versions of channelrhodopsin with greater light sensitivity may increase resolution. As for the hardware, the team is working on versions of the goggles that deliver more accurate and timely stimulation. Potential upgrades include an eye tracker, software to preprocess visual scenes, and even holographs . “Overall, although optogenetic methods have been developed primarily for basic science discovery,” wrote Deisseroth, they’re now heading towards “diverse therapeutic approaches.” The post Blind Patients Recover Partial Vision in Gene Therapy Trial appeared first on SingularityHub .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Where Can I Buy Peppermint Oil in Bulk? Suppliers and Buying Tips Reading Time: 3 minutes Where Can I Buy Peppermint Oil in Bulk? Suppliers and Buying Tips If you’re wondering, “Where can I buy peppermint oil in bulk?”, you have many options, including specialist wholesalers, ingredient distributors, and online marketplaces. Wholesale Botanics, Bulk Apothecary, and Bulk Natural Oils are just a few options worth considering. Walmart also lists larger bottles, while Amazon is another marketplace to check. The best starting point depends on the quantity of the product you need. A larger bottle may suit occasional soap making, but regular production calls for a reliable supplier. Where Can I Buy Peppermint Oil in Bulk? Specialist Suppliers for Bulk Peppermint Oil Consider these suppliers if you’re looking to buy peppermint oil in bulk. Wholesale Botanics Wholesale Botanics lists peppermint oil in 5, 25, 100, and 400-pound sizes, with custom quotes for larger quantities. Buyers have the option to choose between Mentha piperita and Mentha arvensis variants. Wholesale Botanics’ essential oil wholesale service offers consultations and sample packs, enabling you to discuss requirements before placing an order. You can also request a sample of the variant you want to purchase and confirm that testing documents are also provided. Bulk Apothecary Bulk Apothecary offers Japanese and Supreme peppermint oils in 5, 25, and 400-pound options. Shipping is calculated at checkout, so bear that in mind when purchasing. The smaller bottles allow you to test a variety before moving to a larger order. It helps to ask the company’s team about quantities beyond the listed options. New Directions Aromatics New Directions Aromatics offers its Peppermint Essential Oil (Supreme) in sizes that extend up to 396 pounds. This is the Mentha piperita variation, but it also has organic peppermint listings. Availability and dispatch arrangements differ between sizes, so it helps to confirm the selected pack is available. Bulk Natural Oils Bulk Natural Oils offer Piperita and Arvensis peppermint oils as well as organic options. The website lists a minimum spend of $150 on a combination of products. This option might suit businesses purchasing several ingredients together. Shay and Company Shay and Company is a good choice for smaller buys as it offers peppermint oil in smaller bottles in 5- and 10-pound sizes. Orders over 25 pounds require an email inquiry. Its Willamette Valley listing identifies Oregon as the origin, making it worth exploring when sourcing location matters to your product. Where Can I Buy Peppermint Oil in Bulk? Can You Buy on Amazon or Walmart? Walmart’s online listings include peppermint oil in 16-ounce bottles as well as one-gallon containers. This might suit smaller projects that don’t have a large wholesale commitment. Ensure that you check the individual seller, ingredients, and documentation instead of relying on the retailer’s name alone. If you want to purchase peppermint oil on Amazon, search for the quantity you need and check who sells and ships the product. Double-check that the listing describes essential oil and not fragrance oil, extract, or a diluted blend. Check the Oil Before Comparing Prices You would typically come across two main variants: Mentha piperita, which is peppermint, and Mentha arvensis, commonly called cornmint or Japanese peppermint. While both appear in peppermint ranges, their aromas and chemical profiles differ. Make sure that you match the botanical name to your formula instead of substituting whichever costs less. Where possible, request a certificate of analysis, an available batch-specific GC/MS report, and a safety data sheet. These cover specifications, handling hazards, and chemical composition. Request the relevant certification and confirmation of suitability for certified organic, food, or oral care application. Remember that “pure” alone doesn’t establish that an oil meets your requirements. Compare Delivered Cost and Order Size In your comparison between products, factor in shipping, taxes, import charges, and membership fees. Check whether the ounces refer to weight or fluid volume. For international orders, check that the selected quantity can actually be shipped to your country and clearly establish who pays the customs charges. Drum deliveries can involve freight shipping, so ask about unloading requirements as well. For occasional purchases, compare membership savings with subscription costs before signing up for a wholesale plan. Always test a sample in the finished product before scaling up, as peppermint oil can irritate skin, and cosmetics and candles require appropriate safety or performance testing. Confirm lead times, return conditions, and remaining shelf life before paying. Store the oil tightly sealed, away from heat and light, and order only what you can realistically use. Choosing Where to Buy Peppermint Oil in Bulk Amazon and Walmart are worth exploring if you want to purchase a large bottle as a one-time thing. For regular production, specialist suppliers give you more options to discuss specifications and quantities. Start by requesting a sample and a quote for the oil you need. Once you test it in your formula, you can decide whether the pricing, documentation, and availability make it a practical choice for future orders. The post Where Can I Buy Peppermint Oil in Bulk? Suppliers and Buying Tips appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: At 74, she decided to learn something new. Today, at 82, she rides a bike, drives a tractor and shares her adventures on social media! Sukhma’s journey began when a joke turned into a secret learning adventure between her and a family member. Away from the rest of the family, they practised together until she finally learnt to ride. Eight years later, she’s doing much more than riding a bike. She drives a tractor and runs her own social media page, sharing reels of herself riding. She didn’t learn because she had to. She learnt because she wanted to. Sukhma’s story reminds us that curiosity has no expiry date, and age doesn’t have to stop us from trying something we’ve always wanted to do. Συνέχισε να δημιουργεί και να πρωταγωνιστεί στο Pushpavalli και δημιούργησε το Motormouth για να δημιουργήσει περισσότερο χώρο για τις γυναικείες ιστορίες. Στο h…
items.descriptionOriginal: From being body-shamed in school to starring in a Netflix special, Sumukhi Suresh is turning the judgements women face into comedy. She gave up dancing for fear of being laughed at, but eventually found her voice through stand-up comedy. She went on to create and star in Pushpavalli and create Motormouth to make more space for women’s stories. In her Netflix special Hoemonal, Sumukhi tackles body image, dating, being single and the societal pressure on women to become mothers. Through humour, she brings conversations often brushed under the carpet into the spotlight, challenging the expectations women are constantly asked to live up to. Her journey is a reminder that you don’t have to shrink yourself to fit into someone else’s idea of who you should be. Sometimes, the most powerful way to challenge judgement is to laugh at it, speak up and tell your story on your own terms. What do you think women are judged unfairly for the most: their bodies, their age or being single? Tell us in the comments! #SumukhiSuresh #Hoemonal #StandUpComedy #BodyShaming #WomenInComedy #IndianComedy #BodyPositivity #SheTheChange #thebetterindia Subscribe Us Now : https://www.youtube.com/thebetterindia Follow us for more: Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/thebetterindia Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/thebetterindia/ Twitter: https://twitter.com/thebetterindia LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/thebetterindia/ Website: https://www.thebetterindia.com/

items.descriptionOriginal: Researchers in Spain have shown that a modular tire in which tread and casing are designed as separate pieces stays together while in use, provided that it’s properly inflated. “This is an encouraging step toward a more sustainable tire architecture, where the worn tread could potentially be replaced while the main tire structure is reused,” says study team member Farshad Afshari , a PhD researcher at Universidad Carlos III de Madrid (UC3M) and Universidad Politécnica de Madrid (UPM).. A modular automobile tire could be easier to recycle compared to conventional ones, which require time- and labor-intensive separation of rubber treads and sidewalls from steel belts and bead cores. It would also use materials more efficiently, since there would be less material to replace at any given time. A modular tire could also be better for the environment . Conventional rubber tires are a prominent source of microplastic pollution because tiny rubber particles degrade due to friction and enter the air and waterways. But the modular design could open up the possibility of making each component of the tire from safer and more easily recyclable materials. It’s a compelling idea in theory, but would the components of a modular tire actually stay together in practice? Afshari and his collaborators built a scaled-down prototype of their ECOTIRE modular tire concept, in which tread and casing are mechanically interlocked through a series of bumps and hollows like the two halves of a waffle iron. They tested the tire on a custom-built rolling test rig in the lab to see how the tire would fare while varying parameters such as load, turning radius, inflation pressure, and slip. items.descriptionOriginal: Imagine walking through Ziro's lush green forests, hearing birds call from the treetops and spotting colourful butterflies fluttering along the trail. Now imagine someone helping you put a name to the birds and butterflies you see! Most of us know Arunachal Pradesh's Ziro Valley for its famous music festival, sprawling paddy fields and beautiful landscapes . But its forests have a fascinating world of wildlife waiting to be explored. And this October, 630 people got a chance to discover it. At the valley's first Ziro Bird and Butterfly Festival, students, local residents and wildlife enthusiasts headed into the forests for four days of birdwatching, butterfly spotting, nature treks and hands-on learning with conservation experts. Organised by the Hapoli Forest Division alongside the 72nd Wildlife Week, the festival had a simple idea at heart: help people discover the wildlife around them and understand why it needs protecting. And what better place to begin than the forests themselves? Beyond the music, what makes Ziro's forests so special? Ziro's music may draw visitors from across the country, but its surrounding forests have plenty worth exploring, too. Located in Arunachal Pradesh's Lower Subansiri district , the valley is part of the biodiversity-rich Eastern Himalayan landscape, home to a remarkable variety of birds, butterflies, moths and other wildlife. Some are easy to spot. Others require a little patience, curiosity and someone who knows where to look. That's where the festival came in. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Ireland in India (@irelandinindia) Led by Divisional Forest Officer (DFO) Tilling Takar, with support from Deputy Commissioner Oli Perme, the initiative brought forest officials, scientists, schools and community organisations together. The idea was to help people get to know the wildlife living around them. After all, when you can recognise a bird by its call or identify a butterfly fluttering past, even a familiar walk can become an exciting discovery. And the organisers wanted children to be part of that experience from the very beginning. It started with paintbrushes, poems and a promise Before anyone headed into the forest, students from local schools were invited to participate in wildlife-painting, poetry and essay-writing competitions. Organised in collaboration with the Apatani Students' Union, these activities encouraged children to think about nature in their own creative ways. The opening programme at Saint Claret College brought together over 450 people and representatives from 19 local organisations. Together, they pledged to protect the valley's natural heritage. There were exhibitions showcasing local plants and animals, along with sessions on wildlife laws and how to stay safe around reptiles. Traditional music performances, boxing and martial arts demonstrations by local youth groups added to the celebrations. It was a lively start, bringing people of different ages and interests together around a shared love for nature. But the most exciting part was still ahead. From bird calls to butterfly trails, the real adventure begins On the second day, participants swapped the college grounds for a forest trail. Deputy Commissioner Oli Perme flagged off a trek from Manipolyang towards Pange Camp in Tale Wildlife Sanctuary. There was one important rule for the journey: keep it plastic-free and leave no waste behind. It was a practical reminder that enjoying nature comes with the responsibility of looking after it. At Pange Camp, wildlife experts introduced participants to the fascinating world of birds, butterflies and moths. There were exhibitions showcasing local plants and animals, along with sessions on wildlife laws and how to stay safe around reptiles. Photograph: (Nature Web) Specialists associated with Bird Count India, the Ashoka Trust for Research in Ecology and the Environment (ATREE), and the Wildlife Trust of India helped guide the activities. Over the final two days, participants joined early-morning birdwatching walks and butterfly-identification sessions along the Orchid Trail. Think about it. How often have you heard a bird calling from a tree but had no idea which one it was? Or spotted a beautiful butterfly without knowing anything about it? Here, participants had experts to help answer those questions. They learnt how to observe wildlife, recognise different species and understand the habitats these creatures depend on. The evenings brought research presentations and wildlife documentaries, helping connect what participants had seen outdoors with the importance of conservation. And there was plenty to learn. Birds, butterflies and moths all have important roles in nature. Many help plants reproduce through pollination, while others are part of the food chain. Studying them can also help scientists understand changes in forest habitats. Getting to know these creatures is one way to begin caring about their survival. The festival is over. But will the curiosity stay? After four days of activities, the festival concluded at Pange Camp, where competition winners and participants received certificates and awards. During the closing ceremony, DFO Tilling Takar expressed hope that the Ziro Bird and Butterfly Festival would become a regular part of Arunachal Pradesh's annual calendar. And that could make a meaningful difference. A four-day festival cannot protect an entire forest. Wildlife conservation needs continued effort from forest officials, researchers and the communities who share their surroundings with these creatures. But imagine what this experience could mean for a child who has learnt to identify a butterfly for the first time. The next time they spot one near their home, they might stop for a closer look. Someone who attended a birdwatching walk might become curious about the birds visiting their garden. And a traveller who learnt to leave no waste behind might carry that habit into their next forest adventure. These may seem like small things, but they are the kind of awareness the organisers hope to encourage. For now, Ziro will continue to draw visitors with its music, culture and breathtaking landscapes. But its newest festival has given people another reason to explore: to look up into the trees, follow a bird's call, pause for a butterfly and discover the wonderful wildlife that has been here all along. Source: 'Ziro Concludes First Bird and Butterfly Festival with 630 Participants' : By Arunachal24, Published on 10 October 2026 'Ziro Bird and Butterfly Festival begins' : By Arunachal Times, Published on 5 October 2026

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Greening Upwind of Cities Could Cool Megacities by Nearly Half a Degree Reading Time: 3 minutes Greening upwind of cities may offer a simple fix for urban heat, with new research showing strategically placed suburban forests can cool more than half a metropolitan area. Greening upwind of cities draws on a centuries-old planning idea. Researchers behind the new study found inspiration in traditional Chinese village design , where settlements were built backed by mountains, facing water, and surrounded by forest. That layout, known as the mountain-water-forest framework, helped villages stay naturally cooler. Shi-Jie Cao, director of the Center for Sustainable Built Environment at Southeast University in Nanjing, led the team exploring whether this ancient pattern could work for modern megacities. Many cities have already tried planting trees within urban cores to combat heat. Results have often fallen short, leaving some cities sweltering through increasingly hot summers despite those efforts. Cao’s team wondered if location mattered more than volume. Placing vegetation strategically outside a city, rather than scattering it inside, might produce better cooling results. Testing that idea required a different approach than simply counting trees planted downtown. Researchers built a computer model to simulate temperature changes in urban cores during hot summer days. They tested what would happen if suburban land upwind of two Chinese cities, Beijing and Shanghai, were converted into either forest or built-up development. The two cities offered contrasting geography, with Beijing sitting on a plain near mountains and Shanghai positioned along the coast. Results revealed a clear mechanism. Greening upwind of cities creates a mass of cooler air in the surrounding suburbs. Prevailing winds then carry that cooler air directly into the city, lowering temperatures across the urban core without requiring any changes inside city limits. Encouraged by these findings, researchers expanded their analysis to six additional megacities worldwide. Cairo, Kinshasa, São Paulo, Houston, Sydney, and London each represent vastly different climates and urban layouts. Testing across such varied conditions helped determine whether the cooling strategy held up beyond China’s borders. Across all eight cities studied, greening upwind of cities produced an average cooling effect of 0.4 degrees Celsius. That temperature drop applied across at least half of each city’s total area during peak summer heat. Exact results varied by location, but the underlying cooling pathway remained consistent everywhere researchers tested it. A city skyline rises beyond green suburban land, illustrating the wind pathway researchers studied when greening upwind of cities to reduce heat. Photo by Andy Lee on Pexels. Shanghai’s results illustrated the strategy’s limits alongside its potential. Cooling effects there were more modest and localized than in Beijing. Shanghai’s cooling sea breezes simply don’t align well with the areas where suburban trees could realistically be planted, reducing how effectively wind carries cooled air into the city. That finding carries an important caveat for city planners. Cao emphasized that this approach isn’t a blanket call for planting trees everywhere possible. Success depends on cities having consistent wind patterns and available space specifically positioned upwind of urban centers. Available space presents its own complication in many real-world settings. Suburban land upwind of major cities often already hosts housing developments, roads, and industrial facilities. Implementing this strategy would require creative, multi-functional land-use planning rather than simply clearing space for new forests. Local governments and other stakeholders would need to coordinate closely to make such changes possible. Getting buy-in across multiple jurisdictions and property owners adds real-world complexity that no climate model can capture. Political and logistical hurdles may prove just as challenging as the science itself. Beyond the specific temperature findings, Cao pointed to a broader lesson drawn from traditional village design. Cities benefit from thinking about vegetation, wind, topography, and water as one interconnected system rather than isolated green spaces scattered without coordination. That systems-level thinking represents a meaningful shift from how most urban cooling efforts currently operate. As global temperatures continue rising, cities will likely need every available tool to manage heat exposure for residents. Greening upwind of cities offers city planners a research-backed strategy that works with existing wind patterns rather than against them. The approach won’t work everywhere, but where geography cooperates, it could meaningfully ease the burden of urban heat without requiring dramatic changes to how city centers themselves are built. The post Greening Upwind of Cities Could Cool Megacities by Nearly Half a Degree appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.description: Αυτή η ιστορία δημοσιεύτηκε αρχικά από το The Understory. Όταν ήμουν φοιτήτρια στο Πανεπιστήμιο Cornell, διάβασα το βιβλίο «Fraternity Gang Rape» της Peggy Reeves Sanday για μια από τις τάξεις μου. Αυτό το βιβλίο γράφτηκε το 1990, που ήταν πολύ καιρό πριν. Αλλά και πάλι, ήταν; Σήμερα έβγαλα το βιβλίο από το ράφι μου. Ξεφυλλίζοντας το, παρατήρησα ένα νοσηρό patte…
items.descriptionOriginal: This story was originally published by The Understory . W hen I was a student at Cornell University, I read the book “Fraternity Gang Rape” by Peggy Reeves Sanday for one of my classes. That book was written in 1990, which was a long time ago. But then again, was it? I took the book off my shelf today. Paging through it, I noticed a sickening pattern. Parts of it felt ripped from the allegations coming out of the Cornell investigation today: Long nights saturated in alcohol. Women who spend days tunneling through layers of self-blame and shame before concluding they’ve been raped. Prosecutors who do not pursue charges. One example: a 19-year-old woman at a small Midwestern college drank alcohol, had sex with her boyfriend, “fell asleep and the next thing she knew she awoke with a man she didn’t know on top of her.” The more things change, apparently, the less any goddamn thing changes. But wait. At moments of despair like this, I have learned to stop and ask myself: Is it actually true that nothing has changed? There has been some extraordinary reporting done about the Cornell case, including by The Cornell Daily Sun , the student-run newspaper that gave me my first reporting job many years ago. But as usually happens with terrifying news stories, it’s very hard to figure out how to assess the threat — and find proven solutions. How typical was this case? Is sexual assault happening more or less over time? In other words, what is the denominator for whatever fresh horror we are worried about? Most importantly, what actually works to make sexual assault more rare? Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] To answer these questions, I’m going to uncomfortably set aside many other important questions — about accountability, humanity, legality, fairness and barbarity. Those are questions being interrogated in many other places. Here at The Understory, we’re trying to fill gaps that we see in traditional journalism. And one of those gaps is almost always context: How often are horrible things happening, and what can be done to make them more rare? These are the kinds of questions that we know humans need answered, in order to stay sane and take meaningful action in a time of relentless news battering us from near and far. So in that spirit, here is what I have learned so far: Rape reports have been declining in the U.S. since 2021. For 2025, the FBI estimates that 36 rape offenses were reported for every 100,000 people. The number of rapes that get reported to law enforcement each year has been gradually declining every year since 2021 , based on FBI data. This data comes with giant caveats, though. First, the number of actual sexual assaults is far higher than the number that get reported. (Only about 24 percent of sexual assaults were reported to authorities in 2024, according to the National Crime Victimization Survey .) Second, the FBI broadened its definition of rape in 2013, so it is hard to compare statistics going back any further than that. (The current definition includes “penetration, no matter how slight, of the vagina or anus with any body part or object, or oral penetration by a sex organ of another person, without the consent of the victim.”) In general, definitions of rape and sexual assault vary from place to place, making it harder than it should be to track changes over time and to find which cities, states or countries have unusually low (or high) rates. Sexual assault remains appallingly common on college campuses. In 2019, 13 percent of college students reported that they’d experienced some form of sexual assault since they’d arrived on campus. This category is broader than the FBI definition of rape; it includes nonconsensual penetration, attempted penetration, sexual touching by force or inability to consent. This data comes from the 181,752 students who responded to the 2019 Campus Climate Survey (conducted by the Association of American Universities). Importantly, the odds vary tremendously depending on who you are. The rate of sexual assault for women and transgender or nonbinary students was 20 percent — or four times the rate for men. Credit: Zhuoyao Song / Shutterstock The Cornell case is typical in some ways. In most campus sexual assaults, both the victim and the offender have consumed alcohol or drugs. Typically, rape victims are girls and very young women, and the vast majority of perpetrators are male. Victims usually know their perpetrators. At colleges, assaults primarily happen in residences or fraternity houses, according to the Campus Climate Survey (and Cornell’s own 2025 survey on sexual assault). And if a victim reports the offense, official responses are slow and unsatisfying, generally speaking. In all these ways, the Cornell case seems fairly typical. The Cornell case is atypical in other ways. Most sexual assault cases involve just one perpetrator, not multiple, making the Cornell allegations unusual. The other rarity is that the woman in this case reported the incident. And she has continued to push for a reckoning in a civil suit filed this year. To date, none of the accused men has been charged with a crime, and all have denied wrongdoing. Something can be done. And is being done. There is a lot of speculation happening right now about what leads to rape. Can we blame always-accessible, violent porn? Or campus hookup culture and frat-boy privilege? I have hunches about this, like everyone else. But I’m more interested in evidence of change. What actually works to reduce the number of rapes? And guess what? We now have some answers — answers we did not have when I was a student at Cornell. A 2014 study led by Laura Salazar at Georgia State University randomly assigned 743 college men to receive something called the RealConsent online training or a generic online health program. RealConsent featured six 30-minute modules about informed consent, intimate communication skills, the role of alcohol and male socialization in sexual violence, empathy for rape victims and bystander education. Six months later, the men who had received the special training reported intervening more often to stop a peer from engaging in sexually violent or inappropriate behavior. And, most importantly, they reported engaging in less sexual aggression themselves. “The odds for perpetrating among RealConsent participants were 73 percent lower than participants in the comparison condition,” according to the study. The attitudes of these men changed, too. They had greater empathy for rape victims, less hostility toward women and less comfort with other men’s inappropriate behaviors. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime Another program, which has been studied even more extensively, first appeared in The New England Journal of Medicine in 2015. The researchers, led by Charlene Senn at the University of Windsor, randomly assigned a group of first-year female students at three Canadian universities to receive a special training program for resisting sexual assault. The control group got general brochures on sexual assault instead. The training program, known as EAAA (for Enhanced Assess, Acknowledge, Act) featured four three-hour sessions. Students were taught how to assess risk, overcome emotional barriers in acknowledging danger and engage in effective verbal and physical self-defense. In all, 451 women received the EAAA training, and 442 women got the brochures. One year later, the researchers checked in on the women. Get this: women in the training group were 46 percent less likely to report having been raped than women in the control group. They were also 63 percent less likely to report attempted rapes. A subsequent study found that the benefits continued, even two years later. “The program significantly reduced the risk of completed and attempted rape, attempted coercion, and nonconsensual sexual contact over the entire follow-up period,” the study concluded, “yielding reductions between 30 percent and 64 percent at 2 years.” Women who still became victims of sexual violence, despite the training, were less likely to blame themselves than women in the control group. The U.S. Air Force Academy has adopted the program for first-year female cadets. So have many colleges, including Stanford University. Interestingly, Cornell University has tried out this program, too. Cornell facilitators piloted the EAAA program in 2019 and 2020. Then the pandemic came along and on-campus training stopped . Which means it’s unlikely that the students involved in the 2024 case got this training. Last year, Cornell revived the EAAA program with sorority members, as well as a parallel program for fraternity members. You might wonder: Why isn’t every high school student getting proven training like this? There are many reasons, but one reason is that too few people know about these options. When rapes get covered in the media, the reporting almost never includes research like this. It can feel like this kind of violence is inevitable — or the fault of some inherent flaw in the perpetrators. But violence is never inevitable. We, as a society, tend to focus on holding perpetrators accountable after the fact. And this is important, but tragically late. It would be great if laws were clearer, data collection was consistent and police and prosecutors had excellent, trauma-informed training. But it would be infinitely better to prevent more rapes from happening at all. “Despair demands less of us, it’s more predictable, and in a sad way safer,” Rebecca Solnit wrote in Hope in the Dark. “Authentic hope requires clarity — seeing the troubles in this world — and imagination, seeing what might lie beyond these situations that are perhaps not inevitable and immutable.” The post There Are Ways to Reduce Campus Sexual Assaults. Will More Colleges Use Them? appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .
