items.titleOriginal: From 5 Rhinos in 1984 to a Free-Ranging Experiment: What Dudhwa Is Teaching India
items.description: Για δεκαετίες, η διατήρηση των ρινόκερων στο καταφύγιο Dudhwa Tiger στο Uttar Pradesh χτίστηκε γύρω από προστατευμένα περιβόλια. Η προσέγγιση βοήθησε έναν πληθυσμό να ανακάμψει μετά την εξαφάνιση του είδους από την περιοχή, αλλά το επόμενο ερώτημα είναι πιο δύσκολο: μπορούν αυτά τα ζώα να ζήσουν, να αναπαραχθούν και να επιβιώσουν ως ένας πραγματικά ελεύθερος πληθυσμός σε μια λειτουργική γη Terai…
items.descriptionOriginal: For decades, rhino conservation in Dudhwa Tiger Reserve in Uttar Pradesh was built around protected enclosures. The approach helped a population recover after the species had disappeared from the region, but the next question is harder: can these animals live, breed and survive as a genuinely free-ranging population within a functioning Terai landscape? That question is now being tested. In March 2026, four greater one-horned rhinos were moved out of Dudhwa's fenced rehabilitation area into suitable grassland habitat in the reserve. The release took the number of mature rhinos free-ranging in Dudhwa to eight. The state's longer-term plan is to explore the feasibility of having 10 rhinos free-ranging as an initial phase of a wider conservation strategy. The latest census, conducted in June 2026, counted 53 rhinos in Dudhwa: 17 adult males, 25 adult females and 11 calves older than one year. Eight of them were among those released from the rehabilitation enclosures to improve genetic diversity and reduce inbreeding. But the significance of Dudhwa is not simply that there are more rhinos here than there were four decades ago. It is that the reserve is now becoming a test ground for a much larger question: what does it take to move from reintroduction to a resilient rhino population that can sustain itself across the wider Terai? From five rhinos to a larger experiment Dudhwa's rhino story began in 1984, when five rhinos were brought in as part of a reintroduction programme . The population has since grown, demonstrating that the Terai can once again support the species. But numbers alone can conceal the harder ecological questions. A population can grow while remaining vulnerable to genetic limitations, habitat pressures, disease, predation or a lack of connectivity with other populations. For a large herbivore such as the greater one-horned rhino, a viable future depends on much more than a protected patch of land. Amit Sharma, National Lead, Rhino Conservation at WWF India, sees the current phase in Dudhwa as a shift in that direction. "It is a great achievement for rhino conservation in Dudhwa as the rhinos have been allowed free range outside the enclosed area after almost four decades. Even though the initial plans are to release 10 rhinos, the objective should be more than releasing the 10 rhinos — it should be establishing an ecologically functional, demographically viable and genetically resilient free-ranging rhino population." The test now is whether the landscape can support the next generation, and the one after that, without conservation managers having to intervene constantly. What does a rhino need from a landscape? The Terai is a landscape of grasslands, wetlands, swamps, rivers and forests. Rhinos depend heavily on productive grasslands and water, while the mosaic of habitats allows them to feed, wallow and move through the landscape. Dudhwa already has much of this. "Dudhwa already has a successful reintroduction history and the basic ecological foundation : extensive terai grasslands, wetlands, swamps and riparian habitats are already in place," Sharma says. He points to a 2022 analysis which estimated that around 20% of Dudhwa was under grasslands and another 3% under wetlands, marshes and swamps, habitat classes that are critical for a flourishing rhino population. But having these habitats on a map is only the beginning. Instead of asking how Dudhwa can maintain one population, planners may eventually need to ask how Dudhwa, Valmiki, Nepal's Terai and other suitable habitats can function as parts of a larger rhino landscape. Photograph: (WWF India) "The natural water flows must be maintained, and perennial water sources must be secured to maintain the habitat standards. Further, the grassland extent and quality also must be managed to support a good herbivore population, especially for a mega-herbivore like the rhino." That makes habitat management one of the central lessons of Dudhwa. A rhino recovery programme cannot be separated from the health of the grassland itself. If grasslands degrade or natural water flows are disrupted, simply adding more rhinos will not solve the problem. And so the experiment in Dudhwa is also about learning how to manage a landscape before attempting to expand a population beyond it. The real test begins after release There is another difference between rhinos in an enclosure and rhinos that range freely. Once animals move through a larger landscape, conservation managers have to understand where they go, what they eat, how they reproduce, which calves survive and what causes mortality. Sharma says this requires long-term monitoring rather than periodic population counts alone. "For long-term viability of the population through active management, it will be necessary to undertake systematic monitoring for individual identification, reproductive success, calf survival, mortality, home-range use, forage availability and genetic diversity. Non-invasive DNA and technology-based approaches can strengthen population monitoring." In other words, Dudhwa's success will need to be measured in biological terms. Are females producing calves? Are those calves surviving? Are animals using suitable habitat? Is the population genetically healthy? Are rhinos able to expand their range? And can the population continue growing without continual human supplementation? These are the indicators that could determine whether Dudhwa's experience can inform future conservation in the Terai. The landscape does not end at Dudhwa The Terai does not follow state boundaries, and wildlife does not recognise them either. Dudhwa sits within a wider ecological system connected to other forests and protected areas in Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and Nepal. Valmiki Tiger Reserve in Bihar is another important rhino landscape, while rhinos also move across the India-Nepal border. A 2025 Wildlife Institute of India study on the Western Terai Arc Landscape highlighted how roads, development and other land-use changes can disrupt wildlife corridors, affecting the movement of large mammals and potentially isolating populations. Research and modelling under the project have specifically examined rhino and tiger habitat connectivity, and the areas where linear infrastructure could interfere with movement. For rhinos, that connectivity has consequences beyond movement. (1/3) Four greater one-horned rhinos have been released into the wild at Dudhwa Tiger Reserve, taking the free-ranging population to eight and strengthening conservation in India's Terai landscape. @moefcc @DudhwaTR @ManpowerGroupIn @experisitindia #WWFIndia https://t.co/vBt5uekU30 — WWF-India (@WWFINDIA) March 24, 2026 "A landscape-level approach is essential for the long-term recovery of rhinos in the Terai," Sharma says. "Rhinos do not recognise administrative boundaries, and the Katerniaghat–Bardia and Valmiki–Chitwan systems are ecologically interconnected." He points to a pattern already visible on the ground. "Studies have confirmed rhino movement across the India–Nepal border as a natural process to meet ecological requirements. Rhinos from Nepal are observed across the border on the Indian side at Pilibhit, Katerniaghat and Valmiki almost regularly." That changes the conservation question Instead of asking how Dudhwa can maintain one population, planners may eventually need to ask how Dudhwa, Valmiki, Nepal's Terai and other suitable habitats can function as parts of a larger rhino landscape. "It is thus essential to consider the entire area as one conservation unit and manage the rhino population as one single metapopulation or rather as a rhino landscape in the terai belt." But connectivity is not the only challenge. The same landscape that can support rhinos is also under pressure from infrastructure, human activity and climate-related changes. "The omnipresent risk to any rhino population is the threat of poaching arising out of the demand for the rhino horn and, to some extent, its body parts in the international market," Sharma says. But he points to another risk that may become harder to manage because it affects the habitat itself. "However, the predicted risk is the impact that a rapid change in the climate can exert in the region, which can lead to widespread effects in the fragile Himalayan system; the recent floods in Nepal during 2026 are indicative of the likely impacts." For rhinos, climate change is therefore not an abstract future threat. Changes in rainfall, flooding and water availability can alter the grasslands and wetlands on which the species depends. "The habitats in the terai are already under stress due to degradation and any deviation from the climatic pattern may result in drastic changes in the composition and condition of the habitats that may put the survival of the rhinos at risk." Then there is the human landscape around these habitats. "Again, due to multiple developments in the border areas and expansion of human activities, the connectivity with Nepal facilitating safe and active movement of rhinos and wildlife is under increasing threat. Any blockage in the natural connectivity will pose a huge challenge for rhino conservation in the entire Terai region." That means expanding rhino populations will require more than habitat protection. It will also require communities to be part of the conservation landscape. What happens when rhinos meet tigers? Dudhwa has another lesson to offer, and it is less comfortable. In March 2026, a 30-year-old female rhino named Rajeshwari was found dead in a water body in the reserve, with a tiger on her carcass. A post-mortem confirmed that she had died from injuries sustained in the attack. Reports said two sets of tiger pugmarks were found near the site. The incident raised an obvious question: if Dudhwa is trying to build a larger free-ranging rhino population, what happens when those rhinos share the landscape with a strong tiger population? Sharma says predation is part of the ecological reality, but adult rhino predation remains unusual. Dudhwa sits within a wider ecological system connected to other forests and protected areas in Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and Nepal. Photograph: (Indian Express) "Tiger is an apex carnivore in the Indian forest, and it is quite natural for them to prey even on large animals like the rhino or the elephant." "In a park like Kaziranga, where tiger presence ten years back was not that dense, yet the rhinos falling prey to them was not uncommon. However, tigers preying on a healthy adult rhino are relatively rare, as it has been observed that they mostly attempt to attack the calves." For Dudhwa, however, the demographic consequences matter. "Rhino predation by tigers is not new to Dudhwa, and the death of the adult female rhino Rajeshwari in Dudhwa indicates that active predator–prey interactions are an integral component of managing a recovering rhino population within a tiger landscape with a high tiger population." But there is a limit to how much mortality a small or recovering population can absorb. "The rhino population in Dudhwa is limited and still aims for growth; as such, a high rate of predation will negatively impact the demography and population dynamics." Dudhwa's biggest lesson: release is only the beginning A rhino reintroduction cannot be treated as the finish line. "Dudhwa exemplifies a conservation story of return, resilience and the long road from reintroduction to rewilding," Sharma says. "The key lesson from Dudhwa is that reintroduction should be viewed as the beginning of population recovery; it teaches us to plan holistically to achieve a viable free-ranging population." A population of 50, 100 or 200 rhinos can remain vulnerable if it is isolated. For Sharma, resilience means several things happening at once. "The ability of the population to grow without continual human supplementation and connect naturally to be considered as a meta population including Nepal terai and communities to persist without perpetual intensive conflict will also be within the vision." That is why the 10 rhinos proposed for Dudhwa matter less as a number than as a beginning. The real test will come later, when rhinos are counted as members of a connected Terai population that can move, breed, survive, and coexist across a changing landscape.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News River Rights Movement in the UK Gains Ground as Communities Rally to Protect Local Waterways Reading Time: 3 minutes The river rights movement in the UK now connects around twenty grassroots groups working to give rivers legal standing. The river rights movement in the UK is growing steadily, uniting campaigners, co-ops, and community groups behind one shared goal. They want rivers to have real legal standing. Around twenty river groups now work together across England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland. The River Rights Network connects these local efforts under one umbrella. Instead of working in isolation, groups now share strategies, successes, and lessons learned. That collaboration has helped the river rights movement in the UK move faster than any single campaign could alone. Funding from an Arts and Humanities Research Council (AHRC) Curiosity grant has helped the network expand. The grant supports four events, each hosted by a different member group, giving campaigners a direct chance to learn from each other. The first major event took place in Cambridge in September 2024. Friends of the River Cam hosted a workshop focused on rights. A second workshop followed in Sheffield in April 2025, hosted by OPUS Independents, exploring how rivers and their communities get a genuine say in decisions. Network members also joined the March for Clean Water in November 2024. Thousands turned out to call for healthier rivers nationwide. That visibility helps keep the river rights movement in the UK on the national agenda. Local campaigns make up the backbone of this effort. Groups like Love Our Ouse, Friends of the Medway, and Sacred Severn each focus on a specific waterway. Others, including Voices of Water and the Bioregional Learning Centre, bring creative approaches to river advocacy. Love Our Ouse offers one of the clearest examples of what the river rights movement in the UK can achieve. The group helped develop the first Charter of Rights for a UK river to gain formal council backing, with the River Ouse in Sussex officially recognized as a living entity by the Lewes District Council. That milestone shows local advocacy can lead to real institutional change. The river rights movement in the UK reached a milestone when Love Our Ouse helped secure Lewes District Council’s formal recognition of the River Ouse in Sussex as a living entity, making it the first UK river charter to gain official council backing and proving that local advocacy can drive real institutional change. Photo by Mike Bird on Pexels. The Ouse case also highlights why this work matters. Data from the river tracker Top of the Poops recorded sewage pollution there 63 times in 2023 alone, exposing the waterway to 442 hours of contamination across four monitoring sites. Supporters hope the charter will help hold polluters accountable. Josh Levene, who leads the network’s Rivers of Hope project, has spent over 25 years working with river communities worldwide. He directed Love Our Ouse before taking on this wider role. His experience now helps guide new communities through similar processes. Rivers of Hope is the network’s flagship initiative for scaling up this work nationally. The project runs workshops with communities, catchment partnerships, and local councils to help people reconnect with their local river and explore what a rights-based approach could look like. The project follows five clear steps. It raises awareness about what river rights mean in practice and showcases tools, such as river charters and nature guardian programs, that communities can adapt. It also works to reconnect people with rivers they may have grown distant from. From there, Rivers of Hope helps communities weigh their options. Every river faces different pressures, so no single solution fits all. Finally, the project strengthens the broader movement, since each new charter adds weight to the next community’s case. This model already has global precedent to draw from. Rivers in New Zealand, India, and Ecuador have received forms of legal personhood in recent years. Campaigners behind the river rights movement in the UK are adapting those ideas to fit British law and British rivers. The stakes remain significant nationwide. Many English rivers face pollution from sewage overflows, agricultural runoff, and aging infrastructure. Giving rivers a stronger legal voice could change how those long-standing problems finally get addressed. Nearly 20 rivers, from the Dart in Devon to the Tyne in the northeast, now have active local campaigns tied to the network. Some focus on legal recognition, while others prioritize education or council engagement. All share the belief that rivers deserve protection as living systems, not just resources. The success at the River Ouse has already inspired similar efforts elsewhere in England. New groups are welcome to join the river rights movement in the UK at any point. The network continues to grow as more communities decide their rivers are worth fighting for. What began as scattered local campaigns has become a coordinated national effort. Communities are learning from each other, sharing tools, and building a stronger case together. As more rivers gain formal recognition, the movement’s influence on UK water policy looks set to grow. The post River Rights Movement in the UK Gains Ground as Communities Rally to Protect Local Waterways appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: When Daniel Zhang was nine, he watched his grandmother lose her hair to chemotherapy and couldn't understand why medicine could look so much like harm. That confusion never left him, and when his grandfather was later diagnosed with cancer -- and Zhang saw the same bewilderment on his seven-year-old sister's face -- it became the seed of something purposeful. He and his classmate Zachary Tou, both 17, built *Tumor Tactics*, a Pok mon-inspired card game that teaches children cancer biology through the same mechanics they already love -- where, as Zhang explains, "chemotherapy can be a really powerful treatment, but you have to roll a die to determine how effective it is, and you might have to skip your next turn to recover from its side effects." What began as one boy trying to translate grief into language a child could hold has grown into a student-led nonprofit running workshops across San Diego schools, reaching kids from kindergarten through eighth grade. Perhaps most quietly remarkable is what happens at the end of each session: Zhang and Tou open the floor for discussion, and children -- unbidden -- begin sharing their own family stories, needing not just explanation, but the invitation to be heard.

Διαβάστε το πρωτότυπο άρθρο εδώ. Τα σόλο ταξίδια αυξάνονται — και μια βιομηχανία…
items.descriptionOriginal: This article was written by Peter McGraw , a professor of marketing and psychology at the University of Colorado Boulder, for The Conversation — a nonprofit news organization dedicated to sharing the knowledge of researchers and scientists, under a Creative Commons license . Read the original article here . Solo travel is surging — and an industry still largely built for two is taking note. Google reported in April 2026 that online searches involving “solo travel” hit an all-time high this year, with queries for “women solo travel” reaching a 15-year peak. Hilton’s 2026 trends report found that 26% of travelers planned to take a trip alone this year, and that nearly half said they planned to add solo days to the front or back of a family trip. The issue isn’t new. In 1992, marketing researchers identified the solo consumer as an underserved market . But as tourism researchers have documented , the accommodation sector treats double occupancy as the default unit of consumption, which often slaps a “single supplement” charge on customers when they travel without a partner. The industry essentially penalizes travelers for arriving without a second body to fill the other half of a room they aren’t using. The reason why so many hotels, cruise lines, and tour operators still base prices on double occupancy is that their costs — the room, the berth, the coach seat, the guide — don’t fall by half when the second person fails to materialize. But the supplement isn’t just a pricing convention. It’s the clearest signal the industry sends about who it built the product for. I’m a scholar who studies what I call the solo economy : how institutions and markets adapt, or fail to adapt, to the rise of single living. I’ve written before about how retail and restaurants still design for pairs. Travel is further along than most in recognizing this cultural shift. It’s also a useful case because the industry has started on the easy part of the problem but barely touched the rest. Demographics Matter, but Not the Way You’d Think The broader shift toward solo living is real. In 2025, 39.7 million Americans lived alone . That’s 29% of all households, up from 20% in 1975. Married couples, meanwhile, fell to 47% of households from 66% 50 years earlier. Those numbers alone don’t explain solo travel. Some of that decline went to people living alone; some went to unmarried couples, who are still a party of two on a booking page. Married people take trips alone. Single people travel with friends, siblings and parents, and plenty of them have logged serious hours as an extra wheel. Living alone and vacationing alone are different behaviors with different causes. What connects them is the erosion of a single assumption: that every adult arrives with a plus-one. That assumption is weakening at home, and it’s now encountering the booking page. Price Is the Easy Rung One response by the travel industry has been to shave the single supplement. For example, the tour operator Tauck announced this year that it’s waiving the single supplement on a class of its riverboat cabins across more than 250 European river cruise departures and reducing it by up to US$600 on 105 land departures. Another touring company has taken a more committed approach to adjusting its offerings: Aurora Expeditions sets aside 10 dedicated solo cabins on every sailing across its three ships, with no single supplement, through its 2026 and 2027 seasons. Then there’s Norwegian Cruise Line, which was early to the shift. In 2010, it introduced Studio staterooms aboard Norwegian Epic: small cabins designed for one passenger, sold at single-occupancy prices and arranged around a keycard-access Studio Lounge reserved for solo travelers. The trade-off is less private space, but at a price for one, with access to a room full of fellow travelers going it alone. Norwegian then expanded solo categories in 2024 from nine ships to its full 19-ship fleet. But on ships without Studios, much of the expansion was relabeling. Cruise Critic reported that standard double-occupancy rooms would likely be reclassified rather than retrofitted. And by Norwegian’s own account , the Studio Lounge is reserved for guests in Solo Studios — so the fleetwide solo categories come with the discount but not the room full of other solo travelers. That’s the difference between repricing and redesigning. The 2010 Studio was a purpose-built 100-square-foot (9 square-meter) cabin that cost Norwegian something to construct. The 2024 categories are, in many cases, the same rooms as before, with a new label and a discount. The solo traveler pays less than two people would, but it’s still more than half for a room sized and built for two. A cabin sold to one occupies the same space as a cabin sold to two, and the industry still counts berths. There’s a cleaner approach. Yotel sells a room type it calls Solo — 114 square feet (about 10 square meters) in New York City, maximum occupancy one, at the bottom of its price range. Nothing was subtracted to make it. It was built at that size, for that guest, and priced accordingly. That’s what designing for one looks like, and it’s rare enough that a tiny room counts as progress. alvarez—E+/Getty Images Many solo travelers seek control over their experiences and schedules, but they still seek a social component. Traveling Alone Doesn’t Mean Being Alone A common mistake in designing for solo travelers is assuming that solitude is the product. It isn’t. In the same 2026 data showing record interest in solo travel, Google found that searches for “travel groups” and “tour groups” also hit record highs . A Mastercard survey of more than 15,000 consumers across 11 countries found that 39% of international travelers had already taken a trip alone — and 7 in 10 international leisure travelers were interested in solo experiences built to connect them with like-minded people. The contradiction makes sense when you acknowledge that privacy and isolation are two different things. A person can want total control over where to go, when to eat, and when to return to the room — and still want company at dinner. The issue with double-occupancy pricing is that it assumes the customer brings their own company. But when only one person books, the operator has to address the pricing problem — whether or how to discount; and a product problem — how to supply a social component. Waiving a solo supplement solves the first issue, but it ignores the second. Norwegian understood this in 2010 by creating its lounge for solo travelers. The Pitch Is Easier When the Product Is for One For all these changes, travel advertising often still runs on couples: two glasses of wine, two lounge chairs, two silhouettes against a sunset. Sandals Resorts built an entire resort category around the premise. When solo travel does appear, it gets a different script. The traveler is adventurous, on a journey of self-discovery. AARP’s current solo-travel guide emphasizes personal growth and self-reliance. Even Norwegian closes its solo pitch by reassuring the reader that “you’re pretty good company.” The effect is to mark solo travel as exceptional at precisely the moment it stops being exceptional. Nobody reassures a couple that they will enjoy the balcony. Calling a solo traveler “brave” can be a compliment, but it can also reveal the assumption that traveling alone is abnormal, even when that’s changing. That all said, parts of the tourism industry have taken big steps over the past 15 years. But treating solo travelers as an audience rather than an accommodation is harder. It’s about selling them what they have already said they want: control over the trip, and access to other people, on their own terms. Marketing researchers named this opportunity in 1992. Thirty-four years later, the industry is still learning to build for one. Meanwhile, the solo traveler is standing at reception, holding a credit card, waiting for someone to design a room. items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Most building materials are designed to resist the elements, to stay sealed and unchanged for as long as possible. Respyre , a Dutch startup, is working from the opposite premise. The company has developed Mosscrete , a bioreceptive concrete coating that creates conditions for moss to grow directly on vertical surfaces, drawing moisture from rain and air without any soil or irrigation system. The science comes from research at Delft University of Technology , and since its commercial launch, Respyre has applied the technology across eight projects in Belgium and the Netherlands. How moss takes hold Moss doesn’t have roots in the conventional sense; it attaches to surfaces through rhizoids, tiny thread-like structures that cling to the material without penetrating or damaging it. Unlike a traditional green wall , which needs structural support for soil, a built-in watering system, and regular upkeep, Mosscrete sidesteps most of that. And because it’s applied as a coating rather than built in, it can go onto an existing facade just as easily as a new one. The material works especially well on blank or inaccessible walls where conventional planting isn’t an option, and Respyre has been using those spaces to test how the technology holds up under different real-world conditions. Eight buildings, different tests In Kortrijk, Belgium, 450 square meters (about 4,840 square feet) of a new industrial warehouse facade were coated with Mosscrete during construction and integrated with rainwater harvesting, keeping the whole system maintenance-free from day one. A 300-square-meter (about 3,230-square-foot) noise barrier in Hoofddorp, the Netherlands, is being used to test passive greening: moss growing from natural moisture alone, no watering involved. The porous structure of moss may also help absorb sound, which makes the noise barrier a natural fit for the technology. A 260-square-meter (about 2,800-square-foot) social housing facade in Purmerend was one of the first practical applications. Traditional greening options were rejected there as too expensive and maintenance-heavy, and the project helped Respyre work out how bioreceptive facades are best designed and applied. In Haarlem, a 313-square-meter (about 3,370-square-foot) commercial renovation combined Mosscrete with insulation, aiming to both green the facade and improve thermal performance. Research published in June 2026 in the journal Science of the Total Environment found the effect is moisture-dependent: wet moss creates a cooling effect through evaporation, while dry moss can overheat in direct sunlight. In Amsterdam, the technology is being tested on bridge piers where graffiti has been a persistent problem. Moss-covered surfaces are less appealing as targets, and since the site has no irrigation, the project is also tracking how moss develops under ordinary conditions of rain, shade, and humidity. Designing for change Respyre is betting on a different idea of what building materials should do. Most are made to resist change, to stay gray and sealed for decades. Mosscrete is made for the opposite: it works best when moss gradually takes over. Urban greening helps manage stormwater and heat in dense cities, and there’s evidence it supports local biodiversity too. But a building slowly covered in moss doesn’t look like neglect. It looks like something is alive there. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Pumpkin spice lattes, jack-o’-lanterns, and Thanksgiving pies : pumpkins are the unofficial mascots of fall. But behind their seasonal charm lies a deeper, more complicated story that winds through language, history, agriculture, and even a little insult comedy. “ Pumpkins are more popular than ever,” says Cindy Ott , associate professor of history at the University of Delaware and author of Pumpkin: The Curious History of an American Icon. But our obsession with this humble gourd, she notes, is tied less to flavor and more to a nostalgic longing for simpler, rural times. “People are buying these things, even pumpkin spice lattes, because of these attachments, these very old-fashioned ideas about reverence of the small family farm.” A name with roots that twist like a vine The word “pumpkin” has always been more conceptual than botanical. According to Logan Kistler , curator of archaeobotany at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of Natural History, the term refers to squash varieties bred to resemble the round, orange gourds we associate with fall. “Pumpkin isn’t exactly a botanical group,” he explains. Linguistically, the word has had quite a journey. Fiona McPherson of the Oxford English Dictionary traces it from the Greek pepon to the French pompon , which eventually morphed into the English “ pompion ” in the 1500s. “Pumpkin,” as we know it today, first appeared in print in 1647, ironically in reference to the meager diet of early settlers. But while the word took a European path, the plant itself is deeply American. Indigenous peoples across North, Central, and South America cultivated early pumpkin ancestors, domesticating different types of Cucurbita as far back as 10,000 years ago in Mexico. “Pumpkins are part of this genus Cucurbita,” says Kistler, noting that they were farmed widely throughout the Americas long before colonists arrived. From insult to endearment Surprisingly, it didn’t take long for the word “pumpkin” to go from dietary staple to verbal jab. By the late 1600s, it was being used as an insult. “It really did not take long for it to develop this figurative use,” says McPherson. Pumpkin became a shorthand for someone who was conceited, dim-witted, or full of hot air. Cindy Ott adds that gender played a role in the insult’s direction. For women, pumpkin imagery was linked to the body and “natural urges,” seen as a lack of refinement. For men, it implied an empty head. “It’s been used for politicians for hundreds of years,” she notes. A symbol of imagined agrarian purity By the late 19th century, the pumpkin was undergoing a cultural rehabilitation. It shifted from insult to affection, and from staple crop to nostalgic icon. “So Americans move out of the country, into the city, but they like to imagine themselves farmers at heart, many of them,” Ott explains. As industrialization transformed the U.S., the pumpkin came to symbolize the pastoral life being left behind. In poetry, paintings, and festivals, it became a stand-in for tradition and a romanticized vision of national roots. Today, that symbolism is being put to work, literally. Pumpkins are once again supporting small farmers, not as dietary staples but as attractions. Ott calls them “agrarian wonderlands,” where farms market autumnal experiences that hinge on the iconic gourd. “The cool thing about the whole story,” Ott says, “is that these very romantic ideas and myths that a lot of Americans tell themselves about their origin stories are actually helping to rejuvenate the very thing it represents: a small family farm.” Did this solution stand out? items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Commercial Buildings Can Reduce Energy Use and Lower Operating Costs Reading Time: 3 minutes How Commercial Buildings Can Reduce Energy Use and Lower Operating Costs Commercial buildings waste about 30% of their energy, and that’s just an average, according to the U.S. Department of Energy. In practice, that means part of your utility bill is probably paying to heat empty rooms, cool unoccupied offices, light parking lots after everyone has gone home, or keep equipment running on an outdated schedule. While that’s a remarkably high number for energy waste, it’s surprisingly easy to lower it significantly. Often, you can start with low-cost fixes before investing in more sustainable and energy-efficient upgrades. All that is really needed is a fresh, honest look at how the building actually operates. Find Out Where Most of the Waste Goes Before replacing any equipment, look at your data: where does the building actually use energy? Review your utility bills, demand charges, operating schedules, and, where available, interval data from smart meters. Look specifically at peak demand times; staggered startup schedules can significantly reduce demand charges. Also compare energy use against occupancy and production schedules. If consumption barely changes between a busy Monday and an empty Sunday, something deserves investigation. An energy audit or retro-commissioning study can take this further. In plain terms, you are checking whether the building still operates the way its designers intended. Get Serious About Building Controls According to the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE), high-performance control strategies can reduce annual HVAC energy use by 30% across a range of commercial building types. Of course, this doesn’t mean every building will cut its HVAC bill by that exact amount, but it shows why controls deserve more attention than they usually get. Look at temperature setbacks, occupancy schedules, ventilation rates, economizer operation, and simultaneous heating and cooling. A building automation system is only as useful as its programming. If the system has sophisticated controls but nobody checks whether they still match actual occupancy, you have an expensive computer making the wrong decisions. Upgrade Lighting and Control It LED retrofits remain one of the more straightforward commercial efficiency projects, particularly in buildings with old fluorescent or high-intensity fixtures. But swapping fixtures and calling the job finished misses half the opportunity. Add occupancy sensors where spaces sit empty for long periods. Use daylight controls near windows and skylights. Put exterior and parking-lot lighting on appropriate schedules rather than relying on someone to remember to flip a switch. This is also where electrical expertise matters. Whether you operate a warehouse in Texas, an office in Colorado, or need an Albuquerque electrical contractor for a New Mexico facility, look for a provider that can handle both the electrical work and efficiency side of the project. Look Beyond the Big Systems Some of the easiest savings are hidden in ordinary equipment. Plug loads can become a significant energy drain in efficient buildings, particularly where computers, kitchen equipment, vending machines, and other devices remain powered outside working hours. Smart power strips, automatic shutdown schedules, and better equipment procurement can help. This is a good reason to use submeters in larger facilities. Instead of seeing one enormous monthly electricity number, you can separate major loads and identify what changed. Use Maintenance as an Energy Strategy A dirty filter, poorly calibrated sensor, worn weatherstripping, or failing motor doesn’t just create a maintenance problem. It can make equipment work harder and longer. Build energy checks into preventive maintenance rather than waiting for an obvious failure. Inspect: HVAC controls and sensor calibration, Lighting and setback schedules, Equipment operating outside occupied hours, Door seals and building envelope air leaks, Unusual shifts or spikes in consumption. DOE research has found that properly tuned controls alone can produce substantial savings, partly because controls in existing buildings often drift away from their intended settings over time. Not every green upgrade deserves a blank check. Rank projects by expected energy savings, installation cost, maintenance savings, useful life, demand reduction, and available utility incentives. The post How Commercial Buildings Can Reduce Energy Use and Lower Operating Costs appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News The Soil Carbon Sponge Opens a New Path to Cooling the Planet Reading Time: 3 minutes A new report argues that restoring the soil carbon sponge could help cool the planet by rebuilding a hydrological system that has regulated heat for billions of years. The soil carbon sponge, Earth’s living water-management layer, may be one of the most overlooked tools in the fight against climate change. A new report argues that restoring healthy soil could help cool the planet directly. The idea centers on how living soil manages water, not just carbon. Researchers behind the report work with the Conscious Planet Save Soil initiative. Their analysis builds on decades of earlier work by Australian soil scientist Walter Jehne. The report frames water, not carbon alone, as the planet’s primary heat regulator. Water has shaped Earth’s temperature for roughly four billion years. Evaporation and condensation move enormous amounts of heat through the atmosphere. Healthy soil acts like a sponge that keeps this cooling cycle running. Underground fungal networks help build this sponge-like structure over time. Fungi bind soil particles together, creating tiny air pockets that trap water. That structure lets soil absorb heavy rainfall instead of letting it run off the surface. Right now, that sponge is badly damaged across much of the world. About 52 percent of global agricultural land is now considered degraded in some way. In parts of the United States, soil erosion runs up to ten times faster than natural formation. In Europe, an estimated 60-70% of soils are now considered unhealthy. Degraded soil holds less water and supports less plant growth. That shift pushes more solar energy into heating the air instead of evaporating water. Scientists describe this shift using two related terms: latent heat and sensible heat. Latent heat describes energy used to evaporate water, which cools the surrounding air. Sensible heat instead raises air temperature directly, as happens over dry, degraded land. Rebuilding soil organic matter could reverse much of this damage over time. The report estimates that each 1% increase lets a hectare hold 250,000 more liters of water. That stored water supports the plant growth needed for continued evapotranspiration. The report’s authors calculate that healthy evapotranspiration moves about 80 watts of energy per square meter. They compare this to the roughly 0.9 watts per square meter driving current global warming. Restoring the soil carbon sponge, they argue, could offset that imbalance several times over. This calculation reflects a newer and less mainstream approach within climate science. Most researchers still treat cutting greenhouse gas emissions as the primary lever for limiting warming. Even so, many scientists agree that healthy soil provides real, measurable local cooling benefits. Restoring the soil carbon sponge and cutting emissions are not competing strategies but complementary ones, with the report’s authors arguing that land regeneration and decarbonization pursued together can reinforce each other’s benefits across the same climate system. Photo by Sven Hornburg on Unsplash. The report’s authors frame soil restoration as a complement to emissions cuts, not a replacement. Both strategies address different parts of the same climate system. Pursued together, they argue, land regeneration and decarbonization could reinforce each other’s benefits. The report recommends several practical steps for restoring the soil carbon sponge. Cover cropping and mulching can keep bare soil from radiating heat back into the sky. Protecting forests also helps sustain the smaller, regional water cycles that keep landscapes moist. Researchers call these regional patterns small water cycles, distinct from the planet’s larger water cycle. Forests recycle much of their own rainfall internally, moistening the air around them. Losing forest cover can dry out a whole region even without any change in total rainfall. Some cities are already testing these ideas at a smaller scale. A trial in Canberra, Australia, is rewetting soil beneath open grassland to cool nearby streets. Early results suggest that even modest soil restoration can measurably lower local air temperatures. These recommendations echo growing interest in regenerative farming worldwide. Similar cover-cropping and mulching methods are already common practice for many small-scale farmers. Wider adoption could extend these local benefits across much larger areas. None of these steps require waiting on new technology to scale up. Farmers, land managers, and city planners around the world already have the tools to start today. Restoring the soil carbon sponge , one field at a time, could offer valuable climate protection. items.descriptionOriginal: I n August, videos of bulldozers ripping up the mouth of the iconic Santa Elena Canyon in Texas’ Big Bend went viral, propelling one of the country’s most remote national parks into the national spotlight. Construction crews were hard at work in the early stages of cutting a brand-new “patrol road” for law enforcement just feet away from an existing road to the canyon, whose 1,500-foot limestone cliffs, locals argue, form a natural border wall constructed millions of years ahead of schedule. Locals sprang into action, taking shifts monitoring construction and volunteering to rescue endangered plants — including the Chisos Mountain hedgehog cactus and all the spiny plants that provide protective nests for species like the yellow-billed cuckoo — ahead of the bulldozers. A rally was held on the beach in the shadow of the canyon, where people from all walks of life joined hands in the mud. “People think the Rio Grande divides us, but what the river actually does is unite us,” Hillary Pierce, an organizer with No Big Bend Wall, said into the bullhorn while holding a sign that said DON’T BULLDOZE MY CHURCH . items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Klamath River Salmon Comeback Surprises Scientists After Record Dam Removal Reading Time: 3 minutes Tribal advocacy and coordinated science monitoring made the Klamath River salmon comeback possible after a century of blocked rivers. The Klamath River salmon comeback is happening faster than scientists predicted. Chinook salmon have already reclaimed 88% of their historic territory in the upper Klamath River Basin. This progress comes just two years after crews finished removing four hydroelectric dams. A peer-reviewed assessment published in Scientific Reports offers the first quantitative look at how quickly migratory fish can recolonize a river system once barriers come down, and it treats the Klamath as a benchmark for restoration projects worldwide. The dam removal project wrapped up in October 2024. It stands as the largest dam removal effort completed anywhere in the world. Four dams, some over a century old, once blocked salmon from swimming upstream along the Oregon-California border. Researchers tracked the Klamath River salmon comeback using underwater sonar cameras positioned near the former dam sites. In 2024, about 7,700 Chinook salmon swam past the old dam locations. By 2025, that number grew to more than 13,000 fish, and together these salmon made up close to one-fifth of all Chinook returning to the entire Klamath Basin. Think of it like reopening a highway that had been closed for 100 years. Drivers did not just trickle back in. They found the route almost immediately and started using it in growing numbers. The salmon pushed through difficult terrain to get there. They swam through rocky whitewater stretches, climbed fish ladders taller than a two-story building, and crossed a 25,000-acre lake. One fish reached an elevation of 1,250 meters, more than 580 kilometers from the ocean, marking the farthest inland any Klamath salmon has been recorded and underscoring just how far this recovery has traveled. Scientists compared this recovery to other major dam removal projects. The Elwha River in Washington State saw a similar rebound after its dams came down. But the Klamath River salmon comeback reclaimed a larger share of old habitat in less time than any other large-scale project studied so far. Researchers believe geography helped speed things along. The upper Klamath Basin has broad, lake-filled headwaters instead of steep, narrow streams. This creates gentler terrain that suits salmon better than the sharp mountain drops found in many other river systems. The Klamath River salmon comeback is being aided by the basin’s own geography, with broad, lake-filled headwaters creating gentler terrain that suits returning salmon far better than the steep, narrow streams found in most other restored river systems. Photo by Gary Halvorson, Oregon State Archives on Wikimedia Commons . Cold, spring-fed rivers in the newly opened areas also help. These waters stay at steady, cool temperatures year-round. That gives salmon reliable conditions no matter the season or how much rain or snow falls that year. For over a century, four dams cut off salmon from these waters. Combined with overfishing and water withdrawals, the population had dropped by more than 90%. In 2002, roughly a quarter of that year’s entire salmon run died from disease tied to poor water conditions below the dams, a disaster that helped galvanize the movement behind today’s Klamath River salmon comeback. Removing the barriers has already reversed some of that damage. Beyond Chinook, researchers spotted coho salmon, steelhead, and Pacific lamprey exploring the reopened sections of the river. Their numbers remain smaller, but their presence shows the recovery reaches beyond a single species. Tribal nations played a central role in making this possible. The Yurok, Karuk, Klamath, and Shasta Indian Nation communities have relied on Klamath salmon for food, ceremonies, and cultural traditions for generations. Their decades of advocacy helped drive the push to remove the dams and set the Klamath River salmon comeback in motion. Scientists caution that early success does not guarantee lasting recovery. Most Klamath Chinook salmon live two to four years, so researchers need several more seasons before they fully understand how this generation will fare. They also want to see whether salmon start reproducing successfully in the newly reopened streams. One especially hopeful sign involves spring-run Chinook salmon, a variety that vanished from the upper basin decades ago. The newly reconnected cold-water streams could offer the right conditions for this ecotype to return, either naturally or through reintroduction efforts. Researchers plan to keep watching closely during the spring and summer months when these fish would typically appear. The momentum extends well beyond fish counts. River advocates have also pointed to broader gains, from clearer water to the return of native plants along the banks once buried under reservoirs, a shift that occurred as the dam removal project reached completion. What happens in the Klamath now offers guidance for river restoration projects worldwide. As more aging dams reach the end of their working lives, communities elsewhere face similar decisions. This basin shows that when rivers reopen, nature can respond with remarkable speed, and the Klamath River salmon comeback may just be the opening chapter of a much longer recovery story. The fish did not wait for permission. They found their way home. The post Klamath River Salmon Comeback Surprises Scientists After Record Dam Removal appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM An Australian device that splits rooftop solar power across an entire apartment building just won the country’s top design honor. Melbourne-based Allume Energy took the 2026 Australian Good Design Award of the Year for its SolShare system , which its creators describe as a “traffic controller for solar.” The device also won the sustainability award at the same ceremony, held Friday at ICC Sydney, where more than 1,000 entries competed across 13 disciplines. Why apartment solar access matters Homeowners with their own rooftops have driven most of the residential solar boom , but apartment dwellers have largely been on the sidelines. Individual rooftop installations don’t work well in shared buildings: the costs multiply, the wiring gets messy, and you need a separate inverter for each unit. SolShare cuts through that. One rooftop system, one installation, and the device handles distribution to each apartment automatically. Dr. Brandon Gien, chair of Good Design Australia, called it “an amazing piece of technology” and a beautifully designed solution to a complex problem. “Millions of people live in apartments, and many have had limited access to the benefits of rooftop solar ,” he said. “SolShare is a clever Australian design innovation that addresses that problem in a practical way, and it is already delivering benefits at significant scale.” One of the world’s oldest design competitions The Australian Good Design Awards go back to 1958. Past recipients of the top prize include the Cochlear hearing implant (2000), Marc Newson’s economy class seats for the Qantas A380 (2009), the Flow Hive beehive design (2016), and filmmaker James Cameron’s Deepsea Challenger submersible (2012). SolShare now sits in that lineup. Other sustainability winners at the 2026 awards The night’s other awards pointed the same way. Finnish company FabPatch won the fashion and textiles discipline for a rub-on fabric repair system. No Wrap , an Australian-designed reusable pallet securing system, and Holy Carp , a plastic-free compostable alternative to the soy-sauce fish packets in sushi packaging, both won gold in their categories. A ceremonial gathering space at Melbourne’s City Square, designed in collaboration with Wurundjeri elders to make Woi-wurrung language visible and welcome visitors to Country, won for the built environment. Sydney Children’s Hospital’s wayfinding project replaced standard clinical signage with native animals and plants grouped into three local environments: wetlands, sand dunes, and sea cliffs. Gien said the awards are meant to recognize design that can “bring joy to our lives, but not at the expense of the environment.” A small white box on an apartment wall that gets whole buildings into the solar conversation, without requiring anyone to overhaul the roof, is a reasonable candidate for that. items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Hungary’s parliament voted last Tuesday to repeal the 2021 Child Protection Law that banned the portrayal or promotion of homosexuality and transgender identities in schools and media. Within minutes, the EU announced it was releasing €4.2 billion (approximately $4.6 billion) in funds frozen over rule-of-law violations, a connection Budapest had been counting on. From political weapon to political liability Orbán’s government pushed the 2021 law as a child protection measure, framing gay and transgender people as a threat to public morals, and for years it worked. Then his government pardoned the deputy head of a children’s home convicted of covering up his boss’s child sexual abuse crimes, and what had been a political asset became the defining scandal of his final term. Magyar ran his campaign on protecting children in state care and largely sidestepped the LGBTQ rights issue; his party needed conservative votes, and he was not going to risk alienating them. Five years of legislation, unwound in one vote Tuesday’s package went beyond the 2021 law, touching Fidesz-era changes to education policy and assembly rights. Civil rights group Háttér Society , which had been fighting the child protection law for five years, said most of the problems it had flagged in the draft had been fixed. “We are very happy that this got adopted,” said Tamás Dombos of Háttér Society. “We’ve been fighting this so-called child protection law for five years.” The repeal also cleared Hungary’s path to rejoin Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe , two major EU programs suspended during the Orbán years over rule-of-law violations. Tisza holds the same two-thirds parliamentary majority Orbán’s party once had, which meant the package passed without needing to negotiate. Beyond the repeal Háttér Society welcomed the vote, though the group was clear about how much remains unaddressed. It still wants full recognition of same-sex marriage , adoption rights for same-sex couples, and the right of transgender people to change their names on official documents, none of which are in the new legislation. Magyar has been careful in how he frames the issue. “I’m very cautious,” he told Finnish daily Helsingin Sanomat. “As prime minister, it’s my duty to represent all Hungarians, and we have sensitive issues, such as the situation of sexual minorities.” “We are still knocking on a closed door,” Dombos said, “but at least they are listening on the other side.” For a community that spent years being actively targeted, that is a real shift, even if full equality is still a long way off. items.descriptionOriginal: Hear ye, hear ye! You may not be aware, but town criers still exist — and the best of the bunch recently came together to show off their skills in an international competition. Held in Chester, England, the World Town Crier Tournament took place late last month with 25 competitors from eight nations. While town criers date as far back as ancient Greece and Rome, their prevalence in England beginning in the Middle Ages resulted in the image many associate with the role today. Literacy rates were much lower then, so criers were responsible for communicating news, beginning announcements with an exclamation of “oyez,” which is pronounced “oh yay” and derives from a French word meaning “to listen.” Decked out in period attire, the 2026 tournament participants performed three cries: one on their home towns, one on a retail store that sponsored the event, and another on their hotel accommodations. They were judged on vocal power, clarity, showmanship, and audience engagement. Kevin Howarth from Queensland, Australia, was named the overall winner, while Joris Goens of West Flanders, Belgium, took second place. Representing the host country, Christian Ashdown from Surrey, England, came in third. Ashdown spoke to SWNS after the event, describing his win as “a very pleasant surprise.” The 57-year-old noted that “there were some top criers” at the competition — and he would know. He’s been crier of Haslemere, a historic market town in Surrey, for 16 years and has won prior championships. A projects and amenities officer for the Haslemere Town Council, Ashdown said he never intended to be a town crier, but when his predecessor decided to retire in the middle of the busy Christmas period, the mayor called asking if he’d fill in. He hesitantly accepted and eventually fell in love with the role. He’s now the chair of the Ancient and Honourable Guild of Town Criers , which is the largest and oldest body of town criers in the world. Ashdown says there are 117 members and that town crying is becoming more popular as the guild has begun posting on social media. The job mostly consists of greeting people on special occasions and market days, as well as representing the town during contests. Criers must wear a costume, which is usually Georgian-inspired as that was the peak of town crying in England. Because they generally work on a volunteer basis, many hold down other jobs as well. “It had never crossed my mind to become a town crier. I knew what they were, but I didn’t know they still existed,” said Ashdown. “I knew nothing about it, but I have very much embraced it.” He added: “People love it and they thank me. It is all positive which surprised me actually.” Despite the perception of town criers being artifacts of the past, he noted that the position “has never really died off funnily enough. It is something that has never gone away.” He said that common mistakes are saying “oyez” while talking, rather than at the start of a cry with a pause, and focusing too much on volume. He also advises fellow or aspiring criers not to use their voice too much the day before an event, as they’ll need lots of water and throat lozenges. “Try not to scream and shout too much. You have to pace yourself,” Ashdown explained. “Just be nice and clear. It is not necessarily always about the volume; it is enunciation.” This article was originally written by Isobel Williams for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets. The man had slipped the words in quietly, without drawing attention to them, letting them wait until she was ready. What the story reveals is something almost too simple to name: that a caring stranger's gentleness, offered in a few unhurried minutes at a water fountain, can fold itself into a life and stay there. "He didn't say anything," Matsuda recalled. "He just smiled and handed me the origami crane."

items.descriptionOriginal: You’ve finished your morning Nice News read but are still craving some uplifting, thought-provoking media — might we suggest turning to a podcast next? We’re big fans of the medium (so much so that we released a season of our own podcast last year!) and love how these audio shows can inform, inspire, and entertain during mundane moments of the day. We rounded up nine engaging shows that we think are worth a spot on your playlist, whether you’re doing the dishes, walking the dog, or just looking to unwind on the couch. No Such Thing As a Fish Prepare to laugh and be amazed. The recipient of the Heinz Oberhummer Award for Science Communication in 2019, No Such Thing As a Fish features researchers from the BBC’s comedy game show QI who spotlight a trove of hilarious and mind-boggling facts they’ve dug up over the previous week. The episodes are sure to leave you smiling after each listen. “It explains what the Second World War and carrots have to do with each other or how long you have to cook a space egg,” per a statement from the Oberhummer Awards. “And while you listen, laugh, and marvel for 40 minutes, you often don’t notice how much you’ve learned.” On Humans A favorite of Nice News Assistant Editor Rebekah Brandes, On Humans seeks to answer three questions: “Where do we come from? How did we get here? And what kinds of creatures are we?” In each episode, host Ilari Mäkelä interviews scholars primarily about our origins as humans, delving into specific topics like shamans , why we laugh , and the early days of farming . The show “always leaves me feeling smarter and more curious,” Rebekah said. Good Hang With Amy Poehler Amy Poehler isn’t trying to dole out advice or “make you better” — she’s simply looking for a good time. In Good Hang , which won the first-ever Golden Globe for best podcast earlier this year, Poehler interviews celebs and other “fun people” to provide a cozy, relaxed alternative to the plethora of self-improvement-focused media out there. Start with standout episodes featuring Jennifer Lawrence, Seth Meyers, and Tina Fey. Home Cooking Pals Samin Nosrat, author of Salt, Fat, Acid, Heat , and Hrishikesh Hirway, creator and host of the podcast Song Exploder , dished up cooking advice for amateurs with a side of friendly banter in Home Cooking , which ran from 2020-2025. A self-described perfectionist, Nosrat explained to Vogue in 2020 that the show centers a different mindset around cooking: “It’s about putting something out there to make people feel comforted and like they have technical support in the kitchen and some way to pass the time by hanging out with these funny, very dorky friends.” Unconditional With Maggie Lawson Animal lovers know there’s something special about the bonds they share with their pets — and this podcast celebrates exactly that. Hosted by Psych actor Maggie Lawson, the series explores the special connection celebrities like Henry Winkler and Janel Parrish have with their pets, and features interviews with animal experts about the “healing effects” of our furry friends. “Anyone who is obsessed with their pets will feel so seen by this podcast,” said Nice News Writer Marika Spitulski, adding, “I already want to be [Lawson’s] friend and hang out with her dog Linus.” Weirdly Helpful How can we take control of our “news diet”? And what’s considered proper handshaking etiquette in our modern age? These questions and more are answered in Weirdly Helpful , a series of bite-size episodes (each around 20 minutes or less) that spotlight guests who cover unexpected but intriguing ways to make life better. “Thanks for making me feel inspired while giving me concrete steps to evolve,” one reviewer wrote. Happier With Gretchen Rubin In 2024, we picked Gretchen Rubin’s brain about practical ways to lead a happier life — and in her award-winning podcast, the author and happiness researcher shares more strategies, ideas, and personal anecdotes to inspire you to live joyfully. Try one of her “A Little Happier” episodes for a quick fix; each lays out a lesson in five minutes or less. You can also check out her “Move Happier” series, intended to be paired with 26 minutes of movement as part of her Move 26 in ’26 challenge . The Allusionist If you’re a fan of NPR’s “Word of the Week” series, we bet you’ll love The Allusionist , which won smartest podcast at the 2018 British Podcast Awards. In each episode, host Helen Zaltzman dives into the intricacies of language, including the etymology and cultural significance of some of our most used words (and profanities), with a hefty dose of humor. Start with her April 13 episode “Hues” to learn why some of Merriam-Webster’s lexicographers took decades to define certain color names. Get Birding On HBO Max, you can catch Sean Bean ruling his corner of Westeros as the Stark family patriarch in Game of Thrones . On your podcast feed, though, he’s a soothing presence pointing out birds as they fly over his garden. The English actor took over as host for Season 4 of Get Birding , inviting ornithologists into his backyard and beyond to talk all things avian. The biweekly episodes, which you can also watch on YouTube, cover everything from why birdsong makes us feel good to why birds sing at daybreak . In Virginia's Shenandoah Valley, two retired neighbors, John Rice and John Sessler, are doing just that, transforming their farmland into thriving habitats for wildlife. items.descriptionOriginal: A 13-year-old has earned the distinction of being “America’s top young scientist” for 2026, taking first place in 3M’s prestigious Young Scientist Challenge. Raji Doshi, an eighth grader from Farmington, Connecticut, won the contest with an algae-based invention that could help save marine ecosystems. She and nine other finalists aged 11-14 created their prototypes over the summer, each of them working with a mentor to develop their ideas. Raji won the $25,000 grand prize after the challenge’s final events on Oct. 12 and 13, presenting a natural system that addresses ocean acidification by increasing alkalinity and removing carbon dioxide. Ocean acidification, which began during the industrial revolution, is primarily caused by the seawater absorbing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. The change in PH reduces the abundance of carbonate ions: essential structures that many marine lifeforms, like corals and crustaceans, need to build their shells and skeletons. “Raji’s project reminds us that when you’re passionate about something, you can use that interest to change the world,” her mentor, 3M product engineering specialist Deborah Isabelle, said in a press release . “She loves collecting seashells and was distressed that ocean acidification is starting to damage the seashells and the creatures that live inside them.” The contest also recognizes two runners-up, who each received a $1,000 cash prize. The three honorees, all girls, point to promising changes in the STEM arena, where women have historically been underrepresented. Seventh grader Aaisha Asif came in second place for her eco-friendly adhesive made from natural proteins; and ninth grader Sharvi Mahajan took third for her EEG-based device that tracks fatigue and predicts microsleep, alerting drivers and others in high-risk fields. Looking at the full lineup of finalists , it’s clear the future of science is bright. “The 3M Young Scientist Challenge highlights the incredible potential of young people to tackle real-world challenges through science,” said William Brown, 3M Chairman and CEO. “The talent and creativity displayed by this year’s finalists was exceptional, and we congratulate Raji on earning the title of America’s Top Young Scientist.”

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News 5 Top Brands for Comfortable 100% Organic Cotton Bras Reading Time: 5 minutes 5 Top Brands for Comfortable 100% Organic Cotton Bras Spending all day in a truly comfortable bra is already a challenge. Tracking down one made from 100% organic cotton – with legitimate certification to prove it – is even harder. The market for comfortable 100% organic cotton bras has expanded, but quality is all over the place, and plenty of labels that claim “natural” can’t back that up with documentation. Why Organic Cotton Matters for Everyday Comfort Most people don’t realize how chemically loaded a conventional bra can be. Standard synthetics and treated cotton often carry azo dyes, formaldehyde finishes, and PFAS, substances pressing directly against skin for hours every day. The Center for Environmental Health detected BPA in sports bras from major mainstream brands at levels up to 40 times the established safe limit. Certified organic cotton changes that picture. GOTS certification (Global Organic Textile Standard) controls the entire supply chain from farm to finished garment, banning the synthetic pesticides and chemical finishes that standard cotton processing allows. For people with sensitive skin, eczema, or simply a preference for fewer synthetics, a GOTS-certified bra isn’t a luxury; it’s a practical choice. And comfort follows naturally. Organic cotton breathes well, wicks moisture without relying on synthetic coatings, and softens with wear rather than pilling or stiffening. The absence of harsh dyes also means less skin irritation over time. 1. Q for Quinn Q for Quinn is a small, family-owned Canadian brand founded in 2018 by Melita Cyril, who originally designed organic cotton socks for her son’s eczema before expanding into a full line of natural-fiber essentials for adults and children. The brand’s bra and bralette lineup covers several styles: a criss-cross bralette, a pointelle bra, a racerback sports bra, a full bust sports bra, and a shelf tank. Fabrics come in either 95% organic cotton with 5% elastane or 100% organic cotton. The fully cotton styles are biodegradable end-to-end, using natural rubber-cotton elastics and 100% organic cotton thread throughout; pricing starts between $52 and $64, and sizing runs XS through 3XL. Every applicable product carries GOTS certification through Ecocert Greenlife under license 256894. Product pages spell out each component – body fabric, elastic, thread, and closures – so nothing in the construction is hidden. Undergarments are made in certified facilities in Tirupur, India, and the brand excludes chlorine bleach, azo dyes, and formaldehyde finishes from its entire supply chain. Where it fits: Women with sensitive skin, those avoiding chemical exposure during workouts, and shoppers who want full material transparency in a bra, particularly for low-to-medium impact activities like yoga, Pilates, and walking. 2. Roaman’s Roaman’s is a plus-size fashion retailer with roots stretching back decades, now operating as part of FullBeauty Brands and headquartered in Indianapolis. The brand focuses exclusively on sizes 12W through 44W, it doesn’t start from a smaller size and grade up, which makes it genuinely purpose-built for plus-size shoppers rather than an afterthought extension of a standard range. The catalog spans a wide range of women’s clothing, intimates, swimwear, sleepwear, tops, bottoms, and shoes. With over 100 years in women’s fashion, the brand positions itself as an industry leader and pushes fashion-forward designs at prices that don’t require a big budget. Shopping options include the website, a printed catalog, and a store credit card. Roaman’s clothing was used to dress cast members on TLC’s 1,000 lb Sisters , a placement that put the brand in front of its core audience. Customer support runs through phone and email, and the website offers account management, order tracking, and a rewards program. Where it fits: Plus-size shoppers looking for a wide selection of intimates and clothing in one place, with consistent sizing across categories. Worth checking: Roaman’s is a general plus-size fashion retailer. Shoppers seeking certified organic cotton bras should confirm material details before purchasing, as the brand doesn’t position itself around organic certification. 3. Siella Siella is a Canadian lingerie brand launched in 2020 out of Montreal, backed by Chateau Bodywear, a family business with over 75 years of experience manufacturing underwear and lingerie, founded in 1945. That manufacturing depth gives Siella a level of vertical control that newer brands rarely have. The line focuses on wireless bras, underwear, and loungewear, with a stated emphasis on comfort, support, and a second-skin fit. Siella describes its approach as designed by women, blending modern femininity with everyday comfort. Prices range from approximately $25 to $105 USD, with bundle discounts of up to 20% available. Free shipping kicks in on orders over $95. U.S. customer service operates on EST timezone at +1 800-665-0589. The brand emphasizes organic cotton options and benefits from its parent company’s manufacturing infrastructure, which supports tighter control than outsourced production typically allows. Siella has been featured in Diary of a Toronto Girl’s roundup of top lingerie brands. Where it fits: Shoppers who want wireless bras that prioritize everyday comfort and are open to a Canadian brand with a long manufacturing history behind it. Worth checking: Organic cotton certification details aren’t publicly disclosed the same way as some competitors, so shoppers should confirm certification before purchase if that’s a deciding factor. 4. Bestform Bestforms, Inc. is a company founded in 1985 and headquartered in Camarillo, California, with 51 to 200 employees. The company operates as a B2B manufacturer in the business forms and print industry, producing patented membership card products, integrated labels, variable barcoding, unit set forms, continuous forms, and custom labels. Bestforms describes its model as “trade only,” meaning it works through intermediaries rather than direct-to-consumer channels. The company’s tagline is “BestCards, Labels and Digital Solutions, Forms,” and its track record centers on responsive development for commercial printing needs. Bestforms does not appear to operate as a lingerie or apparel retailer. No bra products, organic cotton garments, or related consumer goods appear in the company’s product lineup. Where it fits: Business clients in need of commercial printing, label manufacturing, or custom card production, not a category match for consumers shopping for organic cotton bras. Worth checking: Shoppers searching for lingerie under this name should confirm they’ve reached the correct brand, as the bestform.com domain belongs to a commercial printing manufacturer, not an apparel company. 5. AmpleBosom AmpleBosom is a UK-based online and mail-order retailer founded in 1999 by Sally Robinson, operating from a family-run farm in Old Byland, North Yorkshire. The company specializes in bras, lingerie, swimwear, nightwear, and clothing, with a size range that runs from 28 to 58 in AA through N cups, one of the widest ranges available anywhere in the market. AmpleBosom doesn’t manufacture its own products; instead, it stocks bras and lingerie from established names including Empreinte, Elomi, and Fantasie. The team is estimated at 25 to 100 employees, and the business has stayed independent since it launched. It earned early recognition when the BBC series Inside Dot Coms featured it in 2000, notable for an e-commerce model that was well ahead of the mainstream at the time. Expert bra fitting advice is offered both in-person and virtually. Payment is accepted online, by mail, or by phone; in-store payment isn’t an option. Pricing varies by brand and item, with promotions available throughout the year. Where it fits: Shoppers who need larger or harder-to-find cup sizes and want access to multiple specialty lingerie brands in one place, with expert fitting support available. Worth checking: AmpleBosom is a UK retailer; U.S. shoppers should factor in international shipping costs and delivery times, and should verify whether specific organic cotton options are available among its current brand selection. Bottom Line Brands in the comfortable 100% organic cotton bra space span a surprisingly wide range – certified organic specialists, plus-size fashion retailers, and, in at least one case, a commercial printer that has no business appearing on this list. For shoppers who prioritize verified certification, full material transparency, and construction that’s genuinely gentle on sensitive skin, the real options thin out fast. Roaman’s and Siella both serve comfort-focused buyers but from different angles: Roaman’s through extended plus sizing, Siella through wireless everyday styles. AmpleBosom suits anyone needing an unusually wide cup range paired with professional fitting guidance. Know what matters most to you – certification, sizing, support level, or country of origin, and the right choice gets a lot clearer.
