items.descriptionOriginal: Episode Description: Arielle and Karissa cover ten solutions this week, including 20,000 octopuses hiding in well-studied waters off the California coast, what Indonesian mosque loudspeakers have to do with earthquake survival, and a garden chore you now have a very good reason to skip. If you have questions, comments, feedback, suggestions, or just want to say hi, send a message to: podcast@optimistdaily.com . Want to be part of the Optimism Movement? Become an Emissary . Subscribe to our FREE Daily/Weekly Newsletter and follow us on Instagram , X , and Blue Sky . The Optimist Daily is a project of the World Business Academy. Donate link: https://www.optimistdaily.com/donate-to-support-the-optimist-daily/?lsc=41ef528d Theme and all original music by Marvin Lanes Transcript: Intro Karissa: Hello everyone, I’m Karissa. Arielle: And I’m Arielle. Karissa: And welcome back to The Optimist Daily’s weekly roundup. Arielle: Yes, welcome back. Karissa and I have had a week off because last week we had a wonderful guest episode with #CreateConnectCare. If you missed it, then definitely go check it out. Karissa: Yeah, it was a great episode. I missed sharing the solutions, though, last week. Mm-hmm. And I’m glad to be back with you today, Arielle. Arielle: Yeah, there’s a lot of seasonal solutions and, uh, just some, some fun discoveries that happened this week. But before that, how are you, Karissa? Karissa: Doing well over here. The weather has been so strange all across the globe. We’re already in the middle of October, but you would not know it, at least in California. Arielle: Yeah, it’s been really weird here in the Netherlands as well. Every time I think autumn has arrived, and it’s, like, rainy and gloomy, and I’m kind of getting into my cozy vibe, the next few days are, like, sunny and warm again. Not that I’m complaining. I would not complain about that, but it’s just, it’s a bit hard to get into the seasonal rhythm… I don’t know if our listeners and fellow Optimists are feeling similarly, but I know that I’m just feeling a bit weird. Other than that, nothing to report on my end. Karissa: Yeah. I feel similarly. I guess I’m enjoying a little bit of stillness between the busy summer months and the festive season. We’re gonna go full force into the holidays here, and then this year will be over, so um- Arielle: Yeah. It definitely went by quickly, but there’s still a lot of positive news out there to share before the end of the year. And if you want all of those positive solutions straight to your inbox, then you should consider signing up for our daily or weekly newsletter. You can do that on our website, or the link is in the show notes. Karissa: And if you want these solutions and more on your social media feeds, we’re @optimistdaily on everything except X, where we’re @OdeToOptimism. Arielle: You can also reach me and Karissa directly at podcast@optimistdaily.com. We would love to get any suggestions, comments, questions, feedback, so feel free to shoot us an email. Karissa: Before we go any further, we’d love to thank our Optimist Daily Emissaries who financially support us. If you would like to become an Emissary, the link to do that is in the show notes. If financially supporting us isn’t in your budget right now, we thank our Optimists who share these solutions and follow us on socials. Arielle: Yeah, there are a lot of free ways to support us, and we appreciate everyone who does that. Karissa: And without further ado, Arielle, I think we should dive into this week’s new solutions. Australia’s renewable energy record Karissa: The first one that we had to share this week is “Australia sets a new renewable energy record, with rooftop solar leading the way”. So Australia just hit a new record. Solar- and wind-powered 80% of the entire national grid on a single Saturday. And the wild part about that is that more than half of that came not from massive solar farms, but from panels on people’s rooftops. For about 30 minutes, 4.3 million rooftop solar installations collectively carried more than half of the country’s total power load. The researcher who tracks this called it record season. Conditions were so good, he expects these records to get broken again within weeks. These individual homeowners, and not, like, utility companies, drove a national record, and that’s exciting all in itself. Arielle: Yeah, it really drives home the point that the energy transition doesn’t have to center around big infrastructure. Karissa: Mm-hmm. Arielle: It’s a reminder that, yeah, if there’s small-scale adoption, then that can really add up quickly. Karissa: Absolutely. And with Australia having an 82% renewable target for 2030, this kind of milestone is expected to become routine. So that is optimistic indeed. Performance anxiety & sport psychology Karissa: The next solution is titled “”How to quiet performance anxiety, according to sport psychology””. A sport psychologist who works with NFL teams and Olympic athletes has a pretty counterintuitive take on confidence. You don’t wait until you feel it, you act your way into it first, fake it till you make it, and the feeling follows. So she has a whole toolkit for doing this in the middle of a high-pressure moment, and the technique that an NFL receiver used after a playoff fumble is one of them. I didn’t know about this technique, but it’s called the learn, burn, return method, which is a three-step process for recovering mid-performance from a mistake. Learn one thing from it, use a physical gesture to signal moving on. For example, the Vikings receiver Adam Thielen made the toilet flush gesture famous in a 2020 playoff game, where he’s just kind of pretending to flush the toilet and get rid of that mistake, which is a fun thing. And then reset it all with a certain phrase. The performance anxiety conversation used to live almost entirely in sports, but I mean, now it’s everywhere, whether it’s in job interviews, presentations, creative work, even dating. So I think it’s important to expand upon this concept. But yeah, there’s a lot of great tips in this article from Cindra Kamphoff, who is a PhD in sport and performance psychology, and she gives a lot of great tips here, including writing powerful phrases before a high-stakes moment, which I really liked that one. So go check it out if you want some more pointers. Coral shade experiment Karissa: The next solution is “”How a floating shade can help coral survive a marine heatwave””. Scientists in Florida just published results from an experiment where they literally put little floating umbrellas over coral to protect them from the heat, and it worked. But the lead researcher was pretty blunt. This is triage, not a total solution for coral bleaching. So I loved the images here in this solution, because it really had like… The um- umbrella is kind of a… It, it’s not… I at first pictured an umbrella, like our pop-up umbrella, and I thought that was kind of a cute image, but it’s kind of just a floating, like Arielle: Like a shade, Karissa: basically Shade, yeah. Like a, just a little piece of, um- Arielle: Yeah, like a tarp … Karissa: yeah, a tarp. That’s a great way to explain it. The shaded brain coral started recovering color after these umbrellas were put in, and the unprotected ones kept bleaching through the hottest part of the season. Coral bleaching events used to happen about once a decade, but now they’re happening every five to six years, and reefs don’t have enough time to recover between them. By March 2025, 84% of the world’s reefs had experienced temperatures high enough to cause bleaching. The researcher’s quote in this was so honest, that shading is not a cure-all. This is a solution that is kind of just buying time for the bigger problem. Arielle: Yeah. It’s important to address the root problems, but yeah, if we need more time, which we definitely do, then why not? Karissa: Absolutely. Did you know that coral reefs cover less than 0.2% of the ocean floor, but shelter a quarter of all marine species? So that’s a pretty wild ratio, and we gotta protect them, just like we need to protect the rest of our beautiful planet as well. Skincare mistakes Karissa: The next solution is “”The common skin care mistakes dermatologists say are working against your routine””. Five dermatologists were asked what bad skin habits they most want patients to break, and the answer keeps coming back to the same thing. Most of us are overdoing it when it comes to our skin care routine. And there’s also a pimple popping rule in here that I think a lot of people will appreciate, and I’ll start with that one. It’s the one good squeeze rule for pimples. It’s okay to pop a pimple, but if it doesn’t come out on the first try, stop, because continuing just pushes bacteria deeper and can cause those dark spots that stick around for months. I admit if it has a white head, then I have to pop it. But usually, of course, that comes out with the one good squeeze, and it… I do think it’s, it’s very, um, satisfying, so. Arielle: Yeah. No, I’m so guilty of this. I love popping pimples. Karissa: Me too. Arielle: Um, and I will keep going at it, and I have had that, like, hyperpigmentation thing happen. Mm-hmm. And it’s just not cute. Yeah. And I, I have to abide by this. You know what’s really helped me, though? Those pimple patches. So- Karissa: Yeah, I was gonna say the same thing … Arielle: first of all, they’re fun, so you can have, like, a little purple star or whatever on your face instead of a- Yeah … a bright red glaring pimple. Um, but I do it less for, like, the… Well, of course I, I do it so that the pimple will heal, but it’s more so that my fingers just don’t get on it. Because if I see it- Yeah … then I just wanna squeeze it. Karissa: I resonated with the point that skin care has developed a trend cycle that rivals fast fashion. There’s new ingredients, new products every week, and TikTok routines that keep expanding what we’re, you know, supposed to do. So dermatologists really emphasize that sticking with simple is oftentimes better. Arielle: Mm-hmm. Yeah, and just what works for your skin. Because everyone’s skin is different, and you can’t just be chasing the trends all the time if it doesn’t work for your specific type of skin. So if you have a routine that works for you, then just stick to that. Don’t get, like, you know, uh, distracted by the shiny new serum. Karissa: Mm-hmm. Exactly. Flu shot timing Karissa: Next solution is “”Why October is the best time to get your flu shot this year””. Flu is already showing up in emergency rooms across the West, and the numbers are running about seven times higher than the same week last year. Experts are saying October is the window to get vaccinated, and there’s actually a new mRNA flu vaccine in the mix for the first time, which is a really great breakthrough. So yeah, seven times higher than this time last year is pretty rough. It’s in Western states now, but it’s expected to spread east. And the flu vaccine’s effectiveness data is pretty interesting. 29 to 56% effective against of cases that send people to the doctor, but better against severe illness. The framing here with vaccines in general is to remember it’s keeping you out of the hospital, and keeping you out of the intensive care unit, and keeping you out of the cemetery, which is a quote from the article. About the mRNA flu vaccine, you might recall this term being used for, uh, the COVID vaccine, and it’s now being applied to the flu vaccine for adults 50 and older this season, and it’s supposed to be more effective. Arielle: There was a, a number in this article that kind of broke my heart. It said that last year there were at least 195 child deaths from flu-related causes, and preventing such high numbers could be as simple as just getting vaccinated against the flu. So yeah, and I don’t mean to fearmonger, but it definitely struck a chord with me when I read it. Karissa: Yeah. Tens of thousands of Americans die of flu each season, and that tends to surprise people. I feel like flu deaths are chronically under-discussed. So of course, yeah, like you mentioned, Arielle, not to fearmonger, but get that flu vaccine, and it’s a good time to get it now. Octopus nursery Arielle: Well, on that note, we’re going to bring it to some lighter topics, let’s say. Uh, the first solution that I’m going to share with everyone is titled “Scientists discovered the world’s largest octopus nursery off the California coast”. Scientists were studying one of the most closely monitored stretches of ocean in the world, and somehow missed 20,000 octopuses just hanging out on the sea floor. Turns out there’s a field of hydrothermal springs down there that’s functioning as the world’s largest known octopus nursery, and researchers only found it in 2018. So these hydrothermal springs keep the water warm enough to cut the octopuses’ egg-brooding time from years down to about 1.8 years, which still sounds like a l- a long time to me. Yeah. But if it’s, if it’s cutting more years off of it, then that’s great. And this is why so many octopuses congregate there specifically. The octopuses build their dens from whatever they find on the sea floor, including human objects that have drifted down to the deep sea. This went undetected until 2018 in well-studied water, which raises the question of how many other gatherings like this exist in unmapped thermal fields elsewhere. There’s been growing public fascination, I think, with octopus intelligence and behavior in recent years, and this story lands right in that conversation. And yeah, I, I think I remember when My Octopus Teacher came out, and I think that was kind of when everybody was like, “Oh my gosh, octopuses are actually so, so smart and so cool.” Um, have you seen it, Karissa? Karissa: No, I haven’t, but now I wanna go watch it because I… this solution really, uh, stood out to me this week and I love it, so I’m really interested in learning some more. Arielle: Yeah, this week we have such cute ocean stories, like picturing little corals under their umbrellas and, like a whole bunch of octopuses chilling out. Karissa: Exactly. Arielle: Making babies. So… Karissa: Yeah, fun stuff. Indonesia’s mosque loudspeakers Arielle: The next solution is titled “Indonesia’s mosque loudspeakers might save lives during natural disasters”. A Japanese disaster scientist had an idea 20 years ago while studying earthquakes in Indonesia. What if the country’s mosque loudspeakers, already everywhere and already maintained daily, could double as earthquake warning systems? That pilot is now underway, and the drop-and-cover finding buried in the story is just as interesting. And if you don’t know what I mean by that, just wait. I will get to it. So Indonesia might have only five to 10 seconds of warning before an earthquake hits, and yeah, the mosque loudspeakers tested five times a day by local communities are more reliable than phone networks that can fail the moment the ground starts shaking. What I mean when I say that the mosque loudspeakers are tested five times a day is that, um, the call to prayer happens five times a day, so they definitely know that the speakers are working because the call to prayer is happening. And the drop-and-cover thing that I mentioned earlier is the standard international advice for when there’s an earthquake. You’re supposed to drop low and cover, like get under a table or something. But this advice was meant for places with well-constructed buildings, and in Indonesia, where homes are often unreinforced masonry, the people who survived earthquakes in the past actually ran outside. You know, there is growing conversation in disaster preparedness about community-maintained infrastructure versus centralized government systems, and this is a real case study for why local trust really matters. Indonesia and Japan are both on the Pacific Ring of Fire, but they have very different building standards, so the survival advice gap is a real public health issue, and I’m happy that this is being addressed with infrastructure that already exists and doesn’t really need any extra upkeep since they’re being used all the time. Egg carton reuse Arielle: The next solution is titled “Six smart things to do with an empty egg carton before you toss it in the recycling bin”. Before you toss your next empty egg carton, hear me out. Those 12 little cups, or 10 or six, depending on how many eggs you get, they turn out to be surprisingly useful around the house, and the seed-starting one especially. So that’s one of the uses that I’m going to get into. You just fill each cup with soil, you plant your seeds in them, and then when it’s time, just plant the whole thing into the ground, and then the cardboard breaks down, and the roots never get disturbed. So that would be something that I would do if I had a garden. Karissa: Mm-hmm. Arielle: Another one that I liked was the jewelry organization thing. So you can create little cups for your jewelry, and right now, all of my jewelry is just, like, willy-nilly all over the place in different rooms in tangles. Karissa: Yeah. Arielle: So I don’t need a garden to do that one, so maybe I will try that one out. Karissa: Yeah, I, I love this, and there’s really a big momentum around reducing household waste without buying more eco products, and this is about using what you already have. Japanese sweet potatoes Arielle: The next solution is titled “What sets Japanese sweet potatoes apart, nutritionally speaking?” Japanese sweet potatoes are those, like… They just look like sweet potatoes, but they’re generally kind of longer, I find, and they look purple on the outside, and then when you cut them open, they’re white on the inside. And it turns out that even though they are still sweet potatoes, they are doing completely different things nutritionally than the ones, like the orange ones that so many of us know and love. Karissa: Yeah. Arielle: And the comparison is more interesting than you’d expect. Japanese sweet potatoes are higher in vitamin C and E and anthocyanins, the same pigments that make blueberries and red cabbage dark, while orange ones are the beta carotene champions. They’re complementary, not interchangeable. The fiber content is about four grams per serving, which puts them in, like, a genuinely filling territory for a carb. And luckily, there’s no evidence-based recommendation for how many to eat per week, so you don’t necessarily need to limit yourself if you end up really, really loving Japanese sweet potatoes. The only thing is that dieticians say, um, make sure you don’t, like, hyper-fixate on them, just like on any food, and don’t make them your only kind of vegetable. Have you tried Japanese sweet potatoes before, Karissa? Karissa: Honestly, I don’t think I have. And I’m kind of not the biggest fan of just, like, normal sweet potatoes either, so they’re okay, but, like, I… And if they’re out, like, at a restaurant or something, like, and you know, it’s in front of me, I’ll eat it, but I usually, like… I, I never feel like preparing it myself. But maybe I’ll give Japanese sweet potatoes a try, and maybe I’ll fall in love with them. Overwintering bees Arielle: The last solution that we are going to share with everyone today is titled “What to leave alone in your garden this October to help overwintering bees”. This could be considered a counterintuitive one, but maybe not so counterintuitive for longtime Optimists. The best thing you can do for native bees this fall is put down the rake. All that scraggly stuff you’re about to tidy away, the leaf piles, the hollow stems, the dead-looking cane fruit, that’s where the bees love to be. There are over 3,600 native bee species in the US, and most aren’t honey bees. It’s those solitary wild bees that are in steep decline, and most of them nest in your garden over winter. So don’t compost your cut stems in fall. If bees have already nested inside them, composting kills the larvae still developing in there, and I did not know that. I didn’t realize that there’s, like, little baby bees… inside cut stems. Also, try not to worry yourself about the bare patches of dirt in your lawn if you have them. I know it might look like neglected land, but that’s prime bee nesting habitat, apparently. Ground-nesting bees need bare, un-compacted soil to excavate their nests. Karissa: Wow, I didn’t even realize that there were that many, uh, bee species in the US for one, but, um… native bee decline is an issue that feels kind of, uh, abstract until you realize that the solution is literally just doing less yard work, and I love that because- Mm. Yeah … working in the yard can be such a pain. Arielle: Yeah, I mean, I kinda wish I had one. But it can be, uh, it can be toilsome. And maybe the solution sounds familiar to some people… because we have covered No Mow May before, and I think there have been a few articles about, like, just not raking so much in the fall. Yeah. Um, ’cause that doesn’t just help bees, but it also helps other insects and critters that are important for the ecosystem. Quote & Outro Karissa: Well, Arielle, that was a great roundup of solutions, and before we head off for today, we have a positive quote to leave you off with. Arielle: This one is by Robert Frost, and it is, “The best way out is always through.” Karissa: Simple. Arielle: So yes, that’s, uh, yeah, nice and simple, but hard to do sometimes when you’re faced with a situation that you kinda wanna get out of, but you just have to endure and go through it. Karissa: Exactly. Arielle: Uh, but yeah. Well, on that note, Karissa and I wish all of you a very happy weekend, and we will be back next week with more solutions. Karissa: Until then, stay optimistic. Bye! The post Podcast Transcript October 16th, 2026— Flu is already spreading: why October is the window to get vaccinated, plus nine more solutions first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.title: Τα ηλιακά πάνελ Magenta μπορεί να είναι το πιο έξυπνο κόλπο των αγροβολταϊκών
items.titleOriginal: Magenta solar panels may be agrivoltaics’ cleverest trick yet
items.description: Οι φάρμες λαχανικών και οι ηλιακές φάρμες χρειάζονται πολύ ηλιακό φως και ανοιχτό χώρο. Πώς όμως χωρίζουμε τα περιορισμένα εδάφη μας μεταξύ αυτών των δύο προτεραιοτήτων; Μια κομψή λύση είναι να τοποθετήσετε καλλιέργειες και ηλιακούς συλλέκτες στην ίδια γη—και να μοιραστείτε το ευρύ φάσμα του εισερχόμενου ηλιακού φωτός μεταξύ τους. Μια νέα μελέτη στο Cell Reports Physical Science το κάνει αυτό με φωτοβολταϊκά…
items.descriptionOriginal: Vegetable farms and solar farms both need lots of sunlight and open space. But how do we divide our limited lands between these two priorities? One elegant solution is to put crops and solar panels on the same land—and share the broad spectrum of incoming sunlight between them. A new study in Cell Reports Physical Science does this with photovoltaic cells that are semi-transparent: They capture some wavelengths of sunlight to make electricity, while letting the wavelengths most critical to photosynthesis pass through and reach the plants below. The new study suggests that broccoli can be grown in the magenta shade of these solar panels —without sacrificing the harvest. Agrivoltaic schemes— putting plants and solar on the same land – could help us avoid clearing more land for human use. Climate studies suggest that this might work especially well across a wide sunbathed swath of the United States, from Texas up to Nebraska and west to California . Devoting just one percent of U.S. farmland to agrivoltaics could cover up to 20 percent of the nation’s electricity needs. But traditional photovoltaic panels are opaque—and by shading plants, they can reduce crop yields. So engineers are trying to create new photovoltaic cells that divide the spectrum of sunlight between plants and electricity generation—similar to how governments segment different frequency bands for television, radio, cell phones, and other uses. A 2020 study looked at panels that allow red wavelengths, critical for photosynthesis, to pass through—while harvesting green and blue wavelengths to make electricity. Basil grown under these panels produced similar yields, while spinach yields decreased. But the researchers estimated that by selling both electricity and crops, farmers growing spinach could generate 35 percent more income from the same land. .IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby .postImageUrl , It’s no contest. In the newest study, scientists evaluated a different kind of semi-transparent panel that lets most red and some blue wavelengths pass through—casting a magenta light on the plants—while converting much of the rest to electricity. Broccoli cultivated under them grew more slowly, requiring an additional 25 days for harvest, but produced roughly the same yield. Meanwhile, these magenta sunscreens improved the microclimate below, reducing the “vapor pressure deficit”—a measure of when plants need to halt photosynthesis to avoid excessive water loss. This may have improved the plants’ efficiency in converting sunlight into plant biomass, which increased by 2.8- to 4.5-fold compared to unshaded plants. The shaded plants’ levels of macronutrients such as calcium, magnesium, and phosphorus were either higher than or similar to unshaded plants, while levels of some micronutrients such as iron, copper, and zinc were slightly lower. This was only a preliminary study. Future studies should look at larger plots, farmed across multiple seasons, and in different locations with varying climate and sunlight. It suggests that for now, the future of agrivoltaics might be best seen through rose-colored glasses. items.title: Τι με δίδαξε η άνοια για το να ζω μέσα σε μια βαρετή εποχή
items.titleOriginal: What Dementia Taught Me About Living Through a Callous Time
items.description: Την ώρα που ο πρόεδρος Τζο Μπάιντεν έδειχνε τόσο εμφανή σημάδια γνωστικής παρακμής που αναγκάστηκε να εγκαταλείψει την προεδρική κούρσα το 2024, η άνοια του πατέρα μου χειροτέρευε. Έζησε μαζί μας και όμως έζησε σε μια άλλη πραγματικότητα εντελώς. Ένα που δεν καταλάβαινε πια ότι το φαγητό στο πιάτο του ήταν δικό του και το φαγητό της κόρης μου…
items.descriptionOriginal: J ust as President Joe Biden was showing signs of cognitive decline so conspicuous that he was compelled to drop out of the presidential race in 2024, my own father’s dementia was worsening. He lived with us, and yet he lived in another reality entirely. One where he no longer understood that the food on his plate was his, and the food on my daughter’s was hers. One where he grew agitated when we wouldn’t let him walk in a rainstorm. One where he no longer knew my name. Being in the bizarre world of his deteriorating mind was not unlike reading the headlines each day as the months, and then years, went on. My once sweet and Buddhist dad’s abandonment of norms, his misplaced anger, his seemingly selfish relentlessness, were a product of his disease — the nerve cells in his brain were no longer communicating properly. His context for just about everything fell away. Courtney and her father at Thanksgiving. Credit: John Cary The country’s deterioration was different, a deliberate poisoning more than an organic disease, but the parallels were there. It felt pathological how callous and hard our country had become. But there was also something happening underneath my dad’s deterioration. My whole family was learning to collectively care for him — taking him on drives and scream-singing Tom Petty when he would get sundowners (a medical term for late-day confusion in dementia patients), reading Pema Chödrön aloud to him in the backyard, letting him have our ice cream cones when he would reach for them. And our neighbors were in on the tenderness. They’d call when he wandered too far or help him back home when they found him sitting in their unlocked cars. In our local park, when my dad started helping himself to a plate of sandwiches meticulously arranged on a picnic table, the Japanese family they belonged to welcomed this unkempt, white, six-foot-two stranger to their outing as if he were a long lost relative. Likewise, there has been something happening underneath the deterioration of our country. While the headlines reveal the truth of the matter — data centers bulldozing their way into rural communities, masked federal agents yanking delivery workers off their bikes, industry lobbyists buying legislation that allows them to poison our water and air — there are also young people planting community gardens to tackle gun violence in Milwaukee, Wisconsin; caregivers riding their kids to school in bike buses in Montclair, New Jersey; and folks of all ages gathering for the Black Joy Parade in Oakland, California. While some national figures are trying to flood the zone with so much chaos that we can’t keep up, other Americans are working hard to bring running water and indoor plumbing to those who still don’t have it. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] We’re witnessing a reweaving of local fabric, and a renewed curiosity in one another. Parents watching the resurgence of blatant misogyny are intentionally raising boys who embrace their tender feelings and connections. Famously red Texas has had more data center protests than any other state , so perhaps there is more possibility for labor and climate collaboration than we have understood. Leaders in a wide range of faiths weathered the bitter cold of Minneapolis to join local solidarity protests against ICE raids after the tragic death of Renée Good. It seems we are curious again about what role faith might play in our ethical lives together, how we can build a culture of mutual aid in our very unequal communities, and even how we might better understand the economic pain of those who have been abandoned and stereotyped by mainstream media and the political elite. If the last decade or two has been about expanding our horizons, it feels like this one is becoming about humbly narrowing the aperture on our lives and trying to get right with our neighbors, housed and unhoused alike. At a time when A.I. threatens to unravel us in so many ways, economist E.F. Schumacher’s wisdom from his 1973 book Small Is Beautiful: Economics as if People Mattered feels worth reviving: “I have no doubt that it is possible to give a new direction to technological development, a direction that shall lead it back to the real needs of man, and that also means: To the actual size of man. Man is small, and, therefore, small is beautiful.” In the end, this is what saved my family as we took care of my dad; the small moments in the midst of the chaos where we could register his essence intact, where we could devote ourselves to the sacred practice of showing up for him even when it was hard, when we could rest in the awe of it all. It didn’t cure his illness, but it reminded us of us — the fabric, the tenderness, the main thing. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime I wish that same reminder for our country in the months and years ahead — a way to keep our eye on the systemic harm, while keeping our hands in the dirt of our own communities. There are people in our midst who have lost their way through deep delusion, but there are also better angels: The family that offers a strange old man a sandwich; the organizers fighting for clean water for everyone, no exceptions; the daughters of the revolution baking casseroles for the undocumented families hiding in an attic room of their Minneapolis neighbors’ homes. May we never turn away from the systemic injustice, but may we also turn towards the small and beautiful. It’s all real and deeply interconnected, and deserves our fierce attention. items.description: Αν είστε κάτι σαν εμάς, δεν είστε ακριβώς σε μια ευχάριστη διάθεση αυτή τη στιγμή. Με τις ενδιάμεσες εκλογές στις ΗΠΑ λιγότερο από τρεις εβδομάδες μακριά, μπορεί να αισθάνεστε έτοιμοι για μάχη. Και ποιος θα μπορούσε να σε κατηγορήσει; Φαινομενικά στο ψηφοδέλτιο: το ίδιο το μέλλον της δημοκρατίας, καθοδηγούμενο από ηγέτες που θα διαμορφώσουν την πολιτική για το κλίμα, τεχνητή νοημοσύνη, μετανάστευση, προσιτές τιμές…
items.descriptionOriginal: I f you’re anything like us, you’re not exactly in a congenial mood right now. With the U.S. midterm elections fewer than three weeks away, you might be feeling combat-ready. And who could blame you? Seemingly on the ballot: the very future of the republic, steered by leaders who will shape policy about the climate, A.I., immigration, affordability, wars and many other critical issues. There’s a lot at stake. And yet, for many of us, the way we feel goes beyond those stakes. One part of our brain chugs along analytically, taking stances on legislation, policy and governance. Meanwhile, another part seethes with contempt for those who disagree: They must be stupid, immoral, blind to the facts. Multiply by 340 million, and election season becomes a volatile brew. But there’s hope. While social media algorithms, elected officials, and yes, even our own friends and colleagues, encourage us to close ranks and shut out dissenting voices, others are working in the other direction: reaching out, listening deeply, locating points of connection where they exist, and turning toward those they disagree with, rather than away. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] From now through Election Day, these are the people we’ll journey with. We’ll meet liberals and conservatives who are joining forces despite their differences to oppose data centers and border walls. We’ll talk to students who are turning their college campuses into spaces that welcome an array of opinions, and others participating in cultural exchanges far from their hometowns and comfort zones. We’ll listen in on conversations between “deep canvassers” and the voters they’re hearing out. And we’ll learn how polarization takes hold of the brain — and how, little by little, we can loosen its grip. The Depolarization Project isn’t a call to meet in the middle — it’s an experiment in curiosity. What forces fuel our sense of tribalism? Why do opposing perspectives register as a threat? Can we be open to differences of opinion without compromising our values? Is there hope for those of us who harbor a secret desire to bridge the divides? We know many of you may be skeptical. We hope you’ll take this journey with us regardless, and learn whether we can we fight for what we believe in without closing our minds and our hearts. items.description: Ένα λευκασμένο κοράλλι, απογυμνωμένο από το χρώμα του και σιγά σιγά λιμοκτονεί, μπορεί να ξαναζωντανέψει σε μόλις επτά εβδομάδες -- εάν τεθεί σε επαφή με ένα υγιές δίδυμο. Ερευνητές στο Πανεπιστήμιο του Στάνφορντ ανακάλυψαν πρόσφατα ότι όταν έρχονται σε επαφή γενετικά πανομοιότυπα θραύσματα κοραλλιών, οι ιστοί τους συγχωνεύονται σε αυτό που ο επιστήμονας Ντάνι Κόλινς αποκαλεί «μια διατροφική οδό» και…
items.descriptionOriginal: A bleached coral, stripped of its color and slowly starving, can come back to life in just seven weeks -- if it is placed in contact with a healthy twin. Researchers at Stanford University recently discovered that when genetically identical coral fragments touch, their tissues fuse into what scientist Danny Collins calls "a nutrient highway," and within as little as 36 hours, life-giving algae begin flowing from the healthy fragment into the dying one. The discovery began with a happy accident: a healthy coral slipped against a bleached one in a tank, and someone was paying close enough attention to notice what happened next. The finding won't save coral reefs overnight -- the technique only works between genetic clones, and the ocean keeps warming, which causes coral to bleach. But the findings do open a door. Collins and his team are now exploring whether the algae themselves can be extracted and introduced to bleached corals at scale, without needing the physical bridge at all. While he is clear-eyed about the limits: the real solution is being able to stop coral bleaching in the first place, the horizons feel brighter: "bleached corals aren't a lost cause," he offers.

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Every fall there’s a pull to tidy things up. Cut back the perennials, rake the leaves, clear the beds, put the garden to rest. It feels satisfying, honestly, and spring does seem to start from a cleaner place. The thing is, all that leaf litter, those hollow stems, those patches of scraggly dead plant matter? That’s where the bees are. Over 3,600 bee species are native to the United States, and most of them are not honey bees. It’s the native wild bees, including mason bees, leafcutters, mining bees, long-horned bees, bumble bees, and hundreds of others, that are in steep decline. Most are solitary: each female builds her own nest, lays her eggs, stocks them with food, seals them up, and dies. As Matthew Shepherd , Director of Outreach and Education at the Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation , explains, the offspring “complete most of their life stages in the cell, remaining there until the following year, when they emerge at the same season their mother was active.” That nest is almost certainly somewhere in your garden. Sam Droege , Wildlife Biologist at the USGS, says wild bees are nesting above ground and in the ground somewhere nearby no matter where you live. Ecological landscape designer Kim Eierman puts it plainly: “You may have hundreds or even thousands of individual bees using your landscape. The good news is that you don’t have to do much to give them a place to live.” Most of what they need is already there, and the beauty of this solution is that all you have to do is less. What to do with the fallen leaves Move them rather than bag them. Bumble bee queens hibernate by digging a few inches underground or into leaf mulch, so piling leaves onto flower beds or into a back corner of the yard makes them a winter home. Leaf piles also give fireflies and other small garden creatures a place to wait out the cold. Shepherd’s guidance: remove leaves from anywhere they’re a slip hazard or blocking a drain, but keep them on flower borders, along the base of a hedge, or tucked into a back corner. A rake or broom does the job without the disturbance a leaf blower causes. Think twice before cutting everything back Pruning everything to the ground in fall can cost wild bees their winter home. “Avoiding the typical fall cleanup on plants and keeping stems of perennials and annuals creates nesting opportunities for tunnel-nesting bees such as small carpenter bees and leafcutters,” Shepherd says. The birds appreciate it too; they’ll forage on the seedheads through winter. If a tidy front yard matters to you, Droege has a workable compromise: cut back to about a foot tall instead of to the ground. “A plant needs to be damaged or dead for bees to be able to use it,” he says, so a shorter cut still creates usable nesting structure without looking neglected. If you’re already mid-cleanup, don’t compost what you’ve cut. “If any bees are already nesting in the stems, composting them will cause the end of that cycle,” Droege says. A loose pile left on the ground or behind the shed keeps the cycle going. Eierman adds that pithy stems from elderberry, raspberry, hydrangea, and Joe Pye weed are especially useful to cavity-nesting bees and can be bundled and left in place through winter. Leave brush piles, snags, and cane fruit stems Pruned branches can go into a brush pile rather than the compost. Loose piles don’t do much; Eierman notes they need to be “fairly tight and dense, providing cavities that shelter bees from rain.” Dead or dying trees are candidates for keeping if they’re well away from the house. These are called snags. They develop hollow passages over time as beetles tunnel through the dead wood, and cavity-nesting bees use those passages the following season. A snag that’s too tall to feel comfortable about can be cut back to a manageable height without losing what makes it useful. For cane fruits like raspberries, blackberries, and boysenberries, Droege says the same logic applies. “Cane fruits only fruit in year two,” he says. “Instead of cutting them to the ground, trimming them to a foot tall provides the best nesting material for a whole series of native wild bees.” Leave bare patches of soil undisturbed Most native bees nest in the ground and need bare, uncompacted soil to excavate their nests. “Don’t try to repair all the bare ground — leave the open areas, as bees like to nest there,” says Droege. Sandy or loamy soil in a sunny spot is ideal, but even a few square feet counts. If a bare patch feels too sparse, Eierman says planting very sparsely may still leave enough exposed soil between plants; just skip the mulch or landscape fabric, as both block bees from getting in. Treat it as wild habitat rather than an incomplete garden bed: no tilling, no cleaning up, not even in spring. Keep some flowers going through fall Most bees have wrapped up their nesting cycle by the time temperatures drop, but sweat bees and mining bees are still out foraging late in the season. Goldenrod and asters are the flowers they’re looking for. Having something in bloom through fall, and building toward a range of bloom times from spring through the end of the season, gives different species something to work with at different points in the year. “Expanding your garden for next spring and reducing your lawn is the biggest thing you can do for wild bees ,” Droege says. Eierman says it best: “You may have hundreds or even thousands of individual bees using your landscape. The good news is that you don’t have to do much to give them a place to live.” Leave the leaves. Don’t compost the stems. Keep a corner wild. That’s most of it. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post What to leave alone in your garden this October to help overwintering bees first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .
